1. Lexical + dense hybrid retrieval

1.1 Problem

Dense bi-encoders capture paraphrase and topical similarity but are weak at exact identifiers: product codes, error strings, rare proper nouns, and terms that never appeared in the embedding model's training data. BM25 has the opposite profile. Anthropic's study states plainly that "Embeddings+BM25 is better than embeddings on their own" [12]. Qdrant's survey of sparse retrieval names the domains where lexical matching matters most: medicine, law, and e-commerce with brand names and serial numbers [16]. The same survey notes that "dense retrievers tend to return many false positives" [16]. The engineering problem is how to combine two ranked lists whose scores live on incompatible scales. BM25 scores are unbounded. Cosine similarity in Azure AI Search's HNSW implementation falls in 0.333-1.00 [2].

1.2 Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)

RRF was introduced by Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher at SIGIR 2009 in a paper titled "Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual Rank Learning Methods" [1]. It ignores raw scores entirely. Each document receives

RRF(d) = sum over lists L containing d of  1 / (k + rank_L(d))

with rank starting at 1. The constant k damps the influence of top positions so that a document ranked highly by several retrievers beats one ranked first by only one retriever. The value k = 60 from the original paper has become an industry default:

  • Azure AI Search uses RRF for all hybrid and multi-vector queries. Its documentation states that "the algorithm performs best when you set k to a small value, such as 60" [2]. A document ranked first in two lists scores about 2/61, roughly 0.033.
  • Elasticsearch exposes an rrf retriever with rank_constant defaulting to 60 (minimum 1) and rank_window_size defaulting to the request size. Each child retriever "carries an equal weight" in the base formula, at least two children are required, and scroll, sort and rescore are unsupported. Pagination is stable only while rank_window_size is held fixed [4].
  • Vespa provides reciprocal_rank(x, k) with k defaulting to 60.0 and reciprocal_rank_fusion(a, b, ...) as global-phase normalisers [7].
  • Weaviate's original rankedFusion used 1/(rank + 60) [8].

RRF's strengths are that it needs no training data, is robust to score-scale differences, and is trivially parallel. Its weaknesses follow from discarding score magnitude. A document that one retriever considers an overwhelming match gets no more credit than a marginal one at the same rank. The fused score is also not a relevance probability. In Azure it is bounded by the number of fused queries, with each list contributing at most about 1/k [2]. That makes it useless for absolute thresholds (see Section 6).

Weighted RRF partly addresses the first problem. Azure lets each vector query carry a weight multiplier (default 1.0). Its documentation shows a vector query with weight 0.5 and another with weight 2.0 contributing to the fused ranking alongside an unweighted BM25 list [2].

1.3 Score-normalised linear fusion

The alternative is to normalise each list's scores and take a weighted sum.

  • Weaviate relativeScoreFusion (added in v1.20, default since v1.24) min-max normalises each result set, so the top hit scores 1 and the bottom scores 0. It then combines the two sets with the alpha weight. alpha = 0.5 gives equal weight to vector and keyword search. In Weaviate's internal tests on FiQA, relative score fusion improved recall by about 6% over rank fusion [8].
  • OpenSearch's normalization processor offers min_max (default), l2 and z_score normalisation, with arithmetic_mean (default), geometric_mean or harmonic_mean combination. Weights must lie in [0, 1] and sum to 1.0 (the documentation's example uses [0.3, 0.7]). z_score only works with the arithmetic mean. Min-max can be anchored with explicit lower and upper bounds, so that a list whose best score is still poor is not inflated to 1.0 [11].
  • Elasticsearch's linear retriever supports minmax and l2_norm normalisers, plus none, which the documentation warns leaves scores unnormalised across field groups. In its multi-field mode, lexical and semantic field groups are each normalised to contribute 50% of the final score [5].

The failure mode that bounds options address deserves emphasis. Per-query min-max normalisation always maps the best candidate in each list to 1.0, even when no candidate is relevant. When one retriever returns nothing useful, the normalised scores amplify its noise. Rank-based fusion has the same blind spot, but it does not pretend to carry magnitude.

1.4 Where fusion runs

   Azure AI Search                         Elasticsearch / OpenSearch
   ---------------                         --------------------------
   text query --> BM25 (maxTextRecallSize   retriever tree:
                   default 1000)              rrf | linear
   vector q(s) -> HNSW (k each)                 |-- standard (BM25)
          \          /                           |-- knn (dense)
           RRF (k=60, per-query weights)         |-- sparse (ELSER/SPLADE-like)
             |  top 50 by default              text_similarity_reranker
           semantic ranker (top 50 only)          wraps any retriever,
             |  @search.rerankerScore 0..4        rank_window_size default 10
           response

   Vespa                                   Weaviate
   -----                                   --------
   content nodes: first-phase (all hits)   hybrid(query, alpha)
                  second-phase (100/node)    -> BM25F + vector in parallel
   container:     global-phase (100 total)   -> relativeScoreFusion (default)
                  RRF / normalize_linear        or rankedFusion
                  ONNX cross-encoder         -> optional reranker module

Azure's pipeline illustrates how product limits shape the cascade. A hybrid query returns the top 50 fused results by default. The text side recalls up to 1,000 matches (maxTextRecallSize). Only the top 50 results move on to the semantic ranker, "even if results include more than 50 results" [2][3]. A relevant document at fused rank 51 can therefore never be promoted. Recall at the fusion stage sets the ceiling for everything downstream.

1.5 Lessons

  • Hybrid is the default. Anthropic, Azure, Elastic, Weaviate, Vespa and Qdrant all ship it as a first-class query type [2][4][7][8][12][17].
  • RRF with k = 60 is the zero-configuration baseline. Move to weighted or normalised fusion only with labelled queries to tune against. Weaviate's roughly 6% FiQA recall gain from normalised fusion is an internal benchmark, not a universal law [8].
  • Size each child list deliberately. RRF can only reorder what the children return, and Elastic's pagination stability depends on a fixed window [4].
  • Contextualise chunks before indexing them for BM25. Anthropic prepends 50-100 tokens of LLM-generated context to each chunk before both embedding and BM25 indexing. That costs about $1.02 per million document tokens one time, with prompt caching [12].

2. Learned sparse retrieval (SPLADE and relatives)

2.1 Problem

BM25 suffers from vocabulary mismatch. A query for "pizza" will not match a document that only says "Margherita" [16]. Dense retrieval fixes that but gives up the inverted index, exact-match guarantees and explainability. Learned sparse retrieval trains a transformer to output term weights over a vocabulary. The output is stored in an ordinary inverted index, so it keeps BM25-style serving while learning both term importance and expansion terms.

2.2 Lineage

Qdrant's 2024 survey traces the evolution [16]:

Model Idea Limitation noted
DeepCT Regress an importance weight per word Ground-truth "importance" is ill-defined
DeepImpact Learn per-word impact from relevance labels Uses only the first subword piece
TILDEv2 Token-level impacts One scalar per token cannot separate homonyms
COIL 32-dim vector per term (projected from 768) Costly storage, not a plain inverted index
uniCOIL Back to scalar impacts Loses much of COIL's semantics
SPARTA Expansion over BERT's roughly 30k vocabulary May generalise worse than BM25 off MS MARCO
SPLADE / SPLADE++ MLM-head expansion + sparsity regularisation + distillation See below

External document expansion with docT5query generates queries of about 50-60 words per document. It is slow because it decodes token by token. TILDE cuts expansion time by about 98% relative to docT5query. Qdrant suggests external expansion may be infeasible at production scale, which pushes designs toward internal expansion [16].

2.3 SPLADE architecture

SPLADE (Formal, Piwowarski and Clinchant, SIGIR 2021) "learns query/document sparse expansion via the BERT MLM head and sparse regularization" [14]. Each input token's MLM logits produce a weight for every vocabulary term, and these are pooled into one vocabulary-sized sparse vector. A FLOPS-style regulariser, with separate strengths lambda_q and lambda_d for queries and documents, pushes most weights to zero, which keeps posting lists short [14]. The regularisation strength is the dial between effectiveness and sparsity.

  text --> BERT encoder --> MLM head: logits over |V| ~ 30k terms per token
                                  |
                          pool over tokens + saturate
                                  |
                       sparse vector {term: weight}   (most weights = 0, by FLOPS reg.)
                                  |
            +---------------------+----------------------+
            | documents: indexed offline in an           |
            |   inverted index (Anserini/PISA/Lucene/    |
            |   Qdrant sparse/Elastic, etc.)             |
            | queries: encoded online (or use a          |
            |   lighter/separate query encoder)          |
            +--------------------------------------------+

Published MS MARCO dev MRR@10 for the NAVER checkpoints [14]:

Checkpoint Generation MRR@10
splade_v2_max v2 34.0
splade_v2_distil v2 (distillation) 36.8
splade-cocondenser-selfdistil SPLADE++ 37.6
splade-cocondenser-ensembledistil SPLADE++ 38.3
efficient-splade-V-large (doc + query) Efficient SPLADE 38.8

For comparison, tuned BM25 (k1 = 0.82, b = 0.68) scores 18.7 on the same split [13]. SPLADE v2 [15] added hard-negative mining, cross-encoder distillation and better pre-trained initialisation. SPLADE++ extended the study of those three ingredients [14]. The Efficient SPLADE line (Lassance and Clinchant, SIGIR 2022) targets latency. It uses L1 regularisation on queries, separate query and document encoders, and FLOPS-regularised middle training. Its abstract claims latency within 4 ms of BM25 under the same compute, with less than a 10% MRR@10 drop from state-of-the-art single-stage neural rankers in-domain [14].

2.4 Failure modes and operational notes

  • Licence. The NAVER code and checkpoints are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (non-commercial) [14]. This matters for commercial deployments and is one reason vendors train their own learned-sparse models.
  • Generalisation. Models trained on MS MARCO can generalise worse than BM25 on other domains [16]. BEIR (Thakur et al., NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks) was built to measure exactly this zero-shot gap across lexical, sparse, dense and reranking architectures [43].
  • Query-time cost. Unlike BM25, every query needs a transformer forward pass, and expanded queries produce longer posting-list traversals. Hence the separate lightweight query encoders in Efficient SPLADE [14].

2.5 Cautionary tale: BM42

In July 2024 Qdrant introduced BM42 [17]. It replaced BM25's term frequency with the attention weights of the [CLS] token in a small transformer (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 by default), kept IDF (computed inside the engine so it stays current under updates), and produced very compact vectors: about 5.6 non-zero elements per document, roughly a 13 MB index for about 530k documents in uint8 [17]. The post was later corrected. An evaluation script error had inflated the results, and the corrected note states that BM42 does not outperform other vendors' BM25 implementations. The author now calls it experimental and notes BM25 may remain better for large, unchunked documents [17]. The lesson for readers of retrieval announcements: check vendor-reported sparse-retrieval gains against independent BEIR-style runs before you rebuild an index around them.

3. Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and successors

3.1 Problem

Single-vector bi-encoders compress a passage into one point. Cross-encoders model token-to-token interactions but must run once per query-document pair. Late interaction sits between them. Documents are encoded offline into one vector per token. At query time, each query token is matched to its most similar document token (MaxSim), and the maxima are summed.

score(q, d) = sum over query tokens i of  max over doc tokens j of  (q_i . d_j)

Interactions stay token-level, but document encoding is precomputed, so the method can work as a retriever or as a cheap reranker.

3.2 ColBERT and ColBERTv2

ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, SIGIR 2020) introduced the design [18]. Its abstract reports that it is over two orders of magnitude faster and needs about four orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs per query than BERT-based cross-encoder rerankers (approximate figures from the paper's abstract). ColBERTv2 (NAACL 2022) added residual compression and denoised supervision distilled from a cross-encoder [19]. Each token vector is stored as a centroid ID plus a quantised residual; the repository's examples use nbits=2. The authors found this more robust than their earlier binarisation scheme [21]. The paper reports roughly a 6-10x reduction in index footprint compared with uncompressed ColBERT (approximate, from the abstract) [19]. The project README describes search over large collections in "tens of milliseconds", and a Colab notebook indexes 10,000 passages on a free T4 GPU in about six minutes [21].

3.3 PLAID

PLAID (CIKM 2022) is the retrieval engine for ColBERTv2 [20]. It treats the centroids themselves as a cheap first approximation of each document:

 query tokens (32 x 128-d)
        |
        v
 [1] centroid interaction: score query tokens vs all centroids (K-means codebook)
        |   select candidate passages whose token-centroids score high (IVF probe)
        v
 [2] centroid pruning: drop low-scoring centroids; approximate MaxSim using
        |   centroid scores only (no residual decompression)
        v
 [3] keep top candidates (FastPlaid default n_full_scores = 4096)
        |
        v
 [4] decompress residuals for survivors -> exact MaxSim -> final top-k

The paper reports latency reductions of up to about 7x on GPU and 45x on CPU over vanilla ColBERTv2, with search at the scale of about 140M passages (approximate, from the abstract) [20]. The open-source descendants publish concrete parameters. LightOn's FastPlaid, a Rust reimplementation with PyO3 and tch-rs bindings, defaults to n_ivf_probe = 8 and n_full_scores = 4096. On an H100 it reports 69% to 554% higher QPS than the original PLAID across eight BEIR datasets, with nearly identical NDCG@10 (for example Quora 43 -> 282 QPS at 0.88 vs 0.87 NDCG@10) [22]. PyLate (LightOn, CIKM 2025) is a Sentence Transformers-based training and inference library for ColBERT-style models. It uses FastPlaid as its default index and states about 10x storage reduction via product quantisation with sub-200 ms latency [23].

3.4 XTR, WARP and the CPU path

Google DeepMind's XTR ("Rethinking the Role of Token Retrieval in Multi-Vector Retrieval", NeurIPS 2023) changes training so that the token-retrieval stage itself is more informative. This reduces the need for the expensive gather-and-rescore step [24]. WARP (SIGIR 2025) is a CPU-optimised engine that combines ideas from ColBERTv2/PLAID and XTR [25]. PyLate's documentation warns that WARP's approximations assume XTR-trained models and can degrade results for models not trained that way. It also lists a CPU index, TACHIOM, which it reports beats WARP on ColBERTv2 across build time, quality, latency and index size [23].

3.5 Late interaction as a reranker, and MUVERA

Many production designs avoid a full PLAID index. They store multi-vectors only as a rerank payload behind a single-vector or sparse first stage. Qdrant 1.10 added multi-vector fields with a MAX_SIM comparator and a prefetch query API for exactly this pattern [26]. Their experiments reused an ordinary dense model's output token embeddings as multi-vectors: retrieve the top 50 with the pooled vector, then MaxSim-rerank to the top 10. Results:

  • SciFact NDCG@10: 0.645 -> 0.703 (MiniLM) and 0.682 -> 0.731 (bge-small).
  • TREC-COVID: 0.472 -> 0.638 (MiniLM).
  • ArguAna: reranking hurt, 0.502 -> 0.454 (MiniLM).

The ArguAna drop shows that late-interaction reranking is not monotonically beneficial [26]. Storage is the real cost. MiniLM token vectors are 384-dimensional versus 128 for ColBERT. uint8 scalar quantisation cut memory about 4x with negligible quality loss (SciFact 0.707 -> 0.703) [26].

MUVERA (from Google Research) goes further. It compresses a multi-vector set into one fixed-dimensional encoding (FDE) so that a standard ANN index can serve the first stage, with exact MaxSim as a rerank. On NFCorpus with ColBERTv2, Qdrant measured NDCG@10 of 0.347 for full multi-vector search (1.27 s average), 0.242 for MUVERA alone (0.15 s), and 0.343 for MUVERA plus multi-vector rerank (0.18 s). That is about 7x faster at nearly identical quality. FDEs can be very large, for example 40,960 dimensions in one configuration [27].

3.6 Lessons

  • Late interaction is a storage problem first. Residual compression, product quantisation and scalar quantisation are mandatory, not optional [19][22][26].
  • The centroid trick generalises. Approximate cheaply, prune aggressively, and decompress only survivors. PLAID's structure is itself a miniature cascade.
  • Use multi-vectors as a reranking payload when a full PLAID index is too heavy (Qdrant prefetch, MUVERA plus rerank) [26][27].

4. Cross-encoder rerankers

4.1 Architecture

A cross-encoder concatenates [CLS] query [SEP] passage [SEP], runs full self-attention across both, and maps the output to a relevance score. Because the query is needed at encoding time, nothing can be precomputed. Cost is one forward pass per candidate, linear in the candidate count and quadratic in the joint sequence length. The Sentence Transformers documentation codifies the standard pattern: a bi-encoder or lexical retriever fetches about 100 candidates, and a cross-encoder reranks them [29]. Weaviate's 2022 description is the same two-stage design. It notes that pretrained MS MARCO cross-encoders work out of the box and recommends fine-tuning for out-of-domain data [9].

4.2 The open small-model baseline: MS MARCO MiniLM cross-encoders

The Sentence Transformers model card table is the most-cited speed/quality frontier for compact rerankers [28]:

Model NDCG@10 TREC DL19 MRR@10 MS MARCO dev Docs/sec
ms-marco-TinyBERT-L2-v2 69.84 32.56 9,000
ms-marco-MiniLM-L2-v2 71.01 34.85 4,100
ms-marco-MiniLM-L4-v2 73.04 37.70 2,500
ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 74.30 39.01 1,800
ms-marco-MiniLM-L12-v2 74.31 39.02 960
ms-marco-electra-base 71.99 36.41 340

Two observations follow. First, quality saturates at six layers: L12 is half the speed of L6 for 0.01 points. Second, throughput (hardware unspecified in the source) translates directly into a latency budget. Reranking 100 candidates at 1,800 docs/s is roughly 55 ms of model time. Elastic ships cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 as its documented example of a self-hosted text_similarity model [6].

4.3 Open multilingual and LLM-backbone rerankers

BGE rerankers (BAAI). The FlagEmbedding family spans several tiers [30]: bge-reranker-base and -large (XLM-RoBERTa, Chinese and English); bge-reranker-v2-m3 (built on BGE-M3, multilingual, recommended for efficiency); bge-reranker-v2-gemma (Gemma-2B); and bge-reranker-v2-minicpm-layerwise (MiniCPM-2B). The layerwise model lets callers pick an output layer between 8 and 40 to trade quality for speed, which amounts to an early-exit cascade inside one model. Scores are raw logits. normalize=True applies a sigmoid, so a raw -5.65 becomes about 0.0035 [30].

Qwen3-Reranker (Alibaba, June 2025). Sizes are 0.6B, 4B and 8B, with a 32K context [31]. The model runs as a causal LM given an instruction, a query and a document. The score is the softmax probability of "yes" over {"yes", "no"} at the final position. That makes it instruction-aware: one model can be steered toward, for example, code search or legal relevance. On reranking the top 100 from Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, the 4B model scored 69.76 MTEB-R and 81.20 MTEB-Code, versus 57.03 and 41.38 for bge-reranker-v2-m3 and 58.22 and 58.98 for jina-multilingual-reranker-v2-base [31]. On FollowIR (instruction following) the 4B model scored 14.84, while the 8B scored only 8.05. Bigger was not uniformly better [31].

mxbai-rerank v2 (Mixedbread). Sizes are 0.5B and 1.5B, trained with a three-step recipe that includes reinforcement learning (GRPO), contrastive learning and preference learning. The models support 100+ languages and an 8K default context, extendable to 32K. BEIR average is 57.49 for large-v2 and 55.57 for base-v2, versus 49.32 for the v1 large model. Latency on an A100 is 0.89 s and 0.67 s respectively, under a benchmark setting the README does not fully specify [32].

4.4 Managed rerankers

Cohere Rerank. Cohere's documentation now lists Rerank 4.0 (rerank-v4.0-pro, rerank-v4.0-fast), Rerank 3.5 (rerank-v3.5) and the older split English/multilingual 3.0 models [33]. Rerank 3.5 and 4.0 are single multilingual models trained for 100+ languages [33]. Operational parameters [34]:

  • Context: 4,096 tokens for v3.5 and v3.0 (query capped at 2,048). 32,768 tokens for v4.0 (query capped at 16,384).
  • Long documents: split into chunks that fit the window, each chunk scored, and the maximum taken. A 10,000-token document under v3.5 becomes 3 chunks. A 100,000-token document under v4.0 becomes 4.
  • Limits: up to 10,000 documents per request, and documents x max_chunks_per_doc must not exceed 10,000.
  • Semi-structured input: JSON documents with rank_fields, where field order matters.

Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval pipeline used Cohere's reranker to cut 150 hybrid candidates to 20. It was the step that took the failure-rate reduction from 49% to 67% [12]. Weaviate showed Cohere's reranker can be fine-tuned with as few as 256 unique queries (plus a validation set of at least 64). On a synthetic DSPy-generated dataset of Weaviate blog content, this gave about +8% Accuracy@1, +5% MRR@10 and +4% NDCG@10 over the base model. Training took about 2 hours and the demo cost $0.03 [10].

Azure AI Search semantic ranker. This is a Bing-derived multilingual model applied only to the top 50 fused results [3]. It produces @search.rerankerScore on a 0-4 scale, where 4 means the document fully answers the query. Inputs are summarised per document to about 2,048 tokens (raised from 256 in November 2024), with title and keywords fields capped at 128 tokens each [3]. Field order in the semantic configuration matters because longer text is trimmed [3].

Elastic Rerank. The text_similarity_reranker retriever wraps any retriever. It defaults to the .rerank-v1-elasticsearch endpoint and a rank_window_size of 10, and it can also call Cohere, Google Vertex AI or self-hosted Hugging Face models [6]. Its chunk_rescorer (GA in 9.4) scores the best chunks of long documents instead of truncating them. The documentation warns that oversize chunks can "significantly degrade relevance" [6].

Voyage and Jina. Both sell API rerankers. Anthropic notes Voyage offers one but did not test it [12], and the rerankers library wraps Cohere, Jina, Voyage, MixedBread, Pinecone and others behind one interface [42]. The vendors' own announcement pages could not be retrieved for this chapter, so their claims are not reproduced here. The independent comparison point available is Qwen's table, where jina-multilingual-reranker-v2-base (0.3B) scores 58.22 MTEB-R [31].

4.5 Failure modes

  • Truncation. A 512-token cross-encoder silently drops the end of long chunks. Cohere and Elastic handle this with max-over-chunks scoring [6][34]. For open models, chunk before reranking.
  • Domain shift. MS MARCO-trained rerankers inherit web-search notions of relevance. Weaviate's fine-tuning results and Qwen's instruction prompts are two remedies [10][31].
  • Window ceilings. The reranker can only reorder what reaches it. Azure fixes the semantic-ranker window at 50 [3], and Elastic's default window is 10 [6]. A default window of 10 means the reranker cannot rescue anything ranked 11th or lower. Raise it deliberately.
  • Negative transfer. Qdrant's ArguAna experiment shows that reranking can lower NDCG@10 [26]. ArguAna's counter-argument retrieval task is not what most rerankers were trained for. Always A/B a reranker against the fused first stage.

5. LLM rerankers

5.1 RankGPT: listwise permutation generation

Sun et al. ("Is ChatGPT Good at Search? Investigating Large Language Models as Re-Ranking Agent", EMNLP 2023, Outstanding Paper Award) showed that instruction-following LLMs can rerank directly [35]. The prompt lists numbered passages and asks the LLM to output a permutation such as [2] > [3] > [1]. This is listwise reranking: the model compares candidates against each other rather than scoring each in isolation. Because a context window cannot hold 100 passages, RankGPT uses a sliding window that runs from the back of the list to the front. In the TREC-DL19 setup, 100 BM25 candidates are reranked with window size 20 and step 10 [35]. Each pass bubbles strong passages forward, so the top of the list is resolved last, with the best context.

  BM25 top-100:  [ 1 ............................................ 100 ]
  pass 1:                                              [81 ...... 100]  rerank 20
  pass 2:                                       [71 ...... 90]          step 10
  ...                                     (strong docs bubble forward)
  pass 9:        [ 1 ...... 20]  -> final order of the top 20
  => ~9 LLM calls per query, each with 20 passages in context

RankGPT also introduced permutation distillation. A DeBERTa-v3-base cross-encoder was trained with RankNet loss on ChatGPT-generated permutations for 10K and 100K MS MARCO queries, and the data and a deberta-10k-rank_net checkpoint were released [35]. This pattern, using an expensive LLM as a teacher for a cheap student reranker, recurs throughout the field.

5.2 Open listwise rerankers

The Waterloo rank_llm toolkit (SIGIR 2025 resource paper) packages the open successors and documents pointwise, pairwise and listwise families side by side [36]:

Family Example Reported context/config Notes
Pointwise monoT5, monoELECTRA [41] top 1,000, 512-token context Scores each pair independently
Pairwise duoT5 [41] top 50 O(n^2) comparisons, so only the head of the list
Listwise (open LLM) RankVicuna [37], RankZephyr [38] top 100, 4,096 context 7B open models distilled from GPT teachers
Listwise (seq2seq) LiT5 [39] window 20 for LiT5-Distill T5-based listwise, small context
Listwise (single-token) FIRST [40] 4,096 context Ranks from first-token logits, not full decoding
Listwise (proprietary) RankGPT, RankGemini API Teacher models

The mono-duo split from Pradeep, Nogueira and Lin [41] is itself a cascade. A pointwise model trims 1,000 candidates. A pairwise model, quadratic in cost, then reorders only the top 50. FIRST tackles the main cost of listwise LLM reranking, which is generating the permutation token by token. It reads the ranking from the logits of the first generated identifier, so one decoding step replaces many [36][40].

5.3 Pointwise LLM rerankers blur the line

Qwen3-Reranker's yes/no probability and BGE's Gemma and MiniCPM rerankers are LLM backbones used pointwise [30][31]. They keep the cross-encoder interface (one score per pair, trivially batched, compatible with thresholds) while inheriting LLM instruction following. In 2025-2026 this has become the dominant open design. Full listwise generation is increasingly reserved for offline teaching and for small, high-value candidate sets.

5.4 Failure modes and costs

  • Latency and cost. A 100-candidate sliding window with window 20 and step 10 costs about 9 sequential LLM calls per query (see the diagram). That fits research evaluation and high-value queries, not interactive search at volume.
  • Output brittleness. Generated permutations can omit or duplicate IDs, so parsers must repair them. The RankGPT repo's receive_permutation step exists for this [35].
  • Positional bias. The initial order affects results, which is why the back-to-front window starts from the first-stage ranking.
  • No scores. A permutation carries no calibrated relevance, so thresholding (Section 6) needs a separate signal.

6. Score calibration and thresholding

Every stage emits a number, and almost none of them are probabilities. Yet RAG systems routinely need absolute decisions. Should a chunk enter the prompt? Does the query fall outside the corpus ("I don't know")? Should a dense or sparse result be dropped before fusion? The public guidance:

Stage / product Score semantics Documented guidance
BM25 Unbounded, query-dependent Not comparable across queries; normalise or use ranks [2]
Azure vector (cosine) 0.333-1.00 Threshold property exists; avoid overly granular limits [2][3]
RRF (any engine) At most about n_lists/k Ranking only; never threshold [2]
Weaviate relativeScore Per-query min-max to [0,1] Top hit always 1.0, so do not threshold blindly [8]
OpenSearch min_max [0,1], optional fixed bounds Use lower_bounds/upper_bounds to anchor [11]
Cohere Rerank [0,1], query-dependent Calibrate the threshold on 30-50 queries with borderline docs [34]
Azure semantic ranker 0-4 (4 = fully answers) Distribution drifts with infra and model updates [3]
BGE reranker Logit; sigmoid via normalize=True Sigmoid is monotone, not calibrated [30]
Qwen3-Reranker P(yes) over {yes, no} Probability-shaped, instruction-dependent [31]
Elastic text_similarity Transformed to non-negative Negative maps to (0,1), positive to [1, inf) [6]
LLM listwise Permutation only Needs a separate scorer for cut-offs [35]

Cohere's documentation is the most explicit vendor statement on calibration [34]. The primary output is the rank. Scores are query-dependent, and ratios between scores are "not meaningful". To set a cut-off, pick 30-50 representative queries, pair each with a borderline-relevant document, score them, and use the mean as the reference threshold. Microsoft adds a second caution. Semantic ranker scores can shift slightly for the same query because of infrastructure conditions and model updates, so thresholds should not be "too granular" [3].

Practical patterns that follow:

  1. Calibrate only at the last scored stage. Fused RRF scores and min-max-normalised scores carry no cross-query meaning.
  2. Learn a per-model mapping on in-domain labels: Cohere's borderline-mean recipe, or Platt/isotonic regression on the raw logits. Re-fit it whenever the reranker version changes, given Azure's drift warning [3].
  3. Combine an absolute floor with relative rules: keep at most k chunks, keep only those above the floor, and always keep at least one if the floor is used for answer gating rather than filtering.
  4. Anchor normalisation. OpenSearch-style fixed min/max bounds stop a junk list from being stretched to [0, 1] [11].

7. Multi-stage retrieval cascades

7.1 The pattern

A cascade spends compute where it changes the outcome. Each stage has a recall job (do not lose the relevant item) and a precision job (push it up). Cheap stages see many documents; expensive stages see few. The public systems share a consistent shape:

System Stage 1 Fusion Stage 2 Final to LLM / user
Anthropic Contextual Retrieval [12] Contextual embeddings + contextual BM25 Rank fusion + dedupe Cohere rerank of top 150 Top 20
Azure AI Search [2][3] BM25 (up to 1,000) + HNSW RRF k=60, weighted Semantic ranker, top 50 only top (default 50)
Elasticsearch [4][5][6] standard + knn (+ sparse) rrf or linear text_similarity_reranker (window 10 by default) size
Vespa [7] first-phase on every content node (WAND) global-phase RRF / normalize_linear second-phase (100/node), global-phase ONNX (100) Hits
Qdrant [26][27] Prefetch dense / sparse / MUVERA RRF in Query API MaxSim multi-vector rerank Top 10
Sentence Transformers recipe [29] Bi-encoder or BM25, ~100 n/a MiniLM cross-encoder Top 5
RankLLM / mono-duo [36][41] BM25 top 1,000 n/a monoT5 on 1,000, then duoT5 on 50 or listwise LLM on 100 Top 10-20
PLAID internal [20][22] Centroid IVF probe n/a Centroid-only approx MaxSim, then exact MaxSim on 4,096 Top k

7.2 Vespa's phased ranking as a reference design

Vespa makes the cost model explicit [7]:

      +--------------------------- content node (x N) ---------------------------+
      | matching: WAND / weakAnd limits candidates to top-K per node             |
      |    |                                                                     |
      |    v                                                                     |
      | first-phase: cheap expression on EVERY matched hit (bm25 + closeness)    |
      |    |  rank-score-drop-limit can discard hits                             |
      |    v                                                                     |
      | second-phase: heavier expression (e.g., GBDT, MaxSim) on best 100/node   |
      |    |  total-rerank-count caps the sum across nodes                       |
      +----+---------------------------------------------------------------------+
           v merged
      +--------------------------- stateless container --------------------------+
      | global-phase: best 100 globally (rerank-count / ranking.globalPhase...)  |
      |   - cross-hit normalisers: normalize_linear, reciprocal_rank(k=60), RRF  |
      |   - ONNX cross-encoder inference, optional GPU (gpu-device)              |
      +--------------------------------------------------------------------------+

The placement rules are instructive. First-phase cost scales with hits times expression cost, so it must stay cheap. Large GBDT models are more efficient in second-phase on the content nodes, next to the data. Cross-encoders belong in the global phase on stateless containers, which can use GPUs and see the globally merged list. Normalisers such as RRF only make sense in the global phase, because they need the whole candidate set [7].

7.3 Sizing the stages

The public numbers suggest working defaults:

  • First-stage depth per retriever: 100-1,000. Azure's text recall defaults to 1,000 [2]. RankLLM's pointwise examples use 1,000, and its listwise examples use 100 [36].
  • Rerank window: 50-150. Anthropic retrieved 150 for reranking [12], Azure reranks 50 [3], and Qdrant and Sentence Transformers use about 50-100 [26][29]. Elastic's default of 10 is too small for most RAG workloads [6].
  • Chunks passed to the generator: Anthropic tested 5, 10 and 20 and found 20 best [12].
  • LLM listwise stage: top 20-100, only when latency and cost allow [35][36].

The latency budget composes additively. At about 1,800 docs/s for MiniLM-L6 [28], a 100-candidate rerank costs tens of milliseconds. A 1.5B mxbai model costs on the order of a second per batch on an A100 in Mixedbread's benchmark [32]. A sliding-window GPT-class reranker costs several sequential LLM calls. Each step up must buy measurable quality on your evaluation set.

7.4 Tooling for swapping stages

Because the best reranker is workload-specific, an abstraction layer helps. AnswerDotAI's rerankers library (Clavié, 2024) exposes cross-encoders, ColBERT, T5, LLM pointwise and listwise rankers (RankGPT and RankLLM), FlashRank ONNX models for CPU, and API rerankers (Cohere, Jina, Voyage, MixedBread, Pinecone) behind a single Reranker(...).rank() call [42]. Elastic's retriever trees [5], Qdrant's prefetch [26] and Vespa's rank profiles [7] offer the same flexibility inside the engine, so cascades can be changed per query without redeploying application code.

7.5 Failure modes of cascades

  • Recall leakage. The final ranking cannot exceed first-stage recall. Measure recall@window at each stage boundary, not only NDCG@10 at the end.
  • Window truncation by default settings, such as Azure's 50 and Elastic's 10 [3][6].
  • Mismatched granularity. Chunks larger than the reranker's window are truncated, while chunks too small lose context. Anthropic's contextualisation and Cohere and Elastic's chunk-and-max approach are mitigations [6][12][34].
  • Stage disagreement. A reranker trained on a different notion of relevance (ArguAna counter-arguments, instruction-specific tasks) can undo good first-stage rankings [26][31].
  • Cost creep. Every stage adds latency, and reranking is "resource-intensive" even in managed services [3]. Anthropic explicitly frames reranking as accepting added latency and cost for accuracy [12].

8. Comparison of techniques

Technique Representative Index / state Query-time cost Quality signal (public) Best role
BM25 Lucene, Pyserini Inverted index Very low MS MARCO MRR@10 0.187 [13] Stage-1 recall, identifiers
Dense bi-encoder Any embedding model ANN (HNSW/IVF) Low (1 encode + ANN) Varies by model (Ch. 03) Stage-1 semantic recall
RRF fusion Azure, Elastic, Vespa None Negligible Strong zero-shot default [1] Merge heterogeneous lists
Normalised linear fusion Weaviate, OpenSearch None Negligible ~6% recall over RRF on FiQA (internal) [8] Tuned merge with labels
Learned sparse SPLADE++ Inverted index Low-moderate (query encode) MRR@10 0.383 [14] Stage-1, replaces or joins BM25
Late interaction (full) ColBERTv2 + PLAID Centroids + residuals Moderate NDCG@10 parity PLAID vs FastPlaid [22] High-quality stage 1
Late interaction (rerank) Qdrant MaxSim, MUVERA Multi-vector payload Moderate ~7x faster than full MV, near parity [27] Stage 2 over ANN candidates
Small cross-encoder MiniLM-L6 None ~1,800 docs/s [28] MRR@10 0.390 [28] Stage 2 default
LLM-backbone pointwise Qwen3-Reranker-4B, bge-v2-gemma None High MTEB-R 69.76 [31] Stage 2, instruction-aware
Managed reranker Cohere 3.5/4.0, Azure semantic None (API) API latency Failure rate 2.9% -> 1.9% [12] Stage 2 without MLOps
LLM listwise RankGPT, RankZephyr, FIRST None Very high (multi-call) Teacher-quality rankings [35][36] Stage 3, distillation teacher

Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Ship hybrid by default. BM25 plus dense retrieval, fused with RRF at k = 60, is the most widely shipped zero-configuration baseline (Azure, Elastic, Vespa, Weaviate) and measurably beats dense-only retrieval in Anthropic's study [2][4][7][8][12].
  2. Add a reranker before you change anything else. In Anthropic's study the reranker delivered the largest single step, from 2.9% to 1.9% failure. A six-layer MiniLM cross-encoder already more than doubles BM25's MRR@10 on MS MARCO [12][13][28].
  3. Size windows explicitly. Retrieve 100-1,000 per retriever, rerank 50-150, and send 5-20 chunks to the generator. Check product defaults: Azure's semantic window is 50, and Elastic's reranker window defaults to 10 [3][6][12].
  4. Treat fused scores as ranks, never probabilities. Calibrate thresholds only on the final reranker's scores, per model version, on 30-50 in-domain borderline examples [34]. Expect drift [3].
  5. Choose learned sparse or late interaction for specific reasons. Use SPLADE when you need inverted-index serving with expansion (and check the non-commercial licence of the NAVER checkpoints). Use late interaction when token-level matching matters, and budget for quantisation and centroid-pruned engines (PLAID, FastPlaid, WARP) or MUVERA-style approximation [14][22][25][27].
  6. Use LLMs as teachers more often than as online rerankers. Listwise LLM reranking costs several sequential calls per query. Distil it into cross-encoders (RankGPT -> DeBERTa, RankZephyr, FIRST), or use pointwise LLM-backbone rerankers that keep a batchable per-pair score [31][35][36][40].
  7. Expect rerankers to hurt on some tasks. Qdrant's ArguAna results and Qwen's non-monotone FollowIR scores both show that rerankers can regress on tasks unlike their training data. Gate each stage with an A/B on your own evaluation set [26][31].
  8. Fine-tune or instruct when the domain is unusual. A few hundred labelled queries fine-tuned Cohere's reranker for measurable gains [10]. Instruction-aware rerankers such as Qwen3 can be steered without training [31].
  9. Be sceptical of vendor sparse-retrieval claims. BM42's correction is a reminder to replicate on BEIR-style suites before re-indexing [17][43].
  10. Keep the cascade swappable. Retriever trees, prefetch pipelines, rank profiles and unified reranker APIs let you change stages as models improve each quarter [5][7][26][42].
