  43. N. Thakur, N. Reimers, A. Rücklé, A. Srivastava, I. Gurevych. "BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models." NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks, 2021. https://github.com/beir-cellar/beir (paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08663)

06. Query Understanding and Transformation: HyDE, Multi-Query, RAG-Fusion, Step-Back, Decomposition, Conversational Rewriting, Routing and Self-Query

Overview

Most of a RAG pipeline is designed around documents: how they are parsed, chunked, embedded and indexed (Chapters 02-04). The query gets far less design attention, even though it is the weakest input in the system. Users type short, ambiguous, misspelled or context-dependent text ("what about the second one?"). They mix several questions into one sentence. They state constraints ("from last year", "under three minutes") that belong in a filter rather than in an embedding. And they use vocabulary that differs from the vocabulary of the corpus. A single embedding of the raw string tends to blur all of this together. The AWS Bedrock team describes the effect as the embedding step that "may mask or dilute important components of the query" [27].

Query understanding and transformation is the stage between the user's raw input and the retrievers. Its job is to turn what the user typed into what the retrieval system can act on. This chapter covers the publicly documented designs for that stage:

  1. Generative expansion. HyDE writes a hypothetical answer document and searches with its embedding [1][2]. Query2doc appends a generated pseudo-document to a sparse query [3].
  2. Multi-query and RAG-Fusion. An LLM writes several paraphrases, each is retrieved separately, and the ranked lists are merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) [6][11][12]. This section includes the 2026 debate over whether fusion gains survive reranking [7][8][9].
  3. Abstraction. Step-back prompting asks a more general question first and retrieves for it alongside the original question [5][16].
  4. Decomposition. Least-to-most, Self-Ask, IRCoT, sub-question engines, and the managed query planners in Amazon Bedrock and Azure AI Search [19][25][27][34][35][36].
  5. Learned rewriters. Rewrite-Retrieve-Read, RQ-RAG, DeepRetrieval and Search-R1 train the query writer with retrieval or answer feedback instead of prompting it [4][37][41][42].
  6. Conversational rewriting. Condense-question and history-aware retrievers, and the conversational-search research line (LLM4CS, ConvGQR, CHIQ) [13][22][38][39][40].
  7. Routing. LLM classifiers, embedding-based semantic routers, complexity routers and effort routers [17][21][26][29][32][33].
  8. Structured query construction. Metadata filter extraction and "self-query", in which an LLM turns natural language into a search string plus a typed filter expression [14][15][23][28].

These techniques are composable. A production query layer often stacks several: condense the conversation, route, extract filters, then decompose or expand.

                         QUERY UNDERSTANDING LAYER
  user turn + chat history
          |
          v
  +-------------------+   standalone question   +----------------------------+
  | 1. Contextualize  |------------------------>| 2. Route                   |
  | (condense/rewrite)|                         | (index / tool / effort /   |
  +-------------------+                         |  no-retrieval / model)     |
                                                +-------------+--------------+
                                                              |
              +-----------------------------------------------+
              v
  +---------------------------+     +---------------------------------------+
  | 3. Structure              |     | 4. Expand / transform                 |
  | query text + filter       |---->| multi-query | HyDE | step-back |      |
  | (self-query, implicit     |     | decomposition into sub-questions      |
  |  filters, top_k)          |     +-------------------+-------------------+
  +---------------------------+                         |
                                                        v
                         N retrievals in parallel (dense / BM25 / hybrid, filtered)
                                                        |
                                                        v
                     fuse (RRF / union + dedupe) -> rerank -> truncate -> generator

A note on sources. This chapter relies mainly on primary artifacts: official code repositories for papers, framework source code, and vendor documentation sources. Where a number comes from a paper abstract that could not be re-fetched for this edition, it is marked as such.

1. Taxonomy: what is being transformed, and why

The query-side techniques fall into five families. They differ in what they assume is wrong with the raw query:

Family Diagnosis of the raw query Output Representative designs
Expansion by generation Query and documents look different in embedding space (short question vs long answer passage) A document-shaped string HyDE [1], Query2doc [3]
Paraphrase / multi-query One phrasing misses relevant documents because of vocabulary mismatch N alternative queries MultiQueryRetriever [12], RAG-Fusion [6], Azure query rewrite [24]
Abstraction The query is too specific to retrieve the principles or background it needs A higher-level question Step-back [5]
Decomposition The query contains several information needs, or needs multiple hops Sub-questions, possibly sequential Least-to-most [36], Self-Ask [34], IRCoT [35], sub-question engines [19], Bedrock/Azure planners [25][27]
Contextualization The query is not standalone because it depends on earlier turns A standalone question Condense-question [22], history-aware retriever [13], LLM4CS [38]
Routing The query should go somewhere specific (an index, a tool, a model, an effort level, or no retrieval at all) A decision label, optionally with parameters Semantic router [29], RouterQueryEngine [21], Adaptive-RAG [33], RouteLLM [32]
Structuring The query mixes semantic content with hard constraints Query text + typed filter + limit SelfQueryRetriever [15], auto-retriever [23], Bedrock implicit filters [28]

Each family costs something. All but the embedding-based router add at least one LLM call before retrieval can start, and that call is on the critical path. Measured data on this cost is collected in Section 3.4.

2. Generative expansion: HyDE and Query2doc

2.1 HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings)

Problem. Zero-shot dense retrieval with no relevance labels. Questions and answer passages differ in length, style and vocabulary. An unsupervised encoder such as Contriever therefore places a question far from the passages that answer it.

Architecture. HyDE was introduced by Gao, Ma, Lin and Callan (CMU / Waterloo) in December 2022 and published at ACL 2023 [1]. It splits retrieval into two steps. First, an instruction-following LLM (InstructGPT, text-davinci-003 in the released notebook) is prompted zero-shot to "write a passage to answer the question". Second, the generated passage, not the question, is encoded with the unsupervised retriever, and the nearest real documents are returned. The authors describe the encoder's dense bottleneck as a filter for the hallucinated details in the fake document. The fake passage only needs to sit in the right neighbourhood; its facts do not need to be correct [1][2].

  query q --> LLM ("write a passage that answers q") x N samples
                    |  d1 ... dN  (hypothetical, may contain false facts)
                    v
  encoder f:  v = mean( f(q), f(d1), ..., f(dN) )      # official repo averages q + docs
                    |
                    v
  ANN search over real corpus embeddings --> top-k real documents

Key techniques visible in the reference code [2]:

  • Task-specific prompt templates. The released promptor.py has one template per corpus: "write a scientific paper passage to support/refute the claim" (SciFact), "write a counter argument for the passage" (ArguAna), "write a financial article passage" (FiQA), "write a news passage about the topic" (TREC-News), and a multilingual "write a passage in {lang}" template (Mr.TyDi). The form of the hypothetical document is a design parameter: it should look like the documents in the target corpus.
  • Multiple samples, averaged. HyDE.encode embeds the original query and every generated document, then averages the vectors into a single search vector. The DL19 notebook generates 8 hypothetical documents per query (its output files are tagged 8rep).
  • Frameworks keep the query. LlamaIndex's HyDEQueryTransform defaults to include_original=True. It adds the hypothetical passage to the query's embedding strings and keeps the original string as well [18].

Numbers. The repository's TREC DL19 notebook, run with saved outputs, reports Contriever alone at nDCG@10 0.445, MAP 0.240 and Recall@1000 0.746. Contriever with HyDE (GPT-3, 8 samples) reaches nDCG@10 0.597, MAP 0.404 and Recall@1000 0.873 [2]. That is roughly +15 nDCG points with no training. The paper also claims gains across web search, QA and fact verification, and across languages (e.g. Swahili, Korean, Japanese), with performance "comparable to fine-tuned retrievers" [1].

Failure modes and lessons.

  • Knowledge-bound. HyDE helps only when the LLM knows roughly what an answer looks like. On private or very new corpora, the hypothetical passage can point at the wrong neighbourhood with full confidence.
  • Latency. A full generated passage (and in the reference setup, eight of them) must be written before retrieval starts. This is the most expensive step in the pipeline.
  • Strong-encoder regime. HyDE was designed for the label-free setting. Gains against modern supervised embedders are not established by the primary sources read here, so it should be validated per corpus rather than assumed.
  • Mitigation. Keep the original query in the embedding mix (the default in both the reference code and LlamaIndex) so that a bad hypothesis cannot fully take over the search [2][18].

2.2 Query2doc

Query2doc (Wang, Yang and Wei, Microsoft, EMNLP 2023) applies the same idea to sparse and dense retrieval. It few-shot prompts an LLM to write a pseudo-document, then concatenates it to the original query, repeating the query several times so that it is not outweighed by the longer pseudo-document in BM25. The abstract reports BM25 gains of 3% to 15% on MS MARCO and TREC DL without fine-tuning (figure from the paper abstract, not re-verified here) [3]. The lesson: generative expansion also works for keyword retrieval, and the original query must be explicitly re-weighted against the much longer generated text.

3. Multi-query retrieval and RAG-Fusion

3.1 The basic multi-query retriever

Problem. Distance-based similarity search is sensitive to wording. A relevant chunk phrased differently from the query can fall outside top-k.

Architecture. LangChain's MultiQueryRetriever is the canonical implementation. Its default prompt asks an LLM to "generate 3 different versions of the given user question to retrieve relevant documents from a vector database" so as "to help the user overcome some of the limitations of distance-based similarity search". A line parser splits the output, the retriever runs once per generated query, and the results are de-duplicated by union. The original question is not included unless include_original=True is set [12]. That default is risky, because a poor rewrite then replaces the user's words instead of adding to them. The LangChain "RAG from scratch" teaching notebooks use a five-perspective variant of the same prompt [16].

3.2 RAG-Fusion: multi-query plus Reciprocal Rank Fusion

Origin. Adrian Raudaschl proposed RAG-Fusion in a 2023 article and accompanying repository [6]. It adds two things to plain multi-query: rank-aware fusion and, in its later form, a reranker. An Infineon team reported an industrial evaluation for product-information chat in early 2024 [10].

Reciprocal Rank Fusion. RRF (Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher, SIGIR 2009) scores each document as the sum, over all ranked lists in which it appears, of 1 / (k + rank), with k = 60 [11]. Documents that appear high in many lists rise; one outlier list cannot dominate. LangChain's reference implementation uses exactly fused_scores[doc] += 1 / (rank + k) with k=60 [16], and the RAG-Fusion repository uses the same constant [6].

The current recommended architecture (as of the repository's September-October 2026 write-ups) is more elaborate than the original vector-only demo [6][8]:

                    +--> BM25(q)  ------+
  q ----------------+--> vector(q) -----+
  |                                     |
  +--> LLM: 4 diverse rewrites r1..r4   |
         each ri --> BM25(ri), vector(ri)--> 10 ranked lists
                                        |
                                        v
                      RRF: score(d) = sum 1/(60 + rank_i(d))
                                        |
                              pool of 50 candidates
                                        v
                    reranker (cross-encoder or LLM judge) --> top 5-10 --> LLM

The repository calls this hybrid_diverse+rerank. "Diverse" refers to a rewrite prompt that explicitly asks for different angles, synonyms, and narrower and broader framings [6].

3.3 Does fusion survive reranking? The 2026 evidence

The most useful public evidence on multi-query in production comes from a 2026 exchange.

  • The industry paper. "Scaling RAG Fusion: Lessons from an Industry Deployment" (arXiv 2603.02153, March 2026) reported that on 115 synthetic enterprise-support queries, two-query fusion (the original query plus one LLM rewrite), followed by FlashRank reranking and top-K truncation, matched or slightly underperformed a single-query baseline. Its proposed mechanism is that the reranker re-anchors on the original query, and the rewrite's marginal candidates are squeezed out at truncation. The paper concedes that fusion still helps in "recall-scarce" regimes (as summarized in [7]; the paper is cited as [9]).
  • The replication. Raudaschl replicated the setup on BEIR NFCorpus (3,633 biomedical documents, n=200 queries, paired-bootstrap 95% CIs) and disclosed his stake as the technique's originator [7]. The paper's exact configuration (vector-only, N=1 rewrite, pool of 10) showed no significant lift: +0.005 NDCG@10 [-0.016, +0.027] after a parser bug fix. The strong variant, hybrid_diverse+rerank, did show a significant lift. Against a vector baseline with the same reranker, NDCG@10 rose by +0.027 (bge-reranker-base), +0.015 (FlashRank MiniLM) and +0.025 (bge-reranker-large), all with CIs excluding zero [7].
  • Stronger rerankers do not absorb the gain. With LLM-based "decision model" rerankers, the lift grew rather than shrank: +0.035 to +0.039 with two vendor decision APIs and +0.050 with the strongest one tested [6][8]. Vector-only fusion "collapses toward zero once a strong reranker is added" [6].
  • Answer quality is real but noisy. End-to-end LLM-judge comparisons favoured fusion in all three judge runs but reached significance in only two. The author revised his earlier "measurably better answers" claim to "better retrieval, and probably somewhat better answers" [7].

Three methodological lessons from the replication apply beyond RAG-Fusion:

  1. Parse the rewrites defensively. A rewrite-parser bug caused "for 96 of the 200 queries, two of the four 'rewrites' [to be] the LLM's preamble line and an empty string". In the strict N=1 condition, the preamble was used as the only rewrite for 48% of queries [7]. LangChain's MultiQueryRetriever splits raw output on newlines [12], so the same failure is possible there. Structured output (a JSON array) is the safer contract.
  2. Small samples mislead. The write-up records four reversals between n=30 and n=200 runs [7].
  3. Retrieval-only tables overstate production value. The repository's retrieval-only table shows +0.057 NDCG@10 and +0.089 MRR for hybrid-diverse fusion over a vector baseline. After reranking, the lift is roughly half that or less [6].

3.4 Cost and latency of query expansion

The RAG-Fusion write-up includes the only detailed public per-stage latency breakdown found for this chapter (30 queries, medians, Apple M2 Max laptop, so absolute timings are indicative only) [8]:

Stage Median latency API cost per 1,000 queries
Vector search, top 50 80 ms self-hosted
Hybrid-diverse retrieval (10 lists) 426 ms self-hosted
Rewrite call (4 rewrites, small LLM) 1,557 ms about $0.055
Rerank 50 with bge-reranker-base (laptop GPU) 692 ms self-hosted
Rerank 50 with bge-reranker-large (laptop GPU) 2,162 ms self-hosted
Query-type router call (LLM classifier) 243 ms about $0.017

The author's conclusion: "Fusion's real price is latency, not money". The rewrite call costs about five cents per thousand queries but adds about 1.5 seconds, and "that call sits in front of everything else" [8]. The same source calls hybrid BM25 plus vector search (no rewrites) "close to free and worth doing everywhere" [6].

When multi-query pays. According to [6], fusion earns its cost when (1) user vocabulary diverges from corpus vocabulary, (2) recall matters more than precision, and (3) the downstream consumer can handle topically broad context. Good fits are literature search, patent prior art, e-discovery, long-tail e-commerce and cold-start specialist corpora. Poor fits are FAQ bots, latency-critical voice or autocomplete, code and identifier search, and structured or SQL-backed retrieval.

Routing fusion selectively (see Section 7) is the obvious optimization, but it has not yet been shown to work. An LLM query-type router fused 78% of queries and saved about a fifth of rewrite calls. It did not target the queries where fusion helps, and its own cost exceeded the savings when the rewrite model was cheap. The author proposes a router keyed on a retrieval-weakness signal (for example, a low top reranker score) as the next experiment [6][8].

3.5 Managed multi-query: Azure AI Search generative query rewriting

Azure AI Search ships multi-query as a service feature (preview) [24]:

  • The request sets "queryRewrites": "generative|count-5" (1 to 10 rewrites). Semantic ranking must be on (queryType: semantic), and queryLanguage must be set; the docs list dozens of supported locales.
  • The service sends the query "(or a variation of it)" to a generative model. It retrieves with the original and the rewritten queries, then applies the semantic reranker. Rewrites also apply to vector queries whose text matches the search text.
  • The stated purpose is to correct typos and add synonyms. The sample rewrites the hotel query "newer hotel near the water with a great restaurant" into five variants such as "new waterfront hotels with top-rated eateries".
  • Documented failure mode: "The rewritten queries might not contain all of the exact terms the original query had. This might impact search results if the query was highly specific and required exact matches for unique identifiers or product codes" [24]. This is the same identifier-search weakness noted in [6].

4. Step-back prompting

Problem. Some questions are hard to answer directly because they are full of specifics, such as a particular temperature and pressure in a physics problem, or a person's employer in a particular year. Retrieving for the literal question can return nothing useful, while retrieving for the governing principle or the broader history works.

Technique. Step-back prompting (Zheng et al., Google DeepMind, 2023; ICLR 2024) is a two-step method. The model first generates a step-back question about a higher-level concept or principle, for example "what is the education history of this person?" rather than "which school did X attend between 1954 and 1954?". It then reasons over the answer to that question to solve the original one [5]. The abstract reports that with PaLM-2L, step-back prompting improved MMLU Physics and Chemistry by about 7% and 11%, TimeQA by about 27%, and MuSiQue by about 7% (approximate; abstract figures not re-verified here) [5].

RAG architecture. In retrieval pipelines, the step-back question is used as an extra retrieval query, not as a replacement. LangChain's reference chain retrieves twice in parallel, once with the original question (normal_context) and once with the generated step-back question (step_back_context). Both context sets go into a response prompt that tells the model to use them if relevant and ignore them otherwise [16].

  q ---------------------------------------> retrieve --> normal_context ---+
  |                                                                         |
  +--> LLM (few-shot: "paraphrase to a more generic step-back question")    |
         --> q_sb --> retrieve --> step_back_context ------------------------+
                                                                            v
                                     answer prompt(q, normal_ctx, step_back_ctx)

Fit and failure modes. Step-back suits textbook-style corpora, policies and technical documentation, where principles are written separately from the cases they govern. It costs one extra short LLM call and one extra retrieval. The main failure mode is over-abstraction: the step-back question becomes generic enough to retrieve broad boilerplate that crowds out the specific evidence. Keeping the original-query retrieval in the pipeline, as the reference implementation does, guards against this [16].

5. Query decomposition

Decomposition targets questions that contain more than one information need. They are either parallel ("Where is the waterfront building and how did the whistleblower scandal affect the company?") or sequential, where the answer to one hop is needed to form the next query.

5.1 Research foundations

  • Least-to-most prompting (Zhou et al., Google, 2022) breaks a problem into simpler subproblems and solves them in order, feeding each answer into the next step [36].
  • Self-Ask (Press et al., Findings of EMNLP 2023) names the compositionality gap: models can often answer every sub-question correctly yet fail on the composed question. The model is prompted to ask itself explicit follow-up questions, which can be answered by a search engine, before giving the final answer. The work also introduced the Bamboogle dataset [34].
  • IRCoT (Trivedi et al., ACL 2023) interleaves retrieval with chain-of-thought. Each reasoning sentence becomes the query for the next retrieval step, and the retrieved paragraphs condition the next reasoning step. It was evaluated on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue and IIRC. The paper reports gains of up to about 21 retrieval points and up to about 15 QA points (abstract figures, approximate) [35].

5.2 Framework patterns: answer individually vs. answer recursively

LangChain's teaching material separates two execution strategies [16]:

  PARALLEL ("answer individually")         SEQUENTIAL ("answer recursively")
  q -> LLM -> [s1, s2, s3]                 q -> LLM -> [s1, s2, s3]
        |      |     |                      s1 -> retrieve -> a1
       ret    ret   ret                     s2 + (s1,a1) -> retrieve -> a2
        |      |     |                      s3 + (s1,a1),(s2,a2) -> retrieve -> a3
       a1     a2    a3                      answer(q) = a3 (or synthesize)
        \      |     /
   synthesize(q, Q/A pairs)

The decomposition prompt asks for sub-questions "that can be answered in isolation". The recursive variant passes the accumulated "background question + answer pairs" into each later step. That is the least-to-most / IRCoT pattern, which the notebook cites directly [16].

LlamaIndex's SubQuestionQueryEngine adds tool assignment to decomposition. The question generator receives the user question plus a JSON map of tools (one query engine per data source) and emits sub-questions, each tagged with a tool_name. Its built-in example turns "Compare and contrast the revenue growth and EBITDA of Uber and Lyft for year 2021" into four sub-questions, two routed to uber_10k and two to lyft_10k [19][20]. The sub-questions can run concurrently with asyncio.gather (use_async), and the answers are synthesized afterwards [19]. LlamaIndex also has a StepDecomposeQueryTransform for multi-step sequential querying [18].

5.3 Managed decomposition: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases offers decomposition as a one-line configuration (orchestrationConfiguration.queryTransformationConfiguration.type = "QUERY_DECOMPOSITION") on the RetrieveAndGenerate API. Sub-queries each go "through their own retrieval steps", and "the resulting chunks will then be pooled and ranked together before passing them to the FM" [27]. AWS's sample notebook shows both the failure and the fix. Without decomposition, the compound query about Octank's waterfront building and its whistleblower scandal returned only scandal-related chunks, because the embedding was pulled toward one half of the question. With decomposition, the invocation log shows a <standalone_question> followed by three <query> sub-queries, and the retrieved chunks covered both topics [27]. The <standalone_question> element suggests that conversational contextualization and decomposition run in the same model call.

5.4 Managed decomposition: Azure AI Search agentic retrieval

Azure AI Search's agentic retrieval (Foundry IQ) is the most fully specified public query planner [25][26]:

  retrieve(query, conversation history, reasoningEffort)
       |
       v
  [query planning LLM]  (skipped at "minimal")
       |  focused subqueries + knowledge-source selection
       v
  subqueries run in parallel over knowledge sources
  (keyword | vector | hybrid; indexed indexes or remote sources)
       |  each subquery semantically reranked (L2)
       v
  [medium only] semantic classifier (L3) judges sufficiency
       |  insufficient -> ONE follow-up iteration with revised plan
       v
  merged grounding content (+ optional references, activity log, answer synthesis)
  • Effort levels act as a router over the planner itself [26]. minimal disables LLM planning and searches every knowledge source directly. low (the default) runs one pass of planning and source selection. medium adds a high-precision semantic classifier and at most one retry ("Each iteration adds latency and cost, so the system constrains retry to one pass"). auto starts with a lightweight pass and escalates to planning, up to medium effort, only if grounding is insufficient.
  • Limits (preview): at low, 5,000 answer tokens and up to 50 documents for semantic ranking (10 with L3 classification). At medium, 10,000 answer tokens and 50 documents (20 with L3) [26].
  • Cost model. Billing is per token rather than per query. Microsoft's worked example assumes gpt-4o-mini for planning, 2,000 input tokens of chat context, 350 output tokens per plan, three subqueries per plan and 50 reranked chunks of 500 tokens per subquery. On those assumptions, 2,000 agentic retrievals cost about $3.30 for reranking and $1.02 for query planning, $4.32 in total. Fan-out (number of sources and subqueries) dominates; planning is under a quarter of the cost [25].
  • The docs state the trade-off directly: agentic retrieval "adds latency compared to a single-query pipeline, but it handles query complexity that a single query can't". The examples given are multi-ask questions, dependence on earlier turns, paraphrase and spelling mistakes [25].

5.5 Decomposition in graph and agentic systems

Decomposition also appears inside larger architectures:

  • LazyGraphRAG (Microsoft Research, November 2024) defers all LLM work to query time. Its query-refinement step uses an LLM to "identify relevant subqueries and recombine them into a single expanded query", and to refine subqueries with matching concepts from a concept graph. Each of q = 3-5 subqueries then drives chunk ranking and iterative deepening over communities. Indexing cost is reported as identical to vector RAG and 0.1% of full GraphRAG [43]. The graph-RAG chapter of this atlas covers the full design.
  • Anthropic's multi-agent Research system (June 2025) applies decomposition at the agent level. A lead agent plans, "determining query complexity and subagent count", and spawns subagents with separate search tasks. The prompts include explicit effort-scaling rules: "Simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents". The system outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal research eval. Multi-agent systems used about 15x the tokens of chat interactions [44]. The post also documents a query-formulation failure: agents "default to overly long, specific queries that return few results". The fix was to prompt them to "start with short, broad queries ... then progressively narrow focus" [44].

Decomposition failure modes. (1) Over-decomposition of simple queries, which multiplies cost and latency for no gain. The Anthropic effort rules and Azure's minimal/auto levels both exist to prevent this [26][44]. (2) Sub-questions that lose the shared constraint, such as "for year 2021", so that each one retrieves off-period evidence. (3) Sequential chains in which an early wrong answer contaminates every later query, the error compounding noted in [44]. (4) Unbounded iteration, which Azure caps at one retry [26].

6. Learned query rewriters

Prompted rewriting is easy to build but cannot be tuned against retrieval outcomes. A separate research line trains the rewriter using feedback from retrieval or from the reader.

  • Rewrite-Retrieve-Read (Ma et al., EMNLP 2023) replaces retrieve-then-read with rewrite-retrieve-read. An LLM first generates the search query, and a web search engine (Bing) retrieves the context. To "better align the query to the frozen modules", a small trainable rewriter (T5-based in the paper) is trained by reinforcement learning, using the black-box LLM reader's feedback as reward. Results were reported on open-domain and multiple-choice QA [4].
  • RQ-RAG (Chan et al., COLM 2024) trains a Llama-2-7B model end to end to rewrite, decompose and disambiguate queries. The training data is built by search-augmenting existing data (with DuckDuckGo in the released curation scripts), and both the dataset and the checkpoint are public [37].
  • DeepRetrieval (Jiang et al., 2025) trains a 3B LLM with RL to write queries, using retrieval metrics directly as reward, with no reference rewrites. The model reasons in a <think> block and emits the query in an <answer> block. The reward is tiered by recall (for example, +5.0 for recall of 0.7 or more, down to -3.5 for recall under 0.05 on PubMed search). The authors report 65.07% recall on publication search (previous best 24.68%) and 63.18% on clinical-trial search (previous best 32.11%), and say the 3B model outperforms GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet as a query writer. The method also covers BM25/dense retrieval and SQL search [41].
  • Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025) extends the idea from a single rewrite to interleaved reasoning and search. It uses RL (PPO, GRPO) on veRL to train models to decide when and what to search during multi-turn reasoning, with local sparse or dense retrievers or online search engines as the environment. By late 2025 it had been integrated into veRL, SkyRL and Thinking Machines' Tinker cookbook [42].

Lesson. The research frontier has moved the query writer from a fixed prompt to a policy optimized for retrieval reward. For system designers, the practical takeaway is that a small fine-tuned rewriter (3B-7B) can beat a large prompted model at writing queries. It is also cheaper and faster on the critical path [37][41]. The cost is a training pipeline and a reward signal. The DeepRetrieval reward table, tiered by recall, shows how a reward can be built from retrieval metrics alone [41].

7. Conversational query rewriting

Problem. In multi-turn chat, the latest message is often not retrievable on its own ("and how does that compare to last year?"). Embedding it directly retrieves noise.

7.1 Condense-question and history-aware retrievers

Both major frameworks use the same pattern: an LLM rewrites (chat history + follow-up) into a standalone question, which is then sent to the retriever.

  • LlamaIndex CondenseQuestionChatEngine prompt: "Given a conversation (between Human and Assistant) and a follow up message from Human, rewrite the message to be a standalone question that captures all relevant context from the conversation" [22].
  • LangChain create_history_aware_retriever wraps the rewrite in a RunnableBranch. If there is no chat history, the input is passed straight to the retriever, so the LLM call is skipped. Otherwise the prompt, LLM and string parser produce a search query [13]. This skip is a simple latency optimization: the first turn of every conversation costs no rewrite.
  • Managed services build it into the planner. Azure's agentic retrieval sends "your query and conversation history" to the planning LLM [25]. The Bedrock decomposition logs show a <standalone_question> produced before the sub-queries [27].
  history H = [(u1,a1), ..., (u_{t-1}, a_{t-1})],  follow-up u_t
        |
        +-- H empty? --yes--> retrieve(u_t)
        |
        no
        v
  LLM: rewrite(H, u_t) -> standalone q_t  -->  retrieve(q_t) --> answer(H, u_t, docs)
                                              (answer step still sees the raw turn)

A key design decision is what the answer step sees. The rewritten query is for retrieval only. Generating from the rewritten query alone can lose tone, constraints or meta-requests that appear in the raw turn ("answer in a table"), so the answer prompt should still receive the original message and the history.

7.2 Research line: conversational search

The TREC CAsT and iKAT conversational-search benchmarks led to a series of rewriting methods:

  • LLM4CS (Mao et al., Findings of EMNLP 2023) prompts an LLM to generate several rewrites and hypothetical responses, then aggregates them into one search-intent representation. It defines three prompting modes, Rewrite (REW), Rewrite-Then-Response (RTR) and Rewrite-And-Response (RAR), plus chain-of-thought tailored to intent understanding. It was evaluated on CAsT-19/20/21 with exemplars from CAsT-22 [38]. Generating a hypothetical response alongside the rewrite is HyDE applied to conversation.
  • ConvGQR (Mo et al., ACL 2023) combines generative query rewriting with generated potential answers for query expansion [39].
  • CHIQ (Mo et al., 2024) first improves the conversational history with an LLM (resolving ambiguity, for example) and only then rewrites the query. It was evaluated on TREC iKAT datasets [40].

Failure modes. (1) Over-carrying context: the rewrite drags in entities from earlier turns after the user has changed topic. (2) Under-carrying: pronouns are left unresolved. (3) Latency on every turn after the first. (4) The rewrite becomes the hidden single point of failure. Logging the rewritten query next to the retrieved documents is the minimum needed for debugging, which is why both the Azure activity log [25] and the Bedrock CloudWatch invocation logs [27] expose it.

8. Routing

Routing decides where a query goes before or instead of transforming it. Public designs route on five different axes:

Routing axis Decision Mechanism Example
Data source / index Which index or tool LLM structured output / function calling LangChain RouteQuery [17], LlamaIndex RouterQueryEngine [21]
Intent / guardrail Which pipeline or prompt, or deflect Embedding similarity to example utterances semantic-router [29]
Complexity / strategy No retrieval vs single-step vs multi-step Trained small classifier Adaptive-RAG [33]
Effort How much planning and iteration Service setting plus sufficiency check Azure minimal/low/medium/auto [26]
Model Cheap vs strong LLM Trained router on preference data RouteLLM [32]

8.1 LLM-based logical routing

LangChain's reference router defines a Pydantic schema with a Literal["python_docs", "js_docs", "golang_docs"] field, binds it with with_structured_output (function calling), and branches on result.datasource [17]. LlamaIndex's RouterQueryEngine uses a selector to choose one or several query engines from their text descriptions. The default prompt lists the choices as a numbered set of summaries and asks for the most relevant one "using only the choices above and not prior knowledge". With select_multi=True, it may choose several ("no more than {max_outputs}, but only select what is needed"), and their responses are merged by a TreeSummarize summarizer [21]. These routers are only as good as the descriptions of the destinations. A vague tool description is the most common cause of misrouting.

8.2 Semantic (embedding) routing

Problem. An LLM call to classify every query adds hundreds of milliseconds. The RAG-Fusion benchmark measured 243 ms for a hosted classifier call [8].

Architecture. Aurelio's open-source semantic-router replaces the LLM classifier with nearest-neighbour matching in embedding space [29]. Each Route is defined by a list of example utterances. At query time, the query is embedded once and compared to the utterance vectors (stored locally or in Pinecone/Qdrant). The best route above its score_threshold wins. If none passes, the router returns None, which is an explicit out-of-domain signal [29].

  offline: route r -> utterances u_r1..u_rn -> encoder -> utterance index
  online:  q -> encoder -> sim(q, u_ri) aggregated per route
           best route score >= threshold_r ?  -> route name (static)
                                              -> route + LLM-extracted args (dynamic)
           else -> None (fallback pipeline / general LLM)

Key techniques.

  • Threshold fitting. Default thresholds of 0.5 gave 34.85% accuracy on a larger test set in the library's optimization notebook. Fitting per-route thresholds from labelled (utterance, route) pairs moved them to about 0.22-0.26 and raised accuracy to 90.91%. The notebook warns that optimal values vary greatly by encoder; OpenAI's Ada-002 tends to produce scores in the 0.5-0.8 range [30].
  • Dynamic routes. A route can carry function schemas. After the embedding match, an LLM call extracts the arguments, so the route returns both a decision and parameters. This combines routing and slot filling, and the LLM is called only when the route needs it [31].
  • Hybrid routes (sparse plus dense encoders) and local encoders and LLMs are supported. The library ships a "fully local" healthcare administrative-routing example with threshold optimization across seven workflows [29].
  • As of 2026, the 0.x line (ending at 0.2.0) is in maintenance and a breaking 1.x rewrite of the routing layer is in development, so integrators should pin a version [29].

Failure modes. Embedding routers are fast and cheap, but they match surface similarity. Negation ("not about politics"), rare intents with few utterances, and drift in user language all degrade them. They need a labelled evaluation set and periodic re-fitting, and the None route must be wired to a sensible fallback.

8.3 Complexity routing: Adaptive-RAG

Adaptive-RAG (Jeong et al., NAACL 2024) routes each query to no retrieval, single-step retrieval or iterative multi-step retrieval (IRCoT-style), based on predicted complexity [33]. The router is "a smaller LM trained to predict the complexity level of incoming queries", with labels collected automatically from which strategy actually answered correctly and from dataset biases (single-hop vs multi-hop sources). It was evaluated on single-hop (NQ, TriviaQA, SQuAD) and multi-hop (MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA) QA with FLAN-T5 and GPT readers [33]. The design has been reproduced as LangGraph and LlamaIndex cookbooks [33]. The lesson for production: decomposition and iteration should be gated, not always on. Azure's auto effort level [26] and Anthropic's effort-scaling rules [44] are industrial versions of the same idea.

8.4 Model routing: RouteLLM

Model routing chooses which LLM answers, not where to retrieve. It sits in the same query-understanding layer and uses the same signals. LMSYS's RouteLLM provides routers trained on preference data behind an OpenAI-compatible client. The authors report cost reductions of up to 85% while keeping 95% of GPT-4 performance on MT Bench, and say the routers matched commercial routing offerings while being more than 40% cheaper [32].

9. Metadata filter extraction and self-query

Problem. "Songs by Taylor Swift or Katy Perry about teenage romance under 3 minutes in the dance pop genre" contains one semantic need (teenage romance) and three hard constraints (artist, length, genre). Embedding the whole sentence treats the constraints as soft similarity. That loses precision, and on filtered ANN indexes it wastes the filter support the store already has (Chapter 04).

9.1 LangChain SelfQueryRetriever

The self-query design [14][15] splits the query in two:

  q --> LLM(query-constructor prompt: schema + attribute descriptions
           + allowed comparators/operators + few-shot examples)
     --> {"query": "teenager love",
          "filter": "and(or(eq(artist,'Taylor Swift'), eq(artist,'Katy Perry')),
                         lt(length,180), eq(genre,'pop'))",
          "limit": optional int}
     --> parse into StructuredQuery IR (Comparison / Operation / limit)
     --> store-specific Translator (Pinecone, Qdrant, Chroma, Weaviate, Milvus,
         Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, PGVector, MongoDB Atlas, Neo4j, Redis, ...)
     --> vectorstore.search(query, filter=native_filter, k=limit)

Details of the prompt contract that matter in practice [14]:

  • "The query string should contain only text that is expected to match the contents of documents. Any conditions in the filter should not be mentioned in the query as well." This stops the constraint words from also skewing the embedding.
  • "Make sure that filters only refer to attributes that exist in the data source", only allowed comparators and operators are used, dates use YYYY-MM-DD, and if no filter applies the model must return NO_FILTER.
  • An optional limit field turns "three songs about love" into k = 3.
  • The retriever has use_original_query, which keeps the user's wording for the vector search and uses only the extracted filter [15]. This is a useful hedge when the LLM's shortened query loses meaning.
  • An intermediate representation plus per-store Translator visitors makes the LLM output portable. More than twenty vector stores have built-in translators [15].

9.2 LlamaIndex VectorIndexAutoRetriever

LlamaIndex's auto-retriever adapts the LangChain prompt (the source credits it) to its own VectorStoreInfo / MetadataInfo schema and outputs a VectorStoreQuerySpec with query, filters and optional top_k [23]. It adds operational safeguards:

  • max_top_k (default 10) caps any LLM-requested top_k.
  • If the inferred query string is empty, meaning the request is filter-only, as in "all reports from 2023", it uses empty_query_top_k and an optional default_empty_query_vector.
  • extra_filters are applied unconditionally on top of whatever the LLM produced. They cannot be OR conditions. This is the right place for security and tenancy filters, which must never depend on the LLM [23].

9.3 Structured search schemas with function calling

LangChain's query-construction notebook shows the modern form: a Pydantic TutorialSearch model with separate content_search and title_search strings, plus optional typed range filters (min_view_count, earliest_publish_date, max_length_sec and so on), each described as "Only use if explicitly specified". The model is bound through structured output [17]. Generating two query strings for two fields (a full-text content query and a short, keyword-only title query) is a small but effective pattern for multi-field indexes.

9.4 Managed: Amazon Bedrock implicit (autogenerated) filters

Bedrock Knowledge Bases exposes self-query as implicitFilterConfiguration inside vectorSearchConfiguration. The caller lists metadataAttributes (key, type such as NUMBER/STRING, and a description with possible values, for example "Possible values include ['AMZN']"), and names the model that generates filters (Claude 3.5 Sonnet in the sample) [28]. The documented example: "marketing reports from last year" yields a date filter. AWS recommends CloudWatch log analysis to "verify their consistency across different user query variations" [28], which is an implicit admission that generated filters can vary from one phrasing to the next.

9.5 Failure modes of filter extraction

  1. Over-filtering. The single most damaging error. A wrongly inferred filter (wrong year, misspelled entity value) returns zero or wrong results, and no reranker can recover documents that were filtered out. Mitigations: tell the model to filter only when the constraint is explicit (the "Only use if explicitly specified" pattern [17]), enumerate allowed values in attribute descriptions [28], and fall back to an unfiltered or relaxed search when a filtered search returns too few results.
  2. Value normalization. "Q3", "last year" and "2024" need a reference date and a canonical format. The LangChain prompt forces YYYY-MM-DD [14], but relative dates still need the current date injected into the prompt.
  3. Constraint leakage. Constraint words left in the semantic query double-count. The self-query prompt explicitly forbids this [14].
  4. Security. Access-control filters must be applied outside the LLM, as with extra_filters [23]. An LLM-generated filter is user-influenced input.

10. Side-by-side comparison

10.1 Technique comparison

Technique Extra LLM calls before retrieval Retrievals per query Best for Main failure mode Primary evidence
HyDE 1 (long output; N samples in reference setup) 1 (averaged vector) Zero-shot, label-free corpora; question/passage asymmetry Confident wrong hypothesis on private or new data DL19 nDCG@10 0.445 -> 0.597 [2]
Query2doc 1 (long output) 1 BM25 / sparse stacks Pseudo-doc outweighs query +3-15% BM25 (abstract) [3]
Multi-query (union) 1 (short output) N Vocabulary mismatch Parser junk; drift without original Framework default [12]
RAG-Fusion (hybrid + RRF + rerank) 1 2(N+1) Recall-scarce, jargon-heavy domains ~1.5 s added latency; little gain with vector-only variant +0.015 to +0.050 NDCG@10 after rerank [6][7][8]
Step-back 1 (short) 2 Principle or background questions Over-abstraction MMLU, TimeQA, MuSiQue gains (abstract) [5]
Decomposition (parallel) 1 k sub-queries Multi-ask questions Lost shared constraints; over-decomposition Bedrock sample [27]; Azure planner [25]
Decomposition (sequential / IRCoT) k (interleaved) k Multi-hop questions Error compounding; latency Up to ~21 retrieval points (abstract) [35]
Conversational condense 1 (skipped on turn 1) 1 Multi-turn chat Over- or under-carrying context Framework defaults [13][22]
LLM router 1 (tiny output) 0 extra Several indexes or tools Vague destination descriptions [17][21]
Semantic router 0 (embedding only) 0 extra Intents, guardrails, high QPS Surface similarity; threshold drift 34.85% -> 90.91% after fitting [30]
Complexity router 0 (small classifier) 0, 1 or many Mixed simple and multi-hop traffic Mislabelled complexity Adaptive-RAG [33]
Self-query / implicit filters 1 (structured) 1 (filtered) Catalogues, reports, dated corpora Over-filtering to zero results [14][15][23][28]
Learned rewriter (RL) 1 (small model) 1+ High-volume, domain-specific search Training cost; reward hacking DeepRetrieval recall 65.07% vs 24.68% [41]

10.2 Platform and framework comparison

Capability LangChain [12]-[17] LlamaIndex [18]-[23] Azure AI Search [24]-[26] Amazon Bedrock KB [27][28]
Multi-query / rewrite MultiQueryRetriever (3 by default, original optional) Query transforms queryRewrites: generative|count-N (1-10) Within decomposition
HyDE Cookbook HyDEQueryTransform (keeps original) No (not documented) No (not documented)
Decomposition Notebook patterns SubQuestionQueryEngine (tool-tagged, async) Agentic retrieval query planning QUERY_DECOMPOSITION
Conversational rewrite create_history_aware_retriever (skips on empty history) CondenseQuestionChatEngine, condense-plus-context Planner consumes chat history Standalone question in decomposition
Routing Structured-output router; embedding router RouterQueryEngine + selectors Knowledge-source selection; effort levels incl. auto Not documented
Filter extraction SelfQueryRetriever + 20+ translators VectorIndexAutoRetriever + extra_filters Not documented as automatic implicitFilterConfiguration
Observability Tracing (LangSmith) Verbose / callbacks debug: queryRewrites, activity log CloudWatch invocation logs

11. Cross-cutting failure modes and engineering lessons

  1. The query layer sits on the critical path. Every LLM call before retrieval adds its full latency to time-to-first-token. The measured rewrite cost of about 1.5 s [8] is larger than the retrieval it improves (80-426 ms). Parallelize what can run in parallel (sub-queries [19][25], step-back plus original retrieval [16]), skip work when it is not needed (empty history [13], minimal effort [26]), and use embedding routers instead of LLM classifiers where accuracy allows [29][30].
  2. Always keep the original query in the mix. HyDE averages it in [2]. LlamaIndex keeps it by default [18]. RAG-Fusion searches it alongside the rewrites [6]. Step-back retrieves for it in parallel [16]. Self-query can use it for the vector search [15]. The cases that fail are the ones that replace it: LangChain's include_original=False default [12], and Azure's warning about product codes [24].
  3. Exact identifiers do not survive paraphrase. SKUs, error codes, ticket IDs and legal citations should bypass generative rewriting or be protected by a BM25 leg [6][24].
  4. Use structured output for every transformation. Free-text parsing of rewrites caused a large, silent evaluation error in the most-cited public RAG-Fusion benchmark [7]. Every managed service and the newer framework patterns use JSON or tagged output [14][17][19][27].
  5. Evaluate after the reranker and on answers, with confidence intervals. Gains measured on retrieval alone shrink after reranking, and answer-level gains are noisier still. The 2026 paper and its replication disagreed largely because they tested different variants at different sample sizes [6][7][9].
  6. Gate complexity. Decomposition, iteration and multi-query should be routed on, not always on: Adaptive-RAG [33], Azure auto [26], Anthropic's effort rules [44]. The open problem is choosing the gating signal. Query-type classification did not target fusion wins in [8]; retrieval-confidence signals, such as reranker score or Azure's L3 sufficiency classifier [26], look more promising.
  7. Make the transformation visible. Rewritten queries, generated filters and sub-query plans should be logged next to the results. Azure's debug and activity log, Bedrock's CloudWatch logs and LangSmith traces exist for this purpose [16][24][25][27].
  8. Treat generated filters as untrusted. Tenancy and ACL constraints belong in non-LLM extra_filters-style parameters [23].

Key takeaways for system designers

  • Start with the cheapest wins. Hybrid BM25 plus vector retrieval with RRF costs almost nothing and helps nearly everywhere [6]. A conversational condense step is mandatory for multi-turn chat [13][22]. Self-query filter extraction is mandatory for corpora with meaningful metadata [14][28].
  • Pick query expansion by diagnosis, not habit. HyDE addresses question/passage asymmetry in zero-shot settings [1][2]. Multi-query and RAG-Fusion address vocabulary mismatch in recall-scarce domains [6]. Step-back addresses over-specific questions [5]. Decomposition addresses multi-ask and multi-hop questions [25][27][35].
  • Budget latency explicitly. One rewrite call is about 1-2 s with a small hosted model [8], several times the cost of retrieval itself. Embedding routers run in a single embedding call [29]. Managed planners bill per token, and fan-out across subqueries dominates the cost [25].
  • If you deploy RAG-Fusion, deploy the hybrid variant behind your strongest reranker. Vector-only fusion with one rewrite shows no significant gain after reranking. Hybrid fusion with diverse rewrites shows +0.015 to +0.050 NDCG@10 [6][7][8].
  • Never let a transformation remove information. Keep the original query, protect exact identifiers, apply filters only when explicit, and fall back when filters return nothing [2][12][17][24].
  • Route by complexity. Use no retrieval, single-shot or iterative retrieval as the query requires, with capped iterations (Azure allows one retry [26]) and explicit effort budgets [33][44].
  • Watch the learned-rewriter frontier. RL-trained 3B-7B query writers have outperformed large prompted models on recall-oriented search [37][41], and RL now trains when and what to search during reasoning [42]. For high-volume vertical search, a trained rewriter is becoming a realistic component.
  • Instrument everything. The rewritten query is part of your system's behaviour. Log it, evaluate it, and version its prompt like code [7][24][27].
