08. Agentic and Iterative RAG: Self-RAG, CRAG, FLARE, IRCoT, Adaptive-RAG, ReAct, RL-Trained Search Agents and Agentic Search

Overview

Classic RAG (Chapter 01) is a fixed pipeline: embed the query, retrieve top-k once, put the passages in the prompt, generate. Every design in this chapter breaks one of the assumptions in that sentence.

  • Retrieve once. Multi-hop questions need evidence that can only be found after part of the answer is known. DSP's example is "How many storeys are in the castle David Gregory inherited?". A retrieve-then-read pipeline fetches a passage about the St. Gregory Hotel and answers "nine". The right approach first asks which castle David Gregory inherited [14]. IRCoT, Self-Ask, DSP and ITER-RETGEN turn retrieval into a loop [7][13][14][15].
  • Always retrieve. Many queries need no retrieval, and irrelevant passages can make answers worse. FLARE, DRAGIN, Self-RAG and Adaptive-RAG decide when to retrieve [1][5][9][16].
  • Trust what came back. Retrievers fail silently. Self-RAG and CRAG add an explicit judgment of whether retrieved text is relevant and whether the output is supported. CRAG can then throw the retrieval away and search the web instead [1][3].
  • A human-designed control flow. ReAct hands the loop to the model: think, act (search), observe, repeat [11]. Search-R1 and its successors go further and train that policy with reinforcement learning (RL) against a search engine [21][23][29][30].
  • A pre-built index. Coding agents such as Claude Code mostly skip the vector index. The model searches the live filesystem with grep/find and reads files on demand, which Anthropic calls "just in time" retrieval [36][37][38].

The result is a spectrum. At one end, retrieval is a fixed pre-processing step. At the other, retrieval is one tool among many inside an autonomous agent that decides how many searches to run, what to read and when to stop. This chapter goes along that spectrum in roughly historical order: interleaved multi-hop loops (2022-23), triggered and self-reflective retrieval (2023-24), routing by query complexity (2024), ReAct-style agents, RL-trained search policies (2025-26), multi-agent research systems, and the agentic-search versus indexing debate in coding agents. Query decomposition and learned query rewriting are covered in Chapter 06. Graph-based multi-hop retrieval (HippoRAG) is covered in Chapter 07.

  FIXED PIPELINE                                                      AUTONOMOUS AGENT
  |---------------|----------------|----------------|----------------|---------------|
  Naive RAG     IRCoT / DSP      FLARE / DRAGIN   Self-RAG / CRAG   ReAct, Search-R1,
  (1 retrieval) (loop fixed by   (retrieval fires (model or small   Claude Code,
                 the program)     on uncertainty)  critic grades    multi-agent research
                                                   and corrects)    (model owns the loop)
  control: code ------------------------------------------------------> control: policy
  cost:    1 LLM call + 1 search -----------------------------> 10s-100s of calls/searches

1. A control-theoretic view: four decisions

Every iterative or agentic RAG system makes four decisions, explicitly or implicitly. The designs differ in who makes each decision and what signal they use.

Decision Question Signal used Representative designs
Trigger Retrieve now, or not at all? token probability, attention entropy, learned token, classifier, policy FLARE [5], DRAGIN [16], Self-RAG [1], Adaptive-RAG [9], Search-R1 [21]
Query What to search for? last CoT sentence, predicted next sentence, sub-question, attention-weighted terms, free-form policy output IRCoT [7], FLARE [5], Self-Ask [13], DRAGIN [16], ReAct [11]
Verify Is what came back useful and supporting? critic tokens, trained evaluator, LLM grader Self-RAG [1], CRAG [3], LangGraph graders [18][19]
Stop Enough evidence to answer? answer emitted, budget, max turns, evaluator verdict IRCoT [7], Search-R1 max_turns [21], Anthropic lead agent [33]

The survey by Gao et al. groups the loop variants into iterative retrieval (alternate retrieval and generation, as in ITER-RETGEN), recursive retrieval (refine the query step by step, as in IRCoT) and adaptive retrieval (the model decides when and whether to retrieve, as in FLARE and Self-RAG) [15]. FlashRAG uses a similar split: sequential, conditional (route by query type), branching (parallel paths, merged) and loop pipelines, plus a newer reasoning class for RL-trained search models [17].

2. Interleaved retrieval for multi-hop questions

2.1 DSP and Self-Ask: programmatic and prompted decomposition

Problem. A frozen LM plus a retriever, wired as retrieve-then-read, cannot answer a question whose second hop depends on the first hop's answer [14].

Self-Ask (Press et al., Findings of EMNLP 2023) names the compositionality gap: models can often answer each sub-question correctly but still fail on the composed question. It prompts the model to ask explicit follow-up questions, each of which can be sent to a search engine, before it answers. The paper also introduced the Bamboogle dataset, which later became a standard out-of-domain test for search agents [13][23].

DSP (Demonstrate-Search-Predict) (Khattab et al., Stanford, 2022) writes the pipeline as a program. DEMONSTRATE bootstraps intermediate annotations (hop-1 query, hop-1 passage, hop-2 query) on a few training examples using weak supervision. SEARCH generates hop queries conditioned on earlier passages. PREDICT produces a grounded answer. The authors report 37-120% relative gains over vanilla GPT-3.5, 8-39% over retrieve-then-read and 80-290% over a contemporaneous self-ask pipeline across open-domain, multi-hop and conversational settings [14]. DSP later became DSPy. Its main lesson for designers is that multi-hop control flow can be compiled: demonstrations for every intermediate step are generated instead of hand-written.

2.2 IRCoT: chain-of-thought as the query generator

Problem. For multi-step questions, "what to retrieve depends on what has already been derived", so one retrieval with the original question misses later-hop evidence [7].

Architecture. IRCoT (Trivedi et al., Stony Brook NLP, ACL 2023) alternates two steps until the reasoning chain emits an answer or a step limit is reached:

  question q ---> BM25 (Elasticsearch) ---> paragraphs P0
       |
       v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------+
  | REASON: LLM(q, P_all, CoT so far) -> next CoT sentence s_i      |
  |   if s_i contains "answer is" or i == max_steps: stop          |
  | RETRIEVE: BM25(s_i) -> top-K paragraphs, add to P_all          |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------+
       |  (loop)
       v
  READER: answer from q + collected paragraphs (or read off CoT)

The latest chain-of-thought sentence becomes the next query. It usually names the bridge entity that the original question did not contain. The released code supports Codex and Flan-T5 (base to XXL) as reasoners over BM25 indexes for HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue and IIRC. It also includes baselines for no retrieval (nor) and one-step retrieval (oner) [8].

Results. The paper's abstract reports improvements of up to about 21 points in retrieval recall and up to about 15 points in downstream QA over one-step retrieval (approximate, abstract-level figures) [7]. In FlashRAG's uniform re-implementation (Llama3-8B-Instruct, e5-base-v2, 5 documents), IRCoT gets the best HotpotQA F1 among non-RL "loop" methods: 41.5, against 35.3 for standard RAG. It costs several retrieve-reason rounds per question [17].

Failure modes. (a) Error compounding. A wrong bridge entity in sentence i sends every later retrieval off course. (b) Latency grows linearly with hops, because each round is a sequential LLM call plus a search. (c) The loop runs even on single-hop questions, which motivated Adaptive-RAG (Section 5). Chapter 07 reports that HippoRAG matched or beat IRCoT at roughly 10-30x lower cost by moving the hop into a graph walk.

2.3 ITER-RETGEN and branching variants

ITER-RETGEN (Shao et al., 2023) runs a fixed number of retrieve-read rounds and uses the whole previous generation as the next query. It is "iterative" rather than "recursive" in the survey's terms [15]. Under FlashRAG's settings it reaches 38.3 HotpotQA F1, but only 21.6 on 2WikiMultihopQA, where naive generation without retrieval scores 33.9 [17]. The 2WikiMultihopQA column is a useful warning: several RAG methods score below no-retrieval generation on that dataset in that setup. That is evidence that badly targeted retrieval can hurt reasoning-heavy questions.

3. Uncertainty-triggered retrieval: FLARE and DRAGIN

3.1 FLARE (Forward-Looking Active REtrieval)

Problem. In long-form generation, information needs appear during generation. Retrieving only with the input misses them. Retrieving at a fixed interval (every n tokens) wastes calls and uses stale queries.

Architecture. FLARE (Jiang et al., EMNLP 2023) "actively decides when and what to retrieve using a prediction of the upcoming sentence to anticipate future content". If the tentative next sentence contains low-confidence tokens, that sentence is used as the query. The sentence is then regenerated with the retrieved documents [5][6]. The survey summarizes the trigger as retrieval firing "when the probability falls below a certain threshold" [15].

  context y_<t ---> LLM drafts next sentence s'_t (no retrieval)
                         |
         all token probs >= theta ?  ---- yes ---> accept s'_t, continue
                         | no
                         v
        query = s'_t (the tentative sentence itself)
                         |
                retrieve (BM25 over Wikipedia / Bing)
                         |
        regenerate s_t conditioned on retrieved docs ---> continue

Implementation details. The reference code runs on text-davinci-003, with Elasticsearch over the DPR Wikipedia dump (psgs_w100) and a cached Bing search server for WikiASP. The README warns that "experiments are relatively expensive because FLARE calls OpenAI API multiple times for a single example" [6]. FLARE depends on token log-probabilities. Many hosted chat APIs now expose these only partially or not at all, which limits the design to self-hosted or log-prob-capable models.

Reproduced behaviour. In FlashRAG's uniform setting, FLARE scores almost exactly the same as naive generation (NQ EM 22.5 vs 22.6; HotpotQA F1 28.0 vs 28.4) [17]. This does not contradict the original paper, which used a different model and long-form tasks. It does show that a confidence threshold tuned for one model can leave retrieval almost never triggered on another. The threshold has to be recalibrated per model.

3.2 DRAGIN

DRAGIN (ACL 2024) refines both FLARE decisions. RIND (Real-time Information Needs Detection) decides when to retrieve from the LLM's uncertainty, each token's importance and its semantic significance. QFS (Query Formulation based on Self-attention) builds the query from the tokens the model attends to across the whole context, not just the last sentence [16]. One of its configurations is named attn_entropy. The repository warns about an operational trap common to all these Wikipedia-based reproductions: the Elasticsearch index must hold about 21 million passages (about 11.2 GB). If disk space runs low, indexing stops "silently, with no errors and no logs", and the incomplete index then produces only a "subtle drop in performance" [16]. In production, index-completeness checks belong in the health checks of any iterative RAG system. The iteration hides recall loss because the model can partly compensate from parametric memory.

4. Self-reflective retrieval: Self-RAG

Problem. Indiscriminate retrieval of a fixed number of passages "diminishes LM versatility or can lead to unhelpful response generation", and the output is not guaranteed to be consistent with the passages [1].

Architecture. Self-RAG (Asai et al., UW / AI2 / IBM; arXiv 2023, ICLR 2024) trains one LM to emit four kinds of reflection tokens as ordinary next-token predictions from an extended vocabulary. The 7B and 13B models are released on Hugging Face [1][2]:

Token Input Values Meaning
Retrieve x, or x and y yes, no, continue whether to call the retriever
ISREL x, d relevant, irrelevant passage d helps answer x
ISSUP x, d, y fully, partially, no support output y is supported by d
ISUSE x, y 5..1 overall utility of y

Inference works segment by segment (one sentence per segment in the experiments). At each segment the model first predicts Retrieve. If retrieval is needed, it retrieves K passages, generates K candidate continuations in parallel (one per passage), critiques each with ISREL/ISSUP/ISUSE, and keeps the best candidates by segment-level beam search [1].

  x, y_<t --> [Retrieve?] --no--> generate y_t --> [ISUSE]
                  | yes (or P(yes) > threshold delta)
                  v
          Contriever-MS MARCO: top-K passages d1..dK
                  |
     +------------+------------+-------------+
     v            v            v             v      (parallel, one per passage)
   d1 -> [ISREL] y_t^1 [ISSUP] [ISUSE]   ...   dK -> ... y_t^K
                  |
     score_k = log p(y_t^k) + sum_G w_G * s_G(critique tokens)
                  |
     segment-level beam search (keep top-B) --> next segment

Training pipeline.

  1. Critic data. GPT-4 is prompted with a type-specific instruction to label reflection tokens. The authors collect 4k-20k examples per token type [1].
  2. Critic model C. Llama 2-7B, fine-tuned on these labels. It agrees with the GPT-4 predictions more than 90% of the time on most categories [1].
  3. Generator corpus. C runs offline over 150k instruction-output pairs (Open-Instruct subsets plus knowledge-intensive sets such as NQ, Wizard of Wikipedia, FEVER, ASQA). It inserts Retrieve tokens, retrieved passages and critique tokens [1].
  4. Generator M. Llama 2 7B/13B, trained with the plain LM objective. Retrieved passages are masked out of the loss. Training used 4x A100-80GB, 3 epochs, batch size 128, learning rate 2e-5 [1].

Inserting critiques offline avoids hosting a reward model during training, which the authors say "significantly reduces training costs compared to PPO" [1].

Inference knobs. By default ISREL, ISSUP and ISUSE are weighted 1.0, 1.0 and 0.5. The retrieval threshold is 0.2 for most tasks and 0 for ALCE-ASQA (always retrieve, because citations are required). Inference runs on vLLM [1]. Raising the ISSUP weight raises citation precision but lowers MAUVE fluency. The authors present this as test-time customization without retraining [1].

Results. Self-RAG 13B reaches 55.8 accuracy on PopQA (long-tail subset), 69.3 on TriviaQA, 74.5 on PubHealth, 73.1 on ARC-Challenge, and 70.3/71.3 citation precision/recall on ASQA. Retrieval-augmented Llama2-13B gets 2.3/3.6 citation precision/recall on ASQA, and Ret-ChatGPT gets 65.1/76.6 [1]. Ablations show that removing the retriever or the critic during training causes large drops [1].

Failure modes and lessons.

  • The model is the controller. Changing the retriever, the corpus or the base model means retraining, or at least re-validating that the reflection tokens are still calibrated.
  • In FlashRAG's uniform benchmark, the released selfrag-llama2-7B scores 38.2 EM on TriviaQA. Naive Llama3-8B generation scores 55.7 [17]. A trained controller is tied to its base model, and newer base models can overtake it.
  • The cost is variable. CRAG's authors estimate Self-RAG generation at 26.5-132.4 TFLOPs per token, against a fixed 26.5 for plain RAG, because of the parallel per-passage candidates [3].
  • The lasting contribution is the vocabulary: retrieve / relevant / supported / useful. LangGraph's Self-RAG tutorial re-implements these four decisions as prompted LLM "graders" wired into a state graph, with no fine-tuning [18]. Most production "self-RAG" today means this prompted variant.

5. Corrective retrieval: CRAG

Problem. Self-RAG asks whether retrieval is needed. CRAG (Yan et al., USTC / UCLA / Google DeepMind, 2024) asks a different question: what should the system do when the retriever returns wrong documents? A generator coupled to a weak retriever has "low risk tolerance" [3].

Architecture.

  query x --> retriever --> ~10 docs
                  |
     T5-large retrieval evaluator scores each (x, d_i) pair
                  |
     +------------+--------------------+-------------------------+
     | any score > upper threshold      | all scores < lower      | otherwise
     v                                  v                         v
  CORRECT                            INCORRECT                 AMBIGUOUS
  knowledge refinement:              discard retrieval;        both: refined internal
  decompose docs -> strips,          ChatGPT rewrites x to     + web external
  score strips, drop irrelevant,     keyword query -> web      knowledge
  recompose in order                 search API (prefers
                                     Wikipedia pages) ->
                                     fetch pages -> refine
                  \__________________________|_________________________/
                                             v
                                         generator

Key techniques.

  • Evaluator, not generator, does the judging. A fine-tuned T5-large model scores each question-document pair. On PopQA its accuracy at judging retrieval quality is 84.3%. ChatGPT scores 58.0% zero-shot, 62.4% with CoT and 64.7% few-shot [3]. A small trained classifier beat a large prompted model at this narrow task.
  • Three actions, not two. In preliminary experiments with only Correct and Incorrect, CRAG's efficacy "was easily affected by the accuracy of the retrieval evaluator". The Ambiguous action hedges by combining both knowledge sources [3].
  • Decompose-then-recompose. Documents are split into "knowledge strips" of a few sentences. The same evaluator scores each strip, and only relevant strips are concatenated. This is passage-level filtering before generation [3].
  • Web search as fallback corpus. Queries are rewritten into keywords "to mimic the daily usage of search engine". A commercial web search API (Google Search API in the paper) is used, and authoritative pages such as Wikipedia are preferred, to limit the bias and unreliability of web content [3].

Results and cost. Applied to SelfRAG-LLaMA2-7b, CRAG improves over plain RAG by 7.0 points on PopQA, 14.9 FactScore on Biography, 36.6 on PubHealth and 15.4 on ARC-Challenge [3]. When plain RAG and Self-RAG are also given web search, CRAG still wins in all cases. The authors therefore attribute the gain to the correction mechanism, not to the extra corpus [3]. Measured on PopQA generation only (retrieval excluded), the overhead is small:

Method TFLOPs per token Execution time per instance (s)
RAG 26.5 0.363
CRAG 27.2 0.512
Self-RAG 26.5 to 132.4 0.741
Self-CRAG 27.2 to 80.2 0.908

Source: [3], Table 6. These are rough estimates of the generation phase. Web search latency, often seconds, is not included.

Failure modes. The whole system depends on the evaluator. The authors released the evaluator weights and the knowledge-preparation code, but the evaluator was fine-tuned on PopQA [4]. A judge trained on PopQA will not transfer to a legal or code corpus without new labels. The web fallback also brings in freshness and trust problems that the internal corpus did not have. LangGraph's CRAG tutorial makes the usual production simplification: it skips knowledge refinement, uses an LLM grader for relevance, and runs a web search tool (Tavily) when any document is graded irrelevant [19].

6. Routing by query complexity: Adaptive-RAG

Problem. Single-step RAG is cheap but fails on multi-hop questions. IRCoT-style iteration handles multi-hop but wastes calls on simple ones. Real traffic mixes both [9].

Architecture. Adaptive-RAG (Jeong et al., NAACL 2024) puts a classifier in front of three strategies, all built on the IRCoT codebase: nor_qa (no retrieval), oner_qa (single-step) and ircot_qa (multi-step) [10].

  query --> T5-large complexity classifier --> A: no retrieval   (LLM only)
                                          \--> B: single-step    (BM25 once + LLM)
                                          \--> C: multi-step     (IRCoT loop)

Label generation without annotation. Labels come from two sources. Silver labels record which strategy actually answered each training question correctly; the simplest successful one wins. Binary labels come from the dataset's inductive bias: questions from single-hop datasets (NQ, TriviaQA, SQuAD) are labelled simpler, and questions from multi-hop datasets (MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA) are labelled complex. A separate classifier is trained for each reader LLM (FLAN-T5-XL, FLAN-T5-XXL, GPT) [10]. The classifier learns which pipeline this LLM needs, not an abstract notion of difficulty.

Results. The authors report better overall efficiency and accuracy than the baselines, including other adaptive retrieval approaches [9]. In FlashRAG's re-implementation, Adaptive-RAG falls between standard RAG and IRCoT on HotpotQA (39.1 vs 35.3 and 41.5 F1) [17]. That is the expected trade-off: it gives up some multi-hop accuracy in exchange for skipping the loop on queries routed to A or B.

Practitioner adoption. LangGraph, LlamaIndex and Cohere published Adaptive-RAG cookbooks [10]. LangGraph's version replaces the trained classifier with an LLM router between web search (recent events) and a self-corrective RAG branch over the index [20]. That combination (router, then graders, then fallback) is the most common "agentic RAG" blueprint in framework documentation.

7. ReAct-style retrieval agents

ReAct (Yao et al., ICLR 2023) interleaves free-form thoughts with actions and observations. On HotpotQA and FEVER the actions are calls to a simple Wikipedia API (search an entity, look up a string in the current page, finish with an answer) [11]. The released prompts report, on 500 random dev questions, HotpotQA EM of 29.4 (PaLM-540B) and 30.4 (GPT-3 davinci-002), and FEVER EM of 62.2 and 54 [12]. These numbers are low by 2026 standards. ReAct matters for its interface, not its accuracy. Every current search agent, including Tongyi DeepResearch's evaluation mode and the LangGraph agents used to benchmark code-search tools, still runs a ReAct-shaped loop [31][40].

  Thought: I need the castle David Gregory inherited.
  Action:  search[David Gregory (physician)]
  Obs:     "... inherited Kinnairdy Castle in 1664 ..."
  Thought: Now find how many storeys Kinnairdy Castle has.
  Action:  search[Kinnairdy Castle]
  Obs:     "... a tower house of five storeys ..."
  Action:  finish[five]

(Illustrative trace in ReAct format. The passages are the ones shown in DSP's Figure 1 for this running example [14].)

Anthropic's framing. Anthropic's "Building effective agents" (December 2024) separates workflows, where LLMs and tools are orchestrated "through predefined code paths", from agents, where LLMs direct their own processes and tool use. The basic building block is the "augmented LLM", which generates its own search queries. In the evaluator-optimizer pattern, an evaluator decides whether more searches are needed, and the post gives "complex search tasks that require multiple rounds of searching and analysis" as a fitting example [35]. In these terms IRCoT, FLARE, CRAG and Adaptive-RAG are workflows, and ReAct, Search-R1 and Claude Code are agents.

8. Reasoning models that search: Search-o1 and WebThinker

Long-chain reasoning models (o1, R1, QwQ) brought a new failure mode: knowledge gaps in the middle of a long chain of thought, which show up as hedging and uncertainty [27].

  • Search-o1 (Renmin University, EMNLP 2025) adds an agentic RAG step to the reasoning process. The model emits a search query whenever it hits uncertain knowledge. A Reason-in-Documents module then analyzes the retrieved documents and injects only a refined result back into the chain, to avoid flooding the trace with raw text. Inference is batched: all sequences generate together, search queries are detected and served in batches, and refined documents are spliced back in [27]. It was evaluated on GPQA, MATH500, AMC2023, AIME2024 and LiveCodeBench as well as open-domain QA [27].
  • WebThinker (NeurIPS 2025) adds a Deep Web Explorer that searches and navigates: it clicks links and buttons and follows deeper pages. It also adds a Think-Search-and-Draft mode with tools to draft a section, check the report and edit it, all within the model's thinking. Training uses online DPO on preference pairs built from trajectory correctness, tool usage and output quality [28].

The design point both share is compression at the boundary. Retrieved text is distilled by a separate step before it enters the reasoning context. CRAG's strip filtering and Anthropic's subagents, which "return only the summary" (Section 10), do the same thing at different layers.

9. RL-trained search agents

In 2025 the field moved from prompting a model to search toward training a search policy with outcome-based RL, in the DeepSeek-R1 style. The environment is a search engine. The reward is usually answer correctness alone.

9.1 Search-R1

Architecture. Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025) extends DeepSeek-R1(-Zero)-style RL with interleaved search calls. It is built on veRL and supports PPO, GRPO and REINFORCE, with BM25, dense (flat GPU or ANN CPU) and online search engines behind an HTTP retrieval server [21]. The base-model prompt is short [21]:

Answer the given question. You must conduct reasoning inside <think> and </think>
first every time you get new information. After reasoning, if you find you lack some
knowledge, you can call a search engine by <search> query </search> and it will return
the top searched results between <information> and </information>. You can search as
many times as your want. If you find no further external knowledge needed, you can
directly provide the answer inside <answer> and </answer> ...

Rollout and loss masking. During rollout, generation stops at </search>. The query goes to the retriever (top-3 passages in the published scripts), and the results are spliced back in as an <information> block. Generation then resumes, for up to max_turns rounds (4 in the v0.1 scripts) [21]. The important implementation detail is the information mask. The retrieved tokens appear in the context, but _info_masked_concatenate_with_padding masks them out of the policy-gradient loss. The model is not trained to generate retrieved text, only to reason around it [21].

  prompt | <think>..</think><search>q1</search> | <information>docs</information> | ...
         |<------- policy tokens: in loss ------>|<--- retrieved: masked, no grad ->|
  ... <think>..</think><answer>a</answer>   --> reward = EM(a, gold)  (outcome only)

Reward. Exact match on the final answer (compute_score_em), optionally with a format score. There is no process supervision of individual searches [21].

Results and ecosystem. In FlashRAG's reasoning-pipeline table, the Search-R1 Qwen2.5-7B PPO checkpoint scores 45.2 NQ EM, 54.5 HotpotQA F1 and 59.9 Bamboogle F1. The best non-RL loop method in that benchmark scores 41.5 HotpotQA F1, with a different (Llama3-8B) backbone, so the comparison is only indicative [17]. A follow-up empirical study by the same authors examines reward design, base versus instruct models and search engine choice for these agents [22]. By late 2025 Search-R1 was integrated into veRL, SkyRL and Thinking Machines' Tinker cookbook. The README lists more than 20 derived works, including ZeroSearch, AutoRefine, ParallelSearch, StepSearch and Tree-GRPO [21].

9.2 R1-Searcher and R1-Searcher++

R1-Searcher (Renmin University, March 2025) uses a two-stage outcome-supervised RL schedule with Reinforce++ [23]:

  • Stage 1 teaches the model to invoke search. A retrieve-reward of 0.5 is granted when the model searches and its output is well-formatted.
  • Stage 2 teaches the model to use search. The retrieval requirement is dropped, the answer reward is F1-based, and a format violation costs 2 points.

Training data comes from HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA, bucketed by difficulty according to how many Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct rollouts were needed to answer correctly (<10, 10-20, >20). It is trained against a local KILT Wikipedia index, yet the authors report that it generalizes to Bamboogle with online Google search [23]. Their insights include: outcome reward alone is enough; no SFT cold start is needed for a capable base model; and "LongCoT reasoning after RL is a more effective and efficient test time scaling method than existing tree-search based methods" [23]. R1-Searcher++ adds an SFT cold start, a reward for using internal knowledge when it suffices, and a memorization mechanism that absorbs retrieved facts into the model [24]. That reward is aimed directly at the over-retrieval habit of pure search agents.

9.3 ReSearch / ReCall and ZeroSearch

ReSearch, later renamed ReCall (Agent-RL, 2025), trains reasoning with tool calls via RL "without requiring any supervised data on tool use trajectories or reasoning steps". It generalizes from a search tool to arbitrary Python-defined tools run in a sandbox, trained on MuSiQue plus a synthetic tool-use set [25].

ZeroSearch (Alibaba-NLP, 2025) targets the cost of RL against real search APIs: every rollout fires many paid queries. It first fine-tunes an LLM into a simulated search engine that can return either relevant or deliberately noisy documents. A curriculum rollout then makes the simulated results gradually harder. The authors report that the policy "outperforms real search engine-based models while incurring zero API cost". They release 3B, 7B and 14B simulators and recommend the 14B for stable simulation [26].

9.4 Real-web RL: DeepResearcher, ASearcher, Tongyi DeepResearch, MiroThinker

System Org, year Environment Notable mechanism Reported results (self-reported)
DeepResearcher [29] GAIR-NLP, 2025 live web search end-to-end RL in real web environments up to +28.9 pts over prompt baselines, +7.2 over RAG-based RL agents
ASearcher [30] inclusionAI, 2025 live web fully asynchronous RL; LLM agent that synthesizes QA data >100 tool calls and >400k tokens per trajectory in training; Avg@4 58.7 GAIA, 51.1 xBench-DeepSearch, 74.5 Frames (ASearcher-Web-QwQ, 32B)
Tongyi DeepResearch [31] Alibaba-NLP, Sept 2025 web, Scholar, Python, file parsing agentic continual pre-training + SFT + on-policy GRPO variant; ReAct mode and IterResearch "Heavy" mode 30B-A3B MoE, 128K context
MiroThinker [32] MiroMind, 2025-26 web tools "interactive scaling" (more, deeper tool interactions as a third scaling axis) v1.0 (8B/30B/72B): 256K context, up to 600 tool calls, 47.1% BrowseComp; v1.7: 74.0% BrowseComp

Three engineering lessons recur in these reports:

  1. Trajectory length variance dominates RL systems cost. ASearcher found that long trajectories take dozens more turns, and up to two orders of magnitude more tokens, than short ones. In batch-synchronous RL every batch waits for its longest rollout. Decoupling generation from training removes that idle time and allows turn limits of 128 per trajectory [30].
  2. Data must be hard enough to need search. ASearcher's synthesis agent makes questions harder by fuzzing (obscuring key details) and context injection (adding retrieved facts). It then validates each question for quality, difficulty against a strong reasoning model, and answer uniqueness [30].
  3. Behaviours emerge from the reward. DeepResearcher reports plan formulation, cross-validation across sources, self-reflection, and "honesty when unable to find definitive answers" without these being explicitly supervised [29].

Leaderboard numbers on BrowseComp, GAIA and HLE come from each vendor's own harness, with different tool sets and budgets. Treat cross-system comparisons as approximate.

10. Multi-agent research: Anthropic's Research system

Architecture. Anthropic's Research feature (engineering post, June 2025) uses an orchestrator-worker design [33]:

                         user query
                             |
                  LeadResearcher (Opus 4) --- saves plan to memory
                 /           |            \
         subagent 1     subagent 2  ...  subagent N   (Sonnet 4, own context window,
         web search     web search       web search    3+ parallel tool calls each)
                 \           |            /
                  condensed findings only
                             |
           lead synthesizes; loops if more research is needed
                             |
              CitationAgent attributes claims to sources
                             |
                       final report

Numbers. On an internal research evaluation, Opus 4 as lead with Sonnet 4 subagents beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2%. On BrowseComp, token usage alone explained about 80% of the performance variance; tool-call count and model choice were the other two factors. Agents use about 4x the tokens of chat, and multi-agent systems about 15x. Running 3-5 subagents in parallel, each making 3 or more parallel tool calls, cut research time "by up to 90%" for complex queries [33].

Effort scaling in the prompts. The published lead-agent prompt encodes the scaling rules. A simple fact-finding query gets 1 subagent, a standard query 2-3, a medium one 3-5 and a high-complexity one 5-10, with "maximum 20". Each subagent sets a "research budget" of tool calls and must stay under 20 tool calls and about 100 sources [34]. This is Adaptive-RAG's idea of routing compute by complexity, expressed in natural language rather than as a trained classifier.

Search-strategy lessons. Start with short, broad queries, then narrow, because agents default to over-specific queries that return little [33]. Observed failure modes include spawning many subagents for simple queries, "endless searching for nonexistent sources", duplicated work from vague delegation, continuing to search after results were already sufficient, and preferring SEO content farms over authoritative sources [33]. Evaluation began with about 20 representative queries and an LLM judge scoring factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality and tool efficiency. It judged end states, not prescribed paths [33]. Operationally, agents resume from checkpoints, and rainbow deployments keep long-running agents on their original version [33].

Open implementations follow the same pattern. LangChain's open_deep_research reported an overall score of 0.4344 (rank 6) on the Deep Research Bench leaderboard in August 2025 [43]. Jina's node-DeepResearch reduces the loop to "keep searching, reading webpages, reasoning until an answer is found (or the token budget is exceeded)". It deliberately targets concise answers, not long reports [42].

11. Agentic search vs. indexing: Claude Code and the grep debate

11.1 Claude Code's design

Problem. A codebase changes on every edit. A pre-built embedding index of it is stale by construction. It needs an ingestion pipeline, has to respect .gitignore and permissions, and returns chunks that cut across the units a programmer cares about (functions, call sites).

Approach. Claude Code runs an agentic loop with three phases (gather context, take action, verify results) that "blend together" [37]. Context gathering is plain tool use:

  • Search tools. Grep is built on ripgrep, uses ripgrep regex syntax and respects .gitignore. Glob finds files by name pattern [38]. On macOS, Linux and WSL these two tools are now left out of the default tool set. Claude instead runs find and grep through the Bash tool, which inside Claude's shell are embedded versions of bfs and ugrep [38]. Reading is done with Read (oversized files must be read in ranges or searched) or with cat/head/tail/sed -n [38].
  • Up-front context. CLAUDE.md project instructions and the first 200 lines (or 25 KB) of auto-memory load at session start [37].
  • Code intelligence (optional). Plugins add jump-to-definition, find-references and type errors through language servers [37].
  • Explore subagent. A built-in read-only subagent (Write and Edit denied) for "file discovery, code search, codebase exploration". It is called with a thoroughness level (quick, medium or very thorough) and returns only a summary, which "keeps exploration results out of your main conversation context" [39].

Anthropic's context-engineering post (September 2025) states the rationale. Many AI applications use "embedding-based pre-inference time retrieval". Agents increasingly use "just in time" retrieval instead: they keep lightweight references (file paths, stored queries, links) and load data at runtime with tools, relying on folder hierarchy, naming conventions and timestamps as relevance signals ("progressive disclosure"). Claude Code is described as a hybrid: CLAUDE.md is loaded up front, and glob and grep retrieve just in time, which avoids "stale indexing and complex syntax trees" [36].

  INDEX-FIRST (classic code RAG)          AGENTIC SEARCH (Claude Code)
  repo --chunk--> embed --> vector DB      repo (live filesystem, always current)
          (re-index on change)                    ^          ^          ^
  query --embed--> top-k chunks             grep/rg     find/glob    read ranges
          |                                       \          |          /
          v                                    model plans next probe from results
  LLM answers from k chunks                         (loop; subagent may summarize)
  + 1 round-trip, cheap                     + exact, fresh, no ingestion pipeline
  - stale, chunk boundaries, recall cap     - more tokens, more turns, slower

The same post lists the costs honestly. Runtime exploration "is slower than retrieving pre-computed data". It needs deliberate tool design. Without guidance, agents waste context by misusing tools or chasing dead ends [36]. Anthropic recommends hybrids for less dynamic domains such as legal or finance, and expects designs to rely less on human curation as models improve [36]. The same just-in-time principle applies to tools: Claude Code defers MCP tool definitions and loads them on demand through tool search [37].

11.2 The counter-evidence: semantic search as an added tool

Vector-search vendors have measured the cost side. Zilliz's claude-context is an MCP server that adds hybrid (BM25 + dense) code search, with AST-based chunking and Merkle-tree incremental re-indexing [40]. In its controlled evaluation, a LangGraph ReAct agent on 30 SWE-bench Verified instances (2-file fixes, 15-60 minute difficulty) with GPT-4o-mini, 3 runs per arm, the results were [40]:

Metric grep-only agent + claude-context MCP Change
Retrieval F1 (file localization) 0.40 0.40 none
Tokens per instance 73,373 44,449 -39.4%
Tool calls per instance 8.3 5.3 -36.3%

Retrieval quality was the same. The index saved tokens and turns. This is consistent with Anthropic's own statement that agentic search trades speed and tokens for freshness and simplicity. It is a vendor benchmark with a small model and a small sample. Serena takes a third route: symbol-level retrieval and editing through LSP language servers (40+ languages), or a JetBrains plugin. It aims to replace "fragile text surgery" with reference-aware navigation [41].

Reading the debate. The evidence points to a layered design, not a winner:

  • grep/find is exact and fresh. It is ideal for identifiers, error strings and config keys, and it needs no infrastructure.
  • Embeddings help with conceptual queries ("where do we handle auth?") and lower token cost on very large repositories.
  • LSP gives structural answers (definitions, references) that neither text method gives reliably.
  • Subagents with summaries bound the context cost of whichever method is used [39].

12. Head-to-head under one harness

Most papers in this chapter use different models, corpora and metrics. FlashRAG re-ran many of them with one generator (Llama3-8B-Instruct, 2048 input tokens), one retriever (e5-base-v2, 5 documents) and one prompt [17]. A subset:

Method Type NQ EM TriviaQA EM HotpotQA F1 2Wiki F1 PopQA F1
Naive generation sequential 22.6 55.7 28.4 33.9 21.7
Standard RAG sequential 35.1 58.9 35.3 21.0 36.7
Adaptive-RAG conditional 35.1 56.6 39.1 28.4 40.4
Self-RAG (selfrag-llama2-7B) loop 36.4 38.2 29.6 25.1 32.7
FLARE loop 22.5 55.8 28.0 33.9 20.7
ITER-RETGEN loop 36.8 60.1 38.3 21.6 37.9
IRCoT loop 33.3 56.9 41.5 32.4 45.6

And from FlashRAG's "reasoning pipeline" table, which uses each method's released checkpoint (PopQA reported as EM here) [17]:

Method (checkpoint) NQ EM HotpotQA F1 2Wiki F1 MuSiQue F1 Bamboogle F1
Search-R1 (Qwen2.5-7B, PPO) 45.2 54.5 42.6 29.2 59.9
R1-Searcher (Qwen2.5-7B base) 36.9 49.0 49.1 24.7 57.7
CoRAG (Llama3.1-8B) 40.9 56.6 60.7 31.9 54.1
ReaRAG (9B) 26.3 42.9 41.6 21.2 41.9

What the numbers say:

  1. On single-hop QA (NQ, TriviaQA), iteration adds little over standard RAG. The gains are concentrated in multi-hop sets.
  2. Prompted loops (IRCoT) beat trained-controller designs from 2023 (Self-RAG) on a newer base model. RL-trained 7-8B search policies beat both by about 13 HotpotQA F1 points. The backbones differ, so this is indicative only.
  3. FLARE's trigger and Self-RAG's tokens did not transfer cleanly to a new setup. Methods whose control signal depends on model-internal calibration are the most fragile to swap.

13. Master comparison

Design Year Who controls the loop Trigger / stop signal Training required Retrieval calls per query Main failure mode
Self-Ask [13] 2022-23 prompt follow-up questions none one per sub-question decomposition errors
DSP [14] 2022 program fixed hops bootstrapped demos fixed hops program/task mismatch
IRCoT [7] 2023 program each CoT sentence; "answer is" none one per reasoning step bridge-entity error compounding
FLARE [5] 2023 program + log-probs low-confidence token none 0 to one per sentence threshold calibration; needs log-probs
DRAGIN [16] 2024 program + attention RIND uncertainty score none variable white-box model access
Self-RAG [1] 2023-24 fine-tuned LM Retrieve token, threshold critic + generator SFT 0 to one per segment, K parallel tied to base model; cost variance
CRAG [3] 2024 evaluator + rules T5 confidence, 2 thresholds T5 evaluator 1 + optional web search evaluator domain shift; web trust
Adaptive-RAG [9] 2024 classifier complexity class A/B/C T5 classifier (auto labels) 0, 1 or IRCoT misrouted complex queries
ReAct [11] 2022-23 LLM policy (prompted) model emits finish none open-ended loops, premature finish
Search-o1 [27] 2025 reasoning model model emits search tags none open-ended noisy docs in long CoT (mitigated)
Search-R1 / R1-Searcher [21][23] 2025 RL-trained policy learned; max turns outcome RL few (4-turn cap in Search-R1 v0.1 scripts) reward hacking on EM; over-search
ASearcher / MiroThinker [30][32] 2025-26 RL-trained policy learned; up to 100s of turns large-scale async RL tens to hundreds cost; benchmark-specific harnesses
Anthropic Research [33] 2025 lead LLM + subagents evaluator judgment; budgets none (prompted) many, in parallel 15x tokens; over-spawning
Claude Code agentic search [36][37] 2025-26 LLM agent task completion none open-ended grep/read token cost; dead-end exploration

14. Cross-cutting failure modes

  • Over-retrieval. Agents search when parametric knowledge would do, and keep searching after the evidence is sufficient. Anthropic lists both [33]. R1-Searcher++ adds an internal-knowledge reward for this reason [24], and Adaptive-RAG routes simple queries away from retrieval [9].
  • Under-retrieval. Confidence triggers (FLARE) and learned Retrieve tokens (Self-RAG) can fire too rarely when moved to a new model [17].
  • Error compounding across hops. A wrong intermediate entity poisons later queries (IRCoT, ReAct). Verifiers (CRAG, ISSUP) and cross-source validation (DeepResearcher's emergent behaviour) are the main defences [3][29].
  • Context pollution. Raw retrieved text accumulates in long loops. Search-o1's Reason-in-Documents step, CRAG's strip filtering and subagent summaries all compress at the boundary [3][27][39].
  • Source quality. Web fallbacks bring in SEO content. CRAG prefers Wikipedia [3], and Anthropic had to steer its agents toward authoritative sources [33].
  • Silent recall loss in the substrate. Incomplete indexes degrade results subtly because the model fills gaps from memory [16].
  • Non-determinism and evaluation. Agents take different valid paths. Evaluate end states with rubric-based LLM judges, not step sequences, and start with a small set of real queries [33].
  • Cost and latency. Every loop iteration adds a sequential LLM call plus a search. Multi-agent research uses about 15x chat tokens [33]. Parallel subagents and parallel tool calls are the main latency lever [33].

Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Gate iteration by need. Use a complexity router (a trained classifier as in Adaptive-RAG, or effort rules in the prompt as in Anthropic's lead agent) so that simple queries take the single-shot path. Iteration pays off on multi-hop queries and is mostly overhead on single-hop ones [9][17][34].
  2. Prefer explicit, inspectable graders over model-internal calibration. CRAG's small trained evaluator beat prompted ChatGPT at judging retrieval (84.3% vs at most 64.7%), and it survives a generator swap. Log-prob thresholds and fine-tuned reflection tokens have to be recalibrated when the model changes [3][17].
  3. Have a fallback when retrieval fails. "Retrieval was bad" should be a detectable state with an action attached: rewrite and re-search, switch corpus (web), or abstain. Do not generate from irrelevant context [3][19].
  4. Use the chain of thought as the query generator for multi-hop. IRCoT-style "reason one step, retrieve on that step" remains a strong prompt-only baseline. Cap the number of steps and verify the bridge entities [7][17].
  5. Compress at the boundary. Whether through strip filtering, Reason-in-Documents or subagents that return summaries, keep raw retrieved text out of the main reasoning context [3][27][39].
  6. RL-trained search policies are now the accuracy frontier for open models. The recipe is simple: tags for think/search/answer, a retrieval server, outcome reward, and masking of retrieved tokens from the loss. Budget for rollout cost (ZeroSearch's simulator, asynchronous RL) and for hard, verified training questions [21][26][30].
  7. For live, exact corpora such as code, start with agentic search and add an index only if measurements justify it. grep/find plus subagents avoids staleness and ingestion infrastructure. Add hybrid semantic search or LSP tools when token cost or conceptual queries dominate. Measured savings are about 40% of tokens at equal retrieval quality in one vendor study [36][38][40][41].
  8. Spend tokens deliberately. In Anthropic's BrowseComp analysis, token budget explained about 80% of performance variance. Multi-agent parallelism buys quality and wall-clock time at about 15x chat cost, so reserve it for tasks worth that much [33].
  9. Benchmark under one harness before choosing. Published gains often disappear when methods are re-run with a common model and retriever. FLARE matched naive generation and Self-RAG fell below it on TriviaQA in FlashRAG's re-implementation [17].
