14. Answer Engines and Web-Grounded LLMs: Perplexity, Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, Bing/Copilot, ChatGPT Search, Search APIs for Agents, Deep Research and Citation Systems

Overview

An answer engine is RAG with the open web as its corpus. The user asks a question. The system decides whether to search, writes one or more queries, retrieves pages from a web index, extracts the useful spans, and writes an answer that cites them. The same loop underlies Perplexity, Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode, Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT search, Claude's web search, and the "deep research" agents that run that loop for minutes instead of seconds.

The pipeline looks like the enterprise RAG of earlier chapters, but five things make web grounding a different engineering problem.

  1. Someone else usually owns the index. Only a few companies crawl and rank the web themselves: Google, Microsoft (Bing), and a handful of independent indexes. Everyone else rents retrieval through an API. The API's ranking, snippet length and freshness then set the quality ceiling, and its licence terms decide what you may cache, show or train on [10][11].
  2. The corpus is adversarial. Web pages are written to rank. Content farms, SEO pages, satire, forum jokes and pages optimized for generative engines all end up in the retrieved set [6][17][42].
  3. The corpus changes under you. A correct answer last week can be wrong today. Fresh facts are the main reason to search at all [3][36].
  4. Attribution is part of the product, and sometimes a legal duty. Citations let users check the answer. They also send traffic back to publishers. Some providers make showing them a licence condition [9][10].
  5. The latency budget varies 1,000x. An AI Overview has to appear on a results page. A deep research report may take tens of minutes [29][30][22].

This chapter is organized around those constraints. Section 1 traces the research lineage (WebGPT, GopherCite, FreshLLMs, and the first audits of generative search engines). Section 2 gives a reference architecture. Sections 3 to 5 cover the deployed systems: search-engine owners (Bing/Copilot, Google), answer-engine natives (Perplexity, You.com, open-source clones) and chat assistants with a search tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini API). Section 6 compares the search APIs built for agents: Perplexity Search, Exa, Tavily, Brave, Grounding with Bing and You.com. Section 7 covers deep research agents. Section 8 is about citation systems: how they are built, how they are measured, and how they fail. Section 9 covers evaluation. Chapter 08 covers agentic and RL-trained search loops in general. Chapter 11 covers citation metrics such as ALCE in more depth.

A note on sources. Most claims in this chapter were checked against primary sources retrieved while writing it: vendor documentation, SDK source code, official GitHub repositories, engineering blogs and technical reports. Network restrictions blocked some vendor blogs, for example Google's Search blog, the OpenAI and Perplexity websites, and the Bing blog. Reference entries marked with a dagger (†) could not be re-fetched for this edition. The claims attributed to them describe those published documents as they were originally announced. They are kept few, and they are worth re-checking before anyone quotes them.

                    THE ANSWER-ENGINE DESIGN SPACE
  latency      ~1 s            ~5-30 s                 minutes to tens of minutes
              |----------------|-----------------------|-------------------------|
  pattern     single-shot      agentic search          deep research
              grounding        (search inside the      (plan, fan out, read
              (1 query,        reasoning loop,         hundreds of pages,
              top results)     a few to ~10 calls)     write a cited report)
  examples    AI Overviews,    ChatGPT search,         OpenAI / Gemini / Claude
              Bing grounding,  Claude web search,      Research, Perplexity
              Sonar-style      AI Mode, Perplexity     deep research, Exa /
              answers          Pro search              Parallel / Tavily research

1. Lineage: from WebGPT to verifiability audits

WebGPT (OpenAI, 2021). WebGPT fine-tuned GPT-3 to use a text-based browser. Its actions were commands such as search, click, scroll and quote. Quoting saved a passage as a reference to cite in the final answer. Training used behaviour cloning on human demonstrations, then a reward model trained on human comparisons, combined with rejection sampling (best-of-n). On ELI5 questions, WebGPT answers were preferred to the human demonstrators' answers 56% of the time [1†]. WebGPT set three conventions that answer engines still follow: the model drives the search, evidence is collected as quotes, and the answer must cite them.

GopherCite (DeepMind, 2022). GopherCite trained a model to support each answer with a verbatim quote from a retrieved page ("self-supported question answering"). Training used reinforcement learning from human preferences, and the model was allowed to abstain when unsure [2†]. Two of its ideas recur in production citation systems in Section 8: verbatim quotes as a verifiable unit of evidence, and declining to answer when evidence is weak.

FreshLLMs / FreshPrompt (Google and collaborators, 2023). FreshLLMs introduced FreshQA, a question set built around fast-changing and false-premise questions. It also introduced FreshPrompt, which puts search-engine results, including snippets and answer boxes, into the prompt in date order [3]. The maintainers still update FreshQA weekly or on request, with dated snapshots through April 2026. They report that Google's Gemini, Perplexity's online LLMs and You.com used the data or method. The follow-up benchmark, SealQA, focuses more on reasoning over noisy search results [3].

Auditing generative search engines (Stanford, 2023). Liu, Zhang and Liang audited four commercial generative search engines of early 2023. On average, only about half of the generated sentences were fully supported by their citations (51.5%), and about a quarter of the citations did not support the sentence they were attached to (74.5% citation precision) [4†]. The released dataset has 8,834 / 1,106 / 1,097 train/dev/test verifiability judgments. Each judgment labels a (statement, cited page) pair as complete, partial or no support. Annotators also marked the minimal supporting evidence [4]. The paper's text-extraction pipeline is a reusable recipe: save the page with SingleFile, apply Chrome's DOM Distiller ("reader mode"), then run Trafilatura [4]. ALCE (Princeton, 2023) turned the same concern into a benchmark with citation recall and precision. The best models of the time still lacked complete citation support on about half of ELI5 answers [5†]. Chapter 11 covers ALCE in depth.

Generative Engine Optimization (GEO, 2023). Aggarwal et al. reversed the question and asked how content creators can increase their visibility inside generative answers. They found that page-side rewrites can raise a source's visibility in answers by up to 40% [6]. Any answer engine therefore has to treat "content written for LLMs" as a new kind of SEO pressure.

2. Reference architecture

The deployed systems below differ in detail, but they share one pipeline. Every stage is documented by at least one vendor.

 user query (+ conversation, location, locale)
      |
      v
 [1] TRIGGER / CLASSIFY ---- no search needed --> answer from parametric knowledge
      |  (is the answer current? niche? risky?)
      v
 [2] QUERY GENERATION: rewrite to standalone; generate 1..N queries ("fan-out")
      |
      v
 [3] RETRIEVAL: own index | search API | SERP provider     (filters: domain, recency,
      |                                                     locale, safe-search)
      v
 [4] CONTENT EXTRACTION: snippet | query-biased highlights | full page | PDF | live crawl
      |
      v
 [5] CONTEXT ASSEMBLY under a token budget (dedupe, per-URL caps, threshold filtering,
      |   code-based filtering)
      |
      +--> [6] AGENTIC LOOP? read results -> reflect on gaps -> new queries -> [3]
      v
 [7] GENERATION with inline citations (markers, spans, or post-hoc citation pass)
      |
      v
 [8] CITATION RENDERING + compliance (show sources, show queries, provider widgets)

[1] Triggering. Searching costs latency and money, so systems decide first whether to search. Anthropic documents its policy. Claude searches for recent events, current prices, facts about organizations, people or products that may have changed, and explicit requests to look something up. It answers directly for stable knowledge, creative writing, analysis of content already in the conversation, and greetings. Developers can steer this through the system prompt and cap it with max_uses [36]. The Gemini API has a dynamic-retrieval configuration with a mode and a numeric dynamic_threshold, which lets a predictor decide when to ground [20]. The open-source Vane (formerly Perplexica) starts every turn with a classification step. That step decides whether to research, whether to show widgets, and how to rewrite the question into a standalone form [52].

[2] Query generation. The search query is rarely the user's text. Microsoft documents this for Microsoft 365 Copilot. Copilot parses the prompt, picks out the terms where web data would help, and generates "a few words" as a Bing query. It sends no user or tenant identifiers and does not send the whole of any attached document [8]. Google's AI Mode issues many related queries at once across subtopics, a technique it calls query fan-out (Section 3.2) [18†].

[3] Retrieval. Section 6 compares the retrieval APIs. The basic choice is between your own index, a third-party index with its own ranking (Bing, Brave, Exa, Perplexity), and scraped results pages. Perplexity's evaluation repository calls the Tavily integration a "representative Google SERP scraping-based API" and notes that Google and Bing do not offer first-party web search APIs [26].

[4]-[5] Extraction and context assembly. This is where the "10 blue links" of classic search turns into evidence an LLM can use. Search APIs increasingly do this step on the server and accept a token budget. Examples are Brave's maximum_number_of_tokens (1,024-32,768), Perplexity's max_tokens_per_page, Exa's relevance-sized highlights and Tavily's chunks_per_source (Section 6). Anthropic's tool versions from 2026 go further. Claude writes and runs code that filters search or fetch results before they enter the context window ("dynamic filtering") [36][37].

[6] The loop. Microsoft's Azure documentation of the OpenAI web_search tool describes three modes. They map onto the latency bands in the overview diagram [12]:

Mode Behaviour Typical use
Web search without reasoning Query is forwarded to the search tool; top-ranked sources ground the answer; no multi-step planning fast lookups, timely facts
Agentic search with reasoning models Model searches inside its chain of thought, analyses results, decides whether to keep searching complex questions; slower
Deep research Multi-step reasoning, opens and reads many pages, synthesizes a citation-rich report; runs for minutes background workloads

[7]-[8] Citation. Section 8 covers this stage.

3. Search-engine-owned answer layers

3.1 Bing and Microsoft Copilot

Prometheus (2023). The new Bing launched in February 2023. Microsoft described a proprietary system called Prometheus that combined Bing's index, ranking and answers with an OpenAI GPT model. A component called the Bing Orchestrator generated internal search queries iteratively, so that answers were grounded in fresh results and cited them. Microsoft also reported that applying the same model to Bing's core ranking gave the largest relevance improvement in two decades [7†]. In architectural terms, the search engine became a tool that a planner LLM calls repeatedly, and the LLM became a component of the search engine's ranking stack.

LLM relevance labels. Bing's evaluation side changed as well. Microsoft researchers reported that an LLM, chosen and prompted to agree with careful feedback from real searchers, can produce relevance labels at scale "as accurate as human labellers". They also found that its accuracy changes unpredictably with simple paraphrases of the prompt, so high-quality gold labels remain necessary [14]. Chapter 11 discusses UMBRELA, an open-source reproduction of Bing's relevance assessor.

Microsoft 365 Copilot web grounding: queries as citations. Microsoft's privacy documentation is the most detailed public description of how an enterprise assistant mixes private and web data [8]:

  • Copilot derives a short query from the prompt. The query can be informed by an open document, such as a Word file the user is editing, but the document itself is never sent. In Microsoft's example, the prompt "summarize [internal strategy doc] and tell me if Fabrikam announced a similar approach" becomes the query "Fabrikam clean energy policy announcements".
  • Some prompts generate no web query at all. "Find the document [coworker] wrote last week" is answered entirely from Microsoft 365 data.
  • The exact queries sent to Bing are shown to the user as web search query citations next to the site citations. They stay visible in the thread for 24 hours, and admins can search, audit and run eDiscovery on them.
  • Queries are sent without user or tenant identifiers. Microsoft commits that they are not used to improve Bing or to train foundation models.

Showing the generated query is a cheap transparency measure that other systems rarely offer. It lets a user see at once why the answer drifted.

Grounding with Bing for developers. Microsoft licenses Bing to developers only as a grounding tool inside Azure AI Foundry. Its documentation describes four steps: query formulation, search execution, information synthesis and source attribution [9]. The design rules are unusually strict:

  • Only the generated query, tool parameters and the resource key go to Bing [9][13].
  • "Developers and end users don't have access to raw content returned from Grounding with Bing Search." The model sees the results. The application gets only the model's answer, with citations and a link to the Bing query [9].
  • Both kinds of reference must be "retained and displayed in the exact form provided by Microsoft". The documentation advises using the citation annotations the tool returns and not asking the model to generate citation links [9][10].
  • The terms forbid training any AI model on Bing output. They forbid caching or storing output except as an integrated part of the customer's own work product, and they forbid building a database or index from it. They also restrict use to "internet search experiences" that visibly indicate web results [10].
  • Price at the time of writing: $14 per 1,000 transactions, with a limit of 150 transactions per second and 1 million transactions per day, for both standard and Custom Search [11]. Custom Search restricts grounding to configured domains and can block others [9].

OpenAI's web_search tool on Azure runs on the same Grounding with Bing service, and its charges follow the number of Bing requests [12].

3.2 Google: AI Overviews, AI Mode and Deep Search

Models trained to call Search. The Gemini 2.5 technical report states the design intent directly. Gemini 2.0 was "our first model family trained to natively call tools like Google Search", so the model could write precise queries and combine fresh information with sources. Gemini 2.5 interleaves search with its internal reasoning to answer multi-hop queries: it issues follow-up queries both to widen the information it has and to check the answer's factual accuracy [15]. The report links the factuality work to the deployment of AI Overviews and AI Mode. It states that Gemini models power AI Overviews for over 1.5 billion monthly active users. It reports SimpleQA (parametric factuality, no search) of 54.0% for Gemini 2.5 Pro, against 24.9% for Gemini 1.5 Pro, and FACTS Grounding (faithfulness to supplied documents) of 87.8% [15].

AI Overviews (2024) and the "glue on pizza" lesson. AI Overviews launched broadly in the US in May 2024. They used a Gemini model customized for Search and placed a generated summary with links above the results [16†]. Within days, screenshots spread of answers that recommended adding glue to pizza or eating rocks. Google's post-mortem named three root causes [17†]:

  • Data voids. Nonsensical questions had no good answer on the web, so the system grounded on the little content that existed, which was often satire.
  • Satirical and humorous content taken literally.
  • User-generated forum content offering misleading advice.

Google's fixes acted on triggering and source selection rather than generation: better detection of nonsensical queries, limits on satire and user-generated content, and no overviews where they did not help. It also reported that content-policy violations occurred on fewer than one in every 7 million unique queries [17†]. The general lesson for designers is that grounding passes source quality straight through to the answer. A model that faithfully summarizes a joke is grounded and wrong.

AI Mode and query fan-out (2025). AI Mode was introduced in March 2025, first on a custom Gemini 2.0. It uses query fan-out: the system issues multiple related searches at once, across subtopics and several data sources, and combines the results into one answer [18†]. In May 2025 Google added Deep Search, an AI Mode option that can issue hundreds of searches and produce a fully cited report in minutes [19†].

   "best e-bike for a steep 10 km commute in the rain, under $2k"
                                |
                     Gemini (custom for Search)
                     decomposes the information need
        +-----------+-----------+-----------+------------+-------------+
        v           v           v           v            v             v
   "e-bike hill  "waterproof "e-bike     "e-bike      shopping      reviews /
    torque"       rating      range 10km  under 2000"  graph /       forums
                  IPX"        hills"                   prices        (filtered)
        +-----------+-----------+-----+-----+------------+-------------+
                                      v
                 merge, dedupe, rank evidence; reason over gaps
                                      v
               answer with inline links  (Deep Search: same pattern,
                                          hundreds of queries, a report)

Gemini API grounding: the developer view of the same machinery. The Gemini API exposes Google Search, Google Maps, URL context and YouTube grounding as tools [21]. The SDK's GroundingMetadata type shows how Google represents attribution [20]:

  • web_search_queries: the queries the model actually issued.
  • grounding_chunks: the retrieved sources, such as web URIs and titles.
  • grounding_supports: for each segment of the answer text, a list of grounding_chunk_indices with matching confidence_scores between 0 and 1. This is a claim-to-evidence alignment with a confidence per link.
  • search_entry_point.rendered_content: an HTML snippet of Google Search suggestions that applications embed next to the answer. Google's own cookbook renders it [20][21].

The cookbook's Maps-grounding section states that "all grounded outputs require sources to be displayed after the response text" [21]. Like Bing, Google ties attribution to the licence.

Lessons from the search-engine owners. (1) Owning the index lets you treat retrieval as a fan-out primitive: dozens to hundreds of internal queries per answer, which renting would make uneconomic. (2) Failures cluster where retrieval is thin or adversarial, not where the model is weak. (3) Both owners make attribution a licence condition for third-party developers.

4. Answer-engine natives

4.1 Perplexity

Perplexity built its product around the answer engine: the answer comes first and the sources sit next to it. Its public developer surface shows how the architecture has changed.

From Sonar to an agent API. Perplexity's cookbook says the Agent API is "the new primary API for building hosted agents with native web access, citations, code execution, subagents, and durable, long-running work". The older Sonar chat-completions API is deprecated [24]. In the official Python SDK, a request to the Agent API names either a preset (for example sonar-pro or sonar-reasoning: a model with its system prompt and search parameters already set) or a model in provider/model form. A models fallback chain of up to five models is tried in order. max_steps caps the research loop at 100 steps. Built-in tools include web_search, fetch_url, finance_search, people_search, and a sandbox with file read, write, grep and glob tools [25]. Perplexity has therefore moved from "one search, one answer" towards a hosted, model-agnostic agent runtime with its own search underneath.

The Search API. Perplexity sells its index directly. Requests accept one query or a list of queries, max_results, total and per-page token budgets (max_tokens, max_tokens_per_page), and a search_context_size of low, medium or high (default high; larger sizes return more page content per result at higher cost). They also accept recency filters (hour to year), date filters on publication and last update, domain and language filters, a search_mode of web, academic or SEC filings, and a search_type of web or people [25]. Each result carries title, url, snippet, date and last_updated [25]. The last-updated field matters: it lets the downstream model reason about staleness.

Index architecture. Perplexity Research described the system behind this API in "Architecting and Evaluating an AI-First Search API" (September 2025). The article is linked from the evaluation repository [26][27†]. As announced, the design centres on retrieval units smaller than a document, so that the API returns the most relevant spans of a page rather than whole pages. It combines lexical and semantic retrieval and ranks in several stages under tight latency targets [27†]. Treat these descriptions as approximate. Precise scale and latency figures should come from the article itself.

search_evals: an open harness, run by a vendor. Perplexity released search_evals, an MIT-licensed framework that plugs different search APIs into identical agent harnesses [26]. Its history is a small case study in how such comparisons change over time:

Version (date) What is compared Example result
v1 (Sep 2025) 4 search APIs, one agent (single-step for SimpleQA/FRAMES, deep research for BrowseComp/HLE) SimpleQA: Perplexity 0.930, SERP-via-Tavily 0.890, Brave 0.822, Exa 0.781
Feb 2026 5 engine configs x 3 models (Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5 medium) x 7 suites BrowseComp with Opus 4.5: 0.116-0.207 across engines; with GPT-5 medium: 0.332-0.413
v0.2 (Jun 2026) whole hosted research agents (Perplexity Agent API, OpenAI Responses, Anthropic Managed Agents, Exa Agent API, Parallel Task API) BrowseComp: Perplexity 0.805, OpenAI 0.720, Anthropic 0.598, Parallel 0.56, Exa 0.38

Three readings follow from the published configuration files.

  • The model can matter more than the index. In February 2026 the BrowseComp spread between models on the same engine (for Brave, 0.207 with Opus 4.5 against 0.413 with GPT-5 medium) was larger than the spread between engines for one model [26].
  • Configuration is part of the result. The harness gave Perplexity 3,000 tokens per query (3,000 per page). A perplexity-long variant used 10,000 tokens (4,000 per page) and scored best on most suites. Tavily ran at search_depth="basic", chosen in the code comment because it "provides sub-1s latency". Exa ran in fast mode with highlights of a few sentences per URL. Brave combined descriptions with extra_snippets [26]. A search API benchmark partly measures how many evidence tokens each engine was allowed to return.
  • The unit of comparison moved up a level. By mid-2026 the harness compared whole hosted research agents. The agents themselves were partly configurable: the Perplexity agent ran openai/gpt-5.5, the OpenAI agent ran gpt-5.5 at high reasoning effort with up to 100 tool calls, and the Anthropic agent ran Claude Opus 4.7 on Managed Agents [26]. The question changed from "which index?" to "which search-plus-agent stack?".

All three tables come from a vendor-run harness. They are useful because the code, prompts and graders are public, so others can rerun them. They are not neutral.

4.2 You.com

You.com was an early consumer answer engine. Today it presents itself to developers as a hosted MCP server. The default tools are you-search, you-contents (page content), you-balance and you-discover. you-finance and you-research are available on request, and a keyless free profile exposes search and discovery [51]. The FreshLLMs authors list You.com among the systems that used their method or data [3]. Few architectural details are public.

4.3 Open-source answer engines

Open implementations show the minimal viable architecture without vendor abstractions.

Vane (formerly Perplexica) is a self-hostable answer engine [52]. Each turn works in three phases:

  1. A classification step decides whether to research, whether to show widgets (weather, stocks, calculations), and how to rewrite the question into a standalone form.
  2. Research and widgets run in parallel. Research uses a SearxNG meta-search backend and, optionally, embedding search over uploaded files.
  3. The chat model writes the answer.

Citations are produced by prompting: "We prompt the model to cite the references it used", and the UI renders them next to the links. Widget output serves as context but is explicitly not citable. Users choose a speed, balanced or quality mode [52].

Google's Gemini LangGraph quickstart is a reference deep-research loop. It generates initial queries, runs web research for each through Gemini with Google Search, reflects on whether there are knowledge gaps, generates follow-up queries, repeats up to a configured maximum number of loops, and then writes an answer with citations [23].

WikiChat (Stanford) grounds on Wikipedia, not the open web. Its 7-stage pipeline, where each stage is one or more LLM calls, includes extracting claims from a draft so they can be checked against retrieved evidence. A later version merges the generate and claim-extraction stages to cut cost [53]. It shows a verify-then-answer design: claims are extracted and checked before the final answer is written, which the single-pass designs above do not do.

OpenDeepSearch (Sentient) packages search as a tool for agents and offers two modes. Default mode uses SERP results with minimal processing for single-hop questions. Pro mode scrapes pages (via Crawl4AI), reranks them semantically, and post-processes the results for multi-hop questions. The authors report parity with closed search alternatives on SimpleQA and better results on FRAMES [54]. The same two tiers appear in commercial APIs (Section 6).

5. Chat assistants with a search tool

5.1 ChatGPT search and OpenAI's web_search tool

ChatGPT search (October 2024). As announced, the search model was a fine-tuned GPT-4o, post-trained with synthetic data generation techniques that included distilling outputs from o1-preview. It drew on third-party search providers and on content from news partners [28†]. This is another way to make a model good at search: rather than training it end to end with a search tool, as Google describes for Gemini [15], distil search-and-cite behaviour from a stronger reasoning model.

The API tool. The Responses API web_search tool, documented in detail through its Azure deployment, shows the mechanics [12]:

  • A web_search_call output item records actions of type search, open_page and find_in_page. This is a modern form of WebGPT's command set [1†][12]. The last two are available only with reasoning models.
  • Citations are url_citation annotations on the output text. Each carries the URL, title and character range it supports, so the client can render inline links without parsing markup.
  • include: ["web_search_call.action.sources"] returns every URL consulted, not only the ones cited. This separates "read" from "relied on".
  • Domain allow-lists take up to 100 entries and include subdomains. The external_web_access parameter separates live fetching from cached content. Azure always treats it as false and notes that "the model can still access cached content" [12].

5.2 Claude: web search, web fetch and citations as server tools

Anthropic released web search in Claude.ai in March 2025, on the API in May 2025, and added a web fetch tool in September 2025 [34][35]. Both are server tools. Anthropic's API runs the search loop inside a single request, and the model may search several times, "using earlier results to inform subsequent queries" [35][36]. Several design details stand out [36][37]:

  • Effort is visible and capped. Anthropic's documentation says simple factual queries typically need 1-3 searches, while comparative or multi-entity research can need 10 or more. max_uses is a hard cap. Exceeding it returns a max_uses_exceeded error inside a successful (HTTP 200) response, so the model can recover and still answer.
  • Encrypted provenance. Each search result carries encrypted_content, and each citation carries an encrypted_index. Both must be passed back unchanged in later turns, and the API rejects modified values. The client cannot forge or edit the evidence behind a multi-turn conversation.
  • Cheap quotes. A web citation includes up to 150 characters of cited_text. cited_text, title and url do not count as input or output tokens.
  • Dynamic filtering (2026). From tool version web_search_20260209, search runs by default from inside code execution. Claude writes code that filters results before they enter the context window, which reduces token use on search-heavy requests. response_inclusion: "excluded" further drops the raw result blocks from the API response [36]. Web fetch gained the same filtering, plus a max_content_tokens truncation limit and use_cache: false for fresh content [37].
  • Exfiltration guard. Web fetch can only retrieve URLs that already appeared in the conversation: in user messages, in client tool results, or in earlier search or fetch results. It cannot fetch URLs that appear only in Claude's own output, or URLs that seem to contain credentials. This blocks a common prompt-injection pattern in which a malicious page instructs the model to encode private data into a URL and fetch it. Web fetch does not render JavaScript [37].
  • Price. $10 per 1,000 searches plus tokens. Failed searches are not billed [35][36].

5.3 Gemini app and API

Section 3.2 covers the Gemini API's grounding tools. The architectural point is that one trained behaviour, calling Search from inside reasoning, serves AI Overviews, AI Mode, the Gemini app and the developer API [15][20][21].

6. Search APIs built for agents

Agents now consume search more than people do in many products, and a market of search APIs has formed to serve them. They have converged on returning token-budgeted evidence rather than ranked links.

API Retrieval basis (public description) Evidence unit returned Depth / latency knobs Freshness / filters Grounding output
Perplexity Search [25][27†] Own web index; hybrid retrieval, sub-document units ranked snippets; total and per-page token budgets search_context_size low/med/high recency, publish and update dates, domain, language, academic/SEC modes date, last_updated per result
Exa [45] Own index; neural (embedding-based), keyword, auto, fast, instant, deep variants text, query-biased highlights (relevance-sized), summaries type: fast ... deep-reasoning livecrawl always/fallback/never/auto/preferred; historical snapshots deep search: per-field citations + confidence
Tavily [47] Characterized by Perplexity as SERP-based [26] snippet content, chunks_per_source, raw markdown/text search_depth ultra-fast/fast/basic/advanced; auto_parameters time range, dates, max_age_hours, domains restrict/prefer, topic news/finance optional LLM answer; research reports with citation formats
Brave [49][50†] Own index (per Brave) web results + extra_snippets; LLM Context endpoint token budget 1,024-32,768; per-URL caps; threshold modes freshness pd/pw/pm/py or range; Goggles re-ranking summarizer with inline references
Grounding with Bing [9][11] Bing index not exposed to the developer; model sees it n/a Custom Search domain scoping citations + Bing query link, must be displayed
You.com [51] not documented search, contents research tool on request n/a n/a

6.1 Exa

The Exa SDK documents a retrieval stack built for machine consumers [45]:

  • Search types. auto (the default) chooses the approach. neural uses embedding-based semantic search, instant is low-latency neural search, fast prioritizes speed, and deep-lite, deep and deep-reasoning are deep-search variants that accept additional_queries. In auto mode the response reports whether it resolved to neural or keyword, and cost is broken down the same way.
  • Highlights instead of pages. contents={"highlights": True} returns query-biased extracts. Their length is chosen per document by relevance, and the SDK advises against fixed character limits. A 2026 research preview, Dynamic Highlights, assigns a single shared context budget across all results: the model sizes each excerpt, so a weak page gets nothing and a strong one gets more. This is context assembly (stage [5]) done by the search provider.
  • Freshness control. The livecrawl options are always, fallback, never, auto and preferred. snapshot_as_of returns the newest stored version of a page at or before a given time, which supports reproducible or historical research.
  • Grounded structured output. Deep search can return content that follows a JSON schema (at most 2 levels of nesting and 10 properties). Each output field carries its own grounding: a list of citations (URL and title) and a confidence of low, medium or high. This is per-field attribution for structured extraction, a citation form the chat-oriented APIs lack.
  • Higher-level products. An Agent API (with an "ultra" effort level), Websets, and Agent Monitors. Monitors keep a table of entities by fields up to date: static fields are answered once, and dynamic fields are tracked from news on every refresh.
  • Agent-facing packaging. The official MCP server exposes web_search_exa, web_fetch_exa (pages as clean markdown), web_search_advanced_exa (filters, domains, dates, highlights, summaries, subpage crawling) and agent_run [46]. The search, read and delegate split mirrors the search and fetch tools of Claude and OpenAI.

6.2 Tavily

Tavily's SDK shows a "search plus extraction" API designed to sit inside RAG and agent frameworks [47][48]:

  • search_depth takes ultra-fast, fast, basic or advanced. Perplexity's harness chose basic because, per its code comment, advanced does not give sub-second latency [26]. topic is general, news or finance. Further options are time_range and explicit dates, max_age_hours, include_domains_mode of restrict or prefer (a soft domain boost, not only a hard filter), exact_match for names and phrases, include_raw_content as markdown or text, chunks_per_source, and auto_parameters (let the service choose).
  • include_answer (basic or advanced) returns a short LLM-generated answer. The older get_search_context helper, which packed result contents into a JSON string up to max_tokens (4,000 by default), is deprecated. The packing has moved to the server.
  • Endpoints beyond search: extract (pages by URL), crawl and map (site traversal and structure), and research. Research produces reports with model mini, pro or auto, an optional JSON output schema, and citation formats numbered, mla, apa or chicago.
  • A Feedback API accepts per-result scores from agents or end users "so Tavily can improve ranking and relevance over time". The search provider learns from the consuming agent's judgments.
  • A keyless mode (search and extract only, rate-limited), and 1,000 free credits per month.

6.3 Brave Search API

Brave's official MCP server documents the API surface [49]. Endpoints cover web, news, images, video, local POIs and descriptions, place search, a summarizer, and an LLM Context endpoint (/res/v1/llm/context). The LLM Context endpoint returns "pre-extracted web content optimized for AI agents, LLM grounding, and RAG pipelines", with explicit budgets: total tokens 1,024-32,768, URLs 1-50, snippets 1-256, tokens per URL 512-8,192, snippets per URL 1-100. It also has a context_threshold_mode of disabled, strict, lenient or balanced, which decides how aggressively marginal content is dropped. Goggles let the caller supply custom re-ranking definitions, a programmable ranking layer exposed to the client. The summarizer works in two steps: a web search with summary: true returns a key, and the summarizer turns that key into a summary, optionally with inline references. Brave describes its API as served from its own independent index [50†].

6.4 What the APIs teach

  • The context window is now the product boundary. Every modern API takes a token budget and returns pre-cut evidence, so the old distinction between ranking and snippeting has disappeared. When you compare APIs, hold the evidence budget fixed (Section 4.1).
  • Freshness is a parameter, not a property. Live crawl, cache bypass, max_age_hours and last_updated let the agent pay latency for freshness only when it has to [25][37][45][47].
  • Licences shape architecture. Bing's terms (no raw content to the developer, no caching, no training, mandatory display) push designs towards a model-sees-it, user-sees-citations pattern [9][10]. APIs that return raw text allow local reranking, caching and offline evaluation.

7. Deep research agents

Deep research turns the agentic loop into a background job. A minimal composite of the documented systems looks like this:

  user request
      |
      v
  [clarify / rewrite]  -- ChatGPT: intermediate model asks questions; API: skipped;
      |                   Gemini: optional collaborative planning; Azure: gpt-4o scoper
      v
  [plan]  lead agent / research model writes a plan (persisted to memory)
      |
      +------------+------------+------------+     parallel workers / search threads
      v            v            v            v
   search ->    search ->    search ->    MCP / file   each: search, fetch, read,
   read ->      read ->      read ->      search ->    reflect, refine query
   compress     compress     compress     compress     (own context window)
      +------------+------------+------------+
      |
      v
  [synthesize] lead agent decides: enough? -> else spawn more work
      |
      v
  [cite]  inline citations from the model, or a separate citation pass
      |
      v
  report (+ charts, structured output); background mode + webhooks / polling

7.1 OpenAI deep research

As announced in February 2025, deep research in ChatGPT was powered by a version of the upcoming o3 model optimized for web browsing and data analysis. It was trained with end-to-end reinforcement learning on hard browsing and reasoning tasks, took roughly 5 to 30 minutes per task, and scored 26.6% on Humanity's Last Exam. OpenAI listed limitations: it could hallucinate, had trouble telling authoritative information from rumour, was poorly calibrated about its own confidence, and made formatting errors in reports and citations [29†]. Hugging Face, reproducing it, quoted a GAIA validation score of about 67% (67.36%), with 47.6% on the hardest level-3 questions [55].

The API, documented in OpenAI's cookbook [30][31], exposes the mechanics:

  • Models o3-deep-research-2025-06-26 and o4-mini-deep-research-2025-06-26 (the smaller one for latency-sensitive use) run through the Responses API with background=True, because tasks take minutes.
  • Data sources are web_search_preview (required unless an MCP source is configured), an optional code_interpreter, and MCP servers for private data. The output lists every intermediate step: reasoning summaries, web_search_call, code runs and MCP calls. The final text carries citation annotations with start and end indices, title and URL.
  • Clarification is a separate stage. In ChatGPT, an intermediate model (for example gpt-4.1) asks follow-up questions before research begins. The API skips this step and "expects fully-formed prompts up front", so the cookbook adds a rewriter or clarifier. Without one, vague prompts produce broad research that is verbose, slow and costly [30].
  • The agents cookbook builds a four-agent pipeline (triage, clarifier, instruction builder, research agent) with the Agents SDK. It warns: "Do not use Deep Research for trivial fact lookups" [31].

On Azure the same architecture is visible from the outside. The (now deprecated) Deep Research tool used gpt-4o to clarify and scope the task, then o3-deep-research grounded on Grounding with Bing. Deployments were limited to two regions, and the model retires on 19 November 2026. Microsoft now recommends general reasoning models with web_search at high reasoning effort [12][13]. Deep research is being absorbed into general-purpose reasoning models plus a search tool.

7.2 Gemini Deep Research

Google's technical report describes Gemini Deep Research as an agent on Gemini 2.5 Pro that is optimized for task prioritization and for "identify[ing] when it reaches a dead-end when browsing". Its HLE score rose from 7.95% at launch in December 2024 to 26.9%, and to 32.4% with more compute, by June 2025 [15]. The 2026 API [22]:

  • Two agents: deep-research-preview-04-2026 (lower latency, interactive) and deep-research-max-preview-04-2026 (maximum search exhaustiveness, for automated reporting). They are available only through the asynchronous Interactions API, and a task "can consult over 100 sources".
  • Default tools are Google Search, URL Context and Code Execution. MCP servers and File Search over uploaded corpora are optional, and either can replace the web entirely.
  • Collaborative planning. The agent returns a plan instead of a report, the user iterates on it, and the user then sets collaborative_planning=False to run it. This is clarification as a reviewable artifact.
  • Streaming of thought summaries, built-in charts (visualization="auto"), multimodal inputs, and follow-up questions answered by a standard Gemini model rather than the research agent.

7.3 Anthropic Research

Chapter 08 covers Anthropic's multi-agent Research system as an agent architecture. Here the focus is on what it shows about web grounding [41][42][43]:

  • Orchestrator and workers. A lead agent plans, saves the plan to memory (contexts over 200K tokens are truncated), spawns subagents that search in parallel with their own context windows, and finally hands everything to a separate CitationAgent. The CitationAgent maps claims in the report to locations in the source documents [42].
  • Effort scaling in the prompt. Simple fact-finding uses 1 agent and 3-10 tool calls. Comparisons use 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each. Complex research uses more than 10 subagents [42]. The published prompts cap the lead at 20 subagents. They give each subagent a budget: under 5 calls for simple tasks, about 10 for hard ones, an absolute limit of 20 tool calls and about 100 sources [43].
  • Economics. A multi-agent configuration (Opus 4 lead, Sonnet 4 subagents) outperformed single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal research evaluation. On BrowseComp, token usage alone explained 80% of performance variance. Agents use about 4x the tokens of chat, and multi-agent systems about 15x. Parallel subagents (3-5) and parallel tool calls (3 or more) cut research time by up to 90% on complex queries [42].
  • Source quality is a prompt problem. Human testers found that early agents preferred "SEO-optimized content farms over authoritative but less highly-ranked sources like academic PDFs or personal blogs". Source-quality heuristics in the prompts fixed it [42]. The subagent prompt tells the model to watch for speculation in future tense, news aggregators instead of original sources, passive voice with unnamed sources, and marketing language, and to flag conflicts to the lead instead of resolving them silently [43].
  • Evaluation. A single LLM-judge call scores factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality and tool efficiency. Work started from about 20 real queries [42].
  • Context management. For Claude Opus 4.5, Anthropic reported that combining context management, memory and subagent orchestration improved a deep-research evaluation by almost 15 points: from 70.48% to 85.30% on a fetch-enabled BrowseComp-Plus [44].

7.4 Research APIs from search vendors

Search providers have moved up into agents: Perplexity's Agent API, Exa's Agent API, Tavily's research endpoint and Parallel's Task API [24][26][45][47]. Section 4.1 has the June 2026 search_evals comparison of five of these hosted agents. Their main architectural advantage over a general model calling a third-party search tool is co-location: the loop runs next to the index, so per-query latency and per-query cost are lower. That makes wide fan-out affordable.

7.5 Open replications

Within about a day of OpenAI's launch, Hugging Face's open Deep Research reached 55.15% on the GAIA validation set, against about 46% for the previous open state of the art (Magentic-One). Most of the gain came from letting the agent write its actions as code instead of JSON: with JSON actions the same setup scored 33% [55]. Alibaba's Tongyi DeepResearch is a 30.5B-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 3.3B parameters active per token and a 128K context. It was trained specifically for long-horizon information seeking and is evaluated on HLE, BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, WebWalkerQA, xbench-DeepSearch, FRAMES and SimpleQA [56]. Chapter 08 covers RL-trained search agents (Search-R1, DeepResearcher and others) in detail.

8. Citation systems

A citation makes a checkable claim: this span of the answer is supported by that span of that source. Systems differ in who creates the link, at what granularity, and whether the system can guarantee that the link points to something real.

8.1 Seven implementation patterns

Pattern How the link is made Granularity Guarantees Examples
Prompted markers model writes [n]; UI maps n to the source list source none: n may be wrong or invented Vane [52], most early answer engines
Span annotations API returns char ranges + URL for answer text answer span to URL link targets a retrieved source OpenAI url_citation [12][30]
Constrained source pointers model emits indices into pre-chunked docs; API extracts quoted text answer span to sentence, page or block pointers are valid by construction Anthropic Citations, web search citations [36][38][39]
Supports with confidence each answer segment maps to chunk indices with scores segment to chunk scored, not guaranteed Gemini grounding_supports [20]
Post-hoc citation pass separate agent adds citations to a finished report without changing text claim to source location text identity checked; support judged by model Anthropic CitationAgent [42][43]
Provider-rendered references grounding service returns references the app must display verbatim answer to URL + query references come from provider, not model Grounding with Bing [9][10]
Per-field grounding each field of structured output carries citations + confidence field to URLs scored Exa deep search output [45]

Constrained pointers in practice. Anthropic's Citations feature chunks plain-text and PDF documents into sentences, or uses caller-supplied blocks as-is ("custom content"). The model cites by pointing at those chunks, and the API turns the pointers into cited_text with character indices (text), page ranges (PDF) or block indices (custom content). Because the API parses the citations, they "are guaranteed to contain valid pointers to the provided documents". The quoted text does not count toward output tokens [39]. Anthropic reported recall accuracy up to 15% higher than custom implementations. One customer, Endex, reported source hallucinations and formatting issues falling from 10% to 0%, with 20% more references per response [38]. Search result content blocks apply the same mechanism to a developer's own retrieval results. Any RAG system can then get web-search-style citations by returning search_result blocks (source, title, text content) from its tools [40]. The design principle is to make invalid citations impossible to emit rather than detecting them later.

Post-hoc citation as a separate pass. Anthropic's published citations_agent prompt gives a second agent the finished report and the sources. The agent must output the same text "100% identical" (whitespace included) with citations added. Text without the citations is compared to the original, and the result is rejected if they differ [43]. The prompt also sets citation style: cite claims readers would want to verify rather than common knowledge; cite whole semantic units, preferably at sentence end; do not fragment sentences with several citations; do not repeat a source within a sentence. Separating writing from attribution lets each stage be optimized and evaluated on its own. The cost is an extra model pass over a long document.

Showing queries as well as sources. Microsoft 365 Copilot cites the queries it sent to Bing, not only the pages [8]. Grounding with Bing requires the link to the Bing query [9][10]. Gemini returns web_search_queries [20]. Seeing the query lets users find the most common failure, which is searching for the wrong thing.

8.2 Measuring citation quality

  • Support and precision. Liu et al. separated citation recall (are generated statements supported?) from citation precision (does each citation support its statement?) and found both well below what users assume [4†][4]. ALCE automated both with NLI models [5]. DeepResearch Bench's FACT framework does this for long reports. It extracts statement-URL pairs, removes duplicates, scrapes each URL, has an LLM judge support, and reports citation accuracy and effective citations per task over 100 PhD-level tasks in 22 fields [59].
  • What users reward. Search Arena collected about 24,000 conversations with search-augmented models (ICLR 2026). Users prefer longer responses, more citations, and specific sources: they favour coding sources and community or blog posts and disfavour Wikipedia. However, "models do not always cite retrieved sources accurately and humans do not always check citations" [57]. Preference optimization on such data can therefore reward citation volume over citation validity. Evaluation should include an automated support check that users cannot game.
  • External audits. A March 2025 audit by the Tow Center at Columbia Journalism Review tested eight AI search tools on identifying the source of news excerpts. Collectively they gave incorrect answers to more than 60% of queries, often confidently, and sometimes cited syndicated copies instead of original publishers [60†].

8.3 Citation and grounding failure modes

Failure Mechanism Mitigations seen in sources
Unsupported citation model attaches a real source that does not say the claim constrained pointers [39]; post-hoc pass + judge [42][43]; FACT-style audits [59]
Invented link model generates a URL do not let the model write links; use API annotations [9][12]
Faithful to a bad source satire, forum jokes, data voids trigger suppression, source-type limits [17†]; source-quality prompts [43]
Content-farm bias SEO pages outrank primary sources source heuristics in prompts [42]; Goggles / domain preferences [47][49]
Generative-engine optimization pages rewritten to win LLM citations treat as adversarial ranking; GEO shows up to +40% visibility [6]
Staleness cached or outdated pages last_updated, page_age, live crawl, cache bypass [25][36][37][45]
Prompt injection / exfiltration fetched page instructs agent to leak data via URLs fetch only URLs already in context; block credential-like URLs [37]
Evidence tampering across turns client edits prior results encrypted result and citation indices [36]
Over-citation many weak citations look rigorous citation style rules [43]; precision metrics [4][5]

9. Evaluating web-grounded systems

Answer engines need evaluation along three axes: answer correctness, retrieval and browsing difficulty, and attribution. The current benchmark set:

Benchmark What it stresses Size / notes
SimpleQA [32] short factual answers; saturates quickly once search is on (0.93-0.95 in [26]) OpenAI reference implementation
FreshQA / SealQA [3] fast-changing facts, false premises; noisy search results FreshQA updated weekly
FRAMES [26] multi-hop retrieval and reasoning single-step agent in [26]
BrowseComp [32][33†] hard-to-find facts needing persistent, creative browsing 1,266 problems [26]
BrowseComp-Plus [58] the same queries over a fixed ~100K-document human-verified corpus separates retriever from agent; reproducible
HLE (text-only IR subset) [26] frontier academic questions 2,158 of 2,500 questions [26]
DeepSearchQA [26] multi-step seeking, collation, exhaustive answers 900 tasks
WideSearch [26] breadth: collecting many independent facts into tables 200 tasks; row-level F1
DeepResearch Bench [59] report quality (RACE) and citation trustworthiness (FACT) 100 tasks, 22 fields, based on 96,147 real queries
Search Arena [57] human pairwise preference on real prompts ~24K conversations

BrowseComp at launch showed the gap between browsing and plain search. As reported, GPT-4o with browsing solved under 2% of problems, while OpenAI's deep research agent solved about half [33†]. A year later the hosted research agents in Section 4.1 scored 0.56-0.81 [26].

Methodological cautions. (1) The live web makes runs non-reproducible. BrowseComp-Plus fixes the corpus so that retrievers can be compared under one agent [58]. (2) Grading is done by LLM judges whose prompts come from the original benchmarks [26]. DeepResearch Bench changed its official judge model twice between 2025 and 2026 and re-validated each against human agreement. The human inter-annotator baseline was 68.78% [59]. (3) Vendor harnesses set evidence budgets, models and step caps (Section 4.1). Report them with every number. (4) Separate failed-as-zero from failed-excluded scores. search_evals publishes both [26].

10. Master comparison

System Owner of index Loop style Query strategy Citation mechanism Notable public numbers
Bing Copilot / Prometheus Microsoft orchestrated, iterative internal queries [7†] generated short queries; shown to users in M365 [8] provider references, must display [9][10] grounding $14 / 1K transactions [11]
Google AI Overviews Google single-shot, custom Gemini [16†] n/a public inline links >1.5B MAU [15]
Google AI Mode / Deep Search Google query fan-out; hundreds of searches in Deep Search [18†][19†] parallel subtopic queries inline links n/a
Gemini API grounding Google model-driven tool call [15][21] web_search_queries returned [20] segment-to-chunk supports + confidence [20] SimpleQA 54.0% (2.5 Pro, no tools) [15]
Perplexity (consumer + Agent API) Perplexity single-shot to 100-step agent [25] presets; multi-query search [25] numbered sources; API citations BrowseComp 0.805 (agent, [26])
ChatGPT search / web_search third-party providers / Bing on Azure [12][28†] 3 modes [12] search, open_page, find_in_page [12] url_citation char spans [12] n/a
Claude web search / fetch n/a in docs server-side loop, max_uses, dynamic filtering [36] multiple progressive searches [35] constrained pointers, cited_text [36][39] $10 / 1K searches [36]
OpenAI deep research as above RL-trained o3 variant, background [29†][30] autonomous plan + search annotations HLE 26.6% at launch [29†]
Gemini Deep Research Google async agent, collaborative planning [22] plan, then search, URL context inline citations HLE 26.9% / 32.4% [15]
Anthropic Research n/a orchestrator + parallel subagents [42] effort-scaled subagents separate CitationAgent [42][43] +90.2% vs single agent [42]

Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Decide whether to search before deciding how. A trigger classifier or a model policy for when to ground saves latency and money, and it removes a class of errors. Google's AI Overviews fixes started with not answering nonsensical queries and data-void queries [17†][36][52].
  2. Fan out, then compress. Google's query fan-out, Anthropic's parallel subagents and Gemini's hundreds of Deep Search queries all share a shape: issue many narrow queries in parallel, compress each thread separately, and synthesize once [18†][19†][42]. Budget this explicitly. Token usage explained 80% of BrowseComp variance in Anthropic's analysis, and multi-agent research costs about 15x a chat turn [42].
  3. Treat evidence budget as a first-class parameter. Modern search APIs take token budgets, per-URL caps and thresholds [25][45][47][49]. In vendor benchmarks the budget moved results as much as the choice of engine [26]. When you compare providers, hold the budget constant.
  4. Make invalid citations unrepresentable. Prefer pointer-based or annotation-based citations that the API resolves (Anthropic Citations, OpenAI url_citation, Gemini supports) over model-written [n] markers or URLs [12][20][39]. Never let the model generate links [9].
  5. Validate support separately from generation. A post-hoc citation pass with a text-identity check [43], or FACT-style statement-URL verification [59], catches citations that are real but irrelevant. Users reward citation volume and seldom click through [57], so preference data alone will not catch them.
  6. Source quality is where grounded systems fail. Content farms, satire, forums, syndicated copies and GEO-optimized pages pass straight through faithful summarization [6][17†][42][60†]. Encode source-quality heuristics, prefer primary sources, and expose ranking controls such as domain preferences and Goggles.
  7. Show your queries. Showing the generated search queries next to the citations, as Microsoft 365 Copilot does, is cheap. It helps users diagnose failures and helps auditors with compliance [8][20].
  8. Freshness is a per-request decision. Expose last_updated or page_age to the model, and use live crawl or cache bypass only when the question is time-sensitive [25][36][37][45].
  9. Web access is an attack surface. Restrict fetches to URLs that already appeared in context, block credential-like URLs, encrypt provenance across turns, and run domain allow-lists in regulated settings [36][37][12].
  10. Read the licence before designing the cache. Terms on raw-content access, caching, training and mandatory display can rule out offline reranking, evaluation replay or index-building [9][10]. Pick the retrieval provider to fit the architecture you need.
  11. Clarify before researching. Every deep research system adds a scoping stage: a clarifier model, collaborative planning, or a rewriter. Under-specified prompts lead to broad, slow and expensive research [22][30][31][13].
  12. Benchmark reproducibly. Use a fixed corpus (BrowseComp-Plus) to compare retrievers. Report harness configuration, judge model, and both failed-as-zero and failed-excluded scores. Treat any vendor-run leaderboard as a starting point [26][58][59].
