18. Long-Term Memory Systems for LLMs and Agents: MemGPT/Letta, Mem0, Zep/Graphiti, ChatGPT and Claude Memory, LangMem, and the Write/Read Policies Behind Them

Overview

Classic RAG retrieves from a corpus that someone else wrote and that changes slowly. Long-term memory is a different case. The agent writes the corpus itself, while it runs, from its own conversations and actions. The corpus changes every turn, and facts in it contradict one another as users change jobs, preferences and plans. The read path still looks like retrieval (embed, search, rerank, inject into the prompt). The hard parts move to the write path: what gets stored, in what form, when, by whom, and how newer facts supersede older ones.

This chapter surveys the publicly documented designs, from the research prototypes of 2023 to the production assistant memories of 2025-2026:

  • OS-style tiered memory: MemGPT and its successor Letta, where the model pages information in and out of its own context window with tool calls [1][2][3].
  • Extract-and-consolidate memory layers: Mem0, which turns conversations into atomic facts and reconciles them with an existing store [8][9][10].
  • Temporal knowledge graphs: Zep and its open-source engine Graphiti, which store facts as graph edges that carry validity intervals [12][13][14].
  • Toolkits and taxonomies: LangMem's semantic/episodic/procedural split and its "hot path versus background" write policies [16][17], CoALA [30], Generative Agents [29], A-Mem [32], MemOS [33] and MIRIX [34].
  • Consumer assistant memory: ChatGPT's saved memories and chat-history reference [18][19][21], and Claude's tool-based chat search, memory summaries and topics [22][24].
  • Developer-facing file memory: Anthropic's client-side memory tool, context editing and Claude Code's CLAUDE.md and auto memory [25][26][27][28].

A pattern runs through the whole period. The early designs leaned on complex machinery: vector archival stores, LLM-driven UPDATE/DELETE reconciliation and graph construction. By 2025-2026 several of the strongest results came from simpler substrates: plain files, append-only fact logs and on-demand search over raw transcripts [7][9][26]. Evaluation is contested territory. Vendors publish benchmark numbers that conflict with each other [11][15], so this chapter reports them with their provenance.

                     THE MEMORY LOOP (generic)
  +-----------+   turn    +-------------------+   response
  |   user /  |---------->|   LLM agent       |------------> user / env
  |   env     |           | (context window)  |
  +-----------+           +---------+---------+
                             ^      |  WRITE POLICY
                 READ POLICY |      |  (what / when / who / form)
                 (what to    |      v
                 inject,     |  +---------------------------+
                 when, how   |  | memory store(s)           |
                 much)       +--| profile | facts | graph | |
                                | episodes | files | logs   |
                                +---------------------------+
                                     ^  CONSOLIDATION / FORGETTING
                                     |  (dedupe, invalidate, summarize,
                                     +--  reflect, expire) - often offline

1. Conceptual Foundations: Memory Types and Policies

1.1 Cognitive taxonomies

CoALA (Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents; Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan, Griffiths, 2023, TMLR 2024) borrowed the vocabulary of cognitive science. It describes a language agent as having modular memory components, a structured action space for acting on internal memory and external environments, and a generalized decision procedure [30]. Most later systems use its four-way split: working memory (the active context), episodic memory (past experiences), semantic memory (facts) and procedural memory (skills and behavior, stored either in the weights or in code and prompts) [30].

LangMem turns that split into storage guidance [17]:

Memory type Purpose Agent example Typical storage
Semantic Facts and knowledge User preferences; knowledge triplets Profile or collection
Episodic Past experiences Few-shot examples; summaries of past conversations Collection
Procedural System behavior Core personality, response patterns Prompt rules or collection

LangMem also separates two forms of semantic memory [17]:

  • A collection holds an unbounded set of records that are searched at run time. The system has to reconcile each new fact with what it already holds. "If the system over-extracts, this could lead to reduced precision... If it under-extracts, this could lead to low recall."
  • A profile is a single schema-bound document, such as a Pydantic model of the user's name, preferred name and response style. Each update replaces the current state. A profile is cheap to inject and easy for users to edit by hand, but it keeps no history.

LangMem's guide also says that relevance "is more than just semantic similarity". It argues that recall should combine similarity with a memory's importance and its strength (how recently and how often it was used) [17]. That idea goes back to Generative Agents.

1.2 Generative Agents: the memory stream

Park et al. (2023) built agents for a simulated town around a memory stream: "a long-term memory module that records, in natural language, a comprehensive list of the agent's experiences" [29]. The read policy ranks memories by a weighted combination of three signals:

  • Recency: exponential decay since the memory was last accessed.
  • Importance: an integer score the LLM assigns when the memory is written.
  • Relevance: embedding similarity to the current query.

The consolidation policy is reflection. Periodically the agent synthesizes related observations into higher-level inferences and writes them back into the stream, where they can be retrieved like any other memory [29]. Almost every later system uses these two ideas in some form. Importance-weighted recall and offline reflection reappear as LangMem's "strength", Letta's sleep-time agents and Claude's daily memory synthesis.

1.3 The four policy questions

Whatever the substrate, every memory design answers the same questions:

  1. What to write. Raw transcripts, atomic facts, typed profiles, graph triples, reflections, or free-form notes in files.
  2. When and who writes. The agent can write in the hot path, via tool calls during the turn. A background process can write after the turn or during idle time. LangMem's guide calls these "conscious" and "subconscious" formation: hot-path writes add latency and give the agent one more decision to make, while background writes have "no latency impact" but update with a delay [17].
  3. How to reconcile. Overwrite, UPDATE/DELETE via the LLM, append-only with links, or bi-temporal invalidation.
  4. What and when to read. Always inject a small profile, retrieve per query, or let the agent search on demand through tools.

The sections below show that the major systems differ mostly in how they answer these four questions, not in their embedding models or vector stores.

2. MemGPT and Letta: The LLM as Operating System

2.1 Problem

MemGPT (Packer et al., UC Berkeley, October 2023) started from the fixed context window. Long conversations and large documents do not fit, and naive truncation loses information. The paper borrows virtual memory from operating systems. The LLM gets a small fast tier (the prompt) and large slow tiers (external stores), and it moves data between them itself, using function calls [1].

2.2 Architecture

  +--------------------------- MAIN CONTEXT (prompt tokens) --------------------------+
  | [system instructions] [working context: editable persona/user facts] [FIFO queue] |
  +-----------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
           ^  page in (search results)            |  page out (insert / evict)
           |                                      v
  +--------+---------------------+   +------------+-------------------------------+
  | RECALL STORAGE               |   | ARCHIVAL STORAGE                           |
  | full message log; search by  |   | read/write vector-backed DB of arbitrary   |
  | text / date                  |   | text; semantic search                      |
  +------------------------------+   +--------------------------------------------+
        QUEUE MANAGER: warns at ~70% of window ("memory pressure"); at 100% flushes
        ~half the queue and rewrites a recursive summary  |  FUNCTION EXECUTOR

The main context has three parts [1]:

  • System instructions: read-only. They describe the control flow and the memory functions.
  • Working context: a read/write scratchpad of key facts about the user and the agent's persona.
  • FIFO queue: the rolling message history, headed by a recursive summary of evicted messages.

Outside the prompt, recall storage holds the complete message log and can be searched by content or date. Archival storage is a read/write, vector-backed database for arbitrary text [1]. A queue manager enforces the memory budget. When prompt tokens pass a warning threshold (about 70% of the window, per the paper as summarized in secondary sources), it inserts a "memory pressure" system message so that the model can save important facts. At the limit it flushes the queue, evicting about half the messages and updating the recursive summary [1]. The model can also chain calls: a function call can request an immediate follow-up inference, so a multi-step search runs before the agent answers the user.

2.3 Results

On the paper's Deep Memory Retrieval (DMR) task, built on the Multi-Session Chat dataset, GPT-4 with a fixed context scored 32.1%. GPT-4 under MemGPT scored 92.5% [1]. Secondary summaries report 93.4% for GPT-4 Turbo with MemGPT and 66.9% for GPT-3.5 Turbo with MemGPT, against 35.3% and 38.7% for the corresponding fixed-context baselines. These pairs come from summaries rather than the paper's own table, so treat them as approximate. The paper also reports conversation-opener, document-QA and nested key-value retrieval experiments [1].

2.4 Letta: memory blocks, sleep-time agents, MemFS

The MemGPT authors went on to found Letta, which describes itself as "formerly MemGPT" [2]. Its concepts moved through several stages:

  • Memory blocks. The working context became labeled, size-limited, editable sections of the system prompt (for example persona and human). The agent edits them through memory tools, and a block can be shared across several agents [4][5].
  • Sleep-time agents. A primary agent is paired with a background agent that runs between turns and rewrites the primary agent's memory blocks asynchronously. Letta's documentation describes it as triggering every N steps (5 by default) and labels the feature experimental [5]. The research paper behind it, Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time (Lin, Snell, Wang, Packer, Wooders, Stoica, Gonzalez, 2025), reports these results [6]:
    • About 5x less test-time compute needed for the same accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME.
    • Accuracy gains of up to 13% (GSM-Symbolic) and 18% (AIME) when sleep-time compute is scaled.
    • A 2.5x lower average cost per query when several related queries share the same pre-computation (Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic).
    • The gains are largest when queries are predictable from the context.
  • Filesystem memory. In August 2025 Letta published Benchmarking AI Agent Memory: Is a Filesystem All You Need? [7]. The conversation history was uploaded as a single file and the agent got file tools (grep, a semantic search_files, open, close). With gpt-4o-mini, the agent scored 74.0% on LoCoMo, higher than the 68.5% that Mem0 reported for its best graph variant. Commentators pointed out that search_files is semantic, so "grep" undersells the setup, and that LoCoMo barely tests knowledge updates. Letta itself called framework-to-framework comparison apples-to-oranges [7].
  • Letta Code (2026). The active codebase is now letta-code, and the V1 API server has been retired to an archive branch [2]. Letta Code agents "rewrite their own memory, skills, prompts, and even the harness itself". Memory blocks are now tracked in a git-versioned MemFS that can sync to a GitHub repository. Periodic "dreaming" is configured with /sleeptime, a recall subagent searches past messages, and agent-scoped skills live in MemFS [3].

2.5 Failure modes and lessons

  • Self-management takes model capability. The paper's own numbers show the gap: a weaker model (GPT-3.5 Turbo) reached 66.9% on DMR versus GPT-4's 92.5% [1]. Paging decisions are only as good as the model's judgment about tool use.
  • Hot-path memory editing costs latency. Every memory edit is an extra inference step. Moving consolidation into sleep-time agents is Letta's answer [5][6].
  • Lesson. The OS metaphor survived but the substrate got simpler. MemFS's git-tracked files and the filesystem benchmark both point to plain files plus good tools, rather than bespoke stores, as a strong default [3][7].

3. Mem0: Extract, Consolidate, Retrieve

3.1 Problem and positioning

Mem0 ("mem-zero", YC S24) offers a drop-in memory layer for applications. It scopes memories at the user, session and agent level and ships as a library, a self-hosted server and a managed cloud [9]. Its April 2025 paper, Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory, targets the cost and latency of stuffing entire histories into the prompt [8].

3.2 Original architecture (2025 paper, v1/v2 library)

 new message pair (m_t-1, m_t)
        |
        v
 +------------------- EXTRACTION -------------------+
 | context = async-refreshed conversation summary S |
 |           + last m messages (default m=10)       |
 | LLM -> list of candidate facts                   |
 +-------------------------+------------------------+
                           v
 +-------------------- UPDATE ----------------------+
 | for each fact: vector-search top s similar       |
 | memories (default s=10)                          |
 | LLM tool call -> ADD | UPDATE | DELETE | NONE     |
 +-------------------------+------------------------+
                           v
             vector store (+ graph store for Mem0g)

Extraction runs on each new message pair. Its context is a conversation summary that is refreshed asynchronously, plus a window of recent messages (default 10 per secondary analyses of the paper) [8]. For each candidate fact, the update phase fetches the top-s most similar existing memories and asks the LLM to choose an operation. The library's DEFAULT_UPDATE_MEMORY_PROMPT names them directly: "ADD: Add it to the memory as a new element; UPDATE: Update an existing memory element; DELETE: Delete an existing memory element; NONE: Make no change" [10]. The graph variant, Mem0g, also stores entities and relations in a graph database. Neo4j, Memgraph, Neptune and Kuzu appear among its supported backends [8][9].

3.3 Reported numbers (paper)

On LoCoMo the paper reports these figures [8]:

  • Search latency. Mem0 had the lowest of all compared methods: p50 0.148 s, p95 0.200 s.
  • Total latency. Mem0's median was 0.708 s and its p95 was 1.440 s. The full-context baseline, which passes about 26,000 tokens, had a p50 of 9.870 s and a p95 of 17.117 s.
  • Headline claims. The paper reports 91% lower p95 latency and more than 90% lower token cost than full context.
  • Accuracy. Mem0's companion blog reports an LLM-as-judge score of 66.9% for Mem0, against 52.9% for OpenAI Memory and 58.1% for LangMem, roughly a 26% relative gain over OpenAI [11].
  • Mem0g. The graph variant scored somewhat higher on temporal questions (58.1 vs 55.5) and lower on multi-hop questions. It used about twice the tokens per query (about 4K vs 2K, per the vendor blog) and had higher latency [11].

3.4 The 2026 redesign: ADD-only extraction

In April 2026 Mem0 published a new algorithm that drops the UPDATE/DELETE model [9]. The README lists these changes:

  • Single-pass ADD-only extraction. "One LLM call, no UPDATE/DELETE. Memories accumulate; nothing is overwritten."
  • Agent-generated facts are first-class. Information an agent confirms, such as an action it took, is stored with the same weight as user facts.
  • Entity linking. Entities are extracted, embedded and linked across memories to boost retrieval.
  • Multi-signal retrieval. Semantic, BM25 keyword and entity matches are scored in parallel and fused.
  • Temporal reasoning. Retrieval ranks the right dated instance for questions about current state, past events and upcoming plans.

The new ADDITIVE_EXTRACTION_PROMPT in the codebase says: "Your sole operation is ADD." When a new memory relates to an existing one ("updated/shifted preference, follow-up event, or continuation of a narrative"), the extractor records the old memory's UUID in linked_memory_ids instead of rewriting it [10].

Benchmark (Mem0 managed platform) Old New Tokens/query p50 latency
LoCoMo 71.4 92.5 7.0K 0.88 s
LongMemEval 67.8 94.4 6.8K 1.09 s
BEAM (1M) n/a 64.1 6.7K 1.00 s
BEAM (10M) n/a 48.6 6.9K 1.05 s

Source: Mem0 README [9]. These are self-reported figures for single-pass retrieval with a top-200 budget. Mem0 notes that the managed platform "includes proprietary optimizations not available in the open-source SDK". The evaluation harness is open-sourced.

3.5 Failure modes and lessons

  • Destructive updates lose history. An LLM-chosen DELETE or UPDATE can erase a fact that was still true, or was true at a different time. Without timestamps, the store cannot answer "what did I prefer last year?". The 2026 switch to append-plus-link is, in effect, an admission that lossy reconciliation was the weak point [9][10].
  • Benchmark disputes. Zep argued that Mem0's paper ran Zep incorrectly (wrong user role assignment, wrong timestamp handling). Zep then published a corrected LoCoMo score of 75.14% ± 0.17 for itself, after admitting an error in its own first calculation [15]. Third-party papers report yet other orderings [11]. Treat cross-vendor memory leaderboards as directional at best.
  • Lesson. Separate extraction (high recall, append-only) from read-time resolution (temporal ranking, entity linking). This is the same conclusion Zep reached by a different route.

4. Zep and Graphiti: Bi-Temporal Knowledge Graph Memory

4.1 Problem

Zep (Rasmussen et al., January 2025) argues that enterprise agents need memory that combines conversation with business data and keeps track of when facts held. Static RAG and batch GraphRAG do neither well [12][13]. Graphiti is the open-source engine underneath. Zep's managed service runs Graphiti on a proprietary "Context Graph Engine" and advertises "sub-200ms" retrieval at scale [13].

4.2 Architecture

  EPISODES (raw messages / JSON / text, each with a reference timestamp)
     |  ingest: entity extraction (window of recent messages) -> entity resolution
     |          (embedding + full-text candidate match, LLM dedupe) -> fact (edge)
     |          extraction + dedupe -> temporal extraction -> contradiction check
     v
 +------------------------------------------------------------------------+
 |  Episode subgraph   : raw episodes; every derived fact links back here |
 |  Semantic subgraph  : entity nodes (evolving summaries) + fact edges   |
 |                       edge = (fact text, embedding, valid_at,          |
 |                       invalid_at, created_at, expired_at, episodes[])  |
 |  Community subgraph : clusters of entities with summaries              |
 +------------------------------------------------------------------------+
     |  retrieve: search (cosine | BM25 | breadth-first traversal)
     |            -> rerank (RRF | MMR | node distance | episode mentions |
     |               cross-encoder) -> context constructor (facts + dates)
     v
  prompt context string

The graph has three tiers [12][13]:

  • Episodes: raw data, kept as ground-truth provenance.
  • Semantic entities and facts: the extracted knowledge.
  • Communities: clusters of entities with high-level summaries.

Ingestion is incremental. New episodes are integrated "without requiring complete graph recomputation", in contrast to GraphRAG's batch pipeline [13]. Developers can declare custom entity and edge types as Pydantic models (a "prescribed" ontology) or let the structure emerge from the data (a "learned" one) [13].

4.3 The bi-temporal model

Each fact edge carries two timelines [12][14]:

  • Valid time. valid_at is when the fact became true in the world; invalid_at is when it stopped. The code says "soft deadlines are not invalid_at", and future-tense plans use the episode's reference time.
  • Transaction time. created_at and expired_at record when the system learned the fact and when it retired the edge.

Each edge also stores the reference_time of the episode that produced it, which lets Graphiti resolve relative expressions such as "two weeks ago" [14]. When a new edge contradicts an existing one, the older edge is invalidated, not deleted. The system sorts conflicting edges by valid_at and expires the one that occurred earlier in the real world [12][13]. As a result, both "what is true now" and "what was true at time T" can be answered.

4.4 Retrieval

Graphiti's search configuration defines these options [14]:

  • Edge and node search: cosine_similarity, bm25 and breadth_first_search.
  • Episode search: BM25.
  • Community search: cosine and BM25.
  • Rerankers: reciprocal rank fusion, MMR, node_distance (graph proximity to a focal node), episode_mentions (how often a fact recurs) and a cross-encoder.

Recipes such as COMBINED_HYBRID_SEARCH_RRF and EDGE_HYBRID_SEARCH_NODE_DISTANCE package these choices [14]. The README stresses that retrieval does not depend on LLM summarization at query time. That is how it reaches "typically sub-second" latency, compared with "seconds to tens of seconds" for GraphRAG-style global search [13].

4.5 Reported numbers

All of these are self-reported:

  • DMR. Zep 94.8% vs MemGPT 93.4% [12].
  • LongMemEval with gpt-4o. Zep scored 71.2% against 60.2% for full context, using about 1.6K context tokens instead of about 115K. Median latency was 2.58 s for Zep against 28.9 s for full context, which Zep summarizes as roughly a 90% latency reduction. With gpt-4o-mini, Zep scored 63.8% against 55.4% [12][37].
  • Headline. Zep cites "accuracy improvements of up to 18.5%". The paper reports the largest gains on cross-session synthesis and temporal questions [12].

4.6 Failure modes and lessons

  • Ingestion cost and quality. Every episode triggers several LLM calls (extraction, resolution, dating, invalidation). Graphiti's README warns that providers without structured output, and especially smaller models, can produce "incorrect output schemas and ingestion failures" [13].
  • Entity resolution errors compound. Two nodes for one person, or one node for two people, will corrupt every fact attached to them. This is why resolution uses both embedding and full-text candidate matching [12].
  • Lesson. Time is a first-class retrieval dimension in agent memory. Storing validity intervals is cheap and removes a whole class of "stale fact" errors that similarity search cannot fix.

5. LangMem and LangGraph Memory: A Toolkit View

LangMem (LangChain, 2025) is not a single architecture. It is a set of primitives that apply the policies from Section 1.3 [16][17]:

  • Core functional API (storage-agnostic):
    • create_memory_manager extracts, updates and consolidates memories from conversations. It can produce free-form collections (enable_inserts=True) or schema-bound profiles.
    • create_prompt_optimizer rewrites prompt rules from conversations and feedback. This is procedural memory implemented as prompt evolution.
  • Stateful layer on LangGraph's BaseStore:
    • Store managers persist extracted memories automatically.
    • create_manage_memory_tool and create_search_memory_tool let an agent write and search memory in the hot path.
  • Namespaces segment memories hierarchically, for example by organization, user or app. Templates such as ("memories", "{user_id}") are filled from the run config. Retrieval supports direct key lookup, semantic search and metadata filtering [17].
          HOT PATH (conscious)                 BACKGROUND (subconscious)
  user -> agent --tool: manage_memory--> store <-- memory manager (after turn /
          agent --tool: search_memory--> store      after inactivity; reflects,
          (+latency, +tool-choice burden)           consolidates; no added latency)

The guide's write-policy table sums up the trade-off. Active formation has higher latency and immediate updates, and suits critical context. Background formation adds no latency but updates with a delay, and suits pattern analysis and summaries [17]. Episodic memory in LangMem means storing successful interactions: the situation, the reasoning and why it worked, for later use as few-shot examples. That is a narrower and more actionable meaning than "a log of past chats" [17].

6. Consumer Assistant Memory: ChatGPT

6.1 Timeline and controls

OpenAI launched ChatGPT memory in 2024 as user-visible saved memories. On April 10, 2025 it expanded memory to "reference all past conversations" for Plus and Pro users [18]. The feature now has two settings. Reference saved memories covers details the user explicitly asked ChatGPT to remember. Reference chat history draws on past chats, and OpenAI notes that what it remembers from them "can change over time" [19]. Saved memories persist until the user deletes them, and turning the setting off does not erase what is already stored [19]. On June 3, 2025 free users got a lighter version that provides "short-term continuity across conversations" [20].

6.2 Reverse-engineered architecture

OpenAI has not published the internals. In December 2025, Manthan Gupta probed ChatGPT in conversation and reported that, at least at that time, it did not appear to run retrieval over a vector index of past conversations. He found a structured context assembled for each message [21]:

  [system + developer instructions]
  [session metadata]        device/env info; injected per session, not persisted
  [user memory]             explicit long-term facts (saved memories)
  [recent conversations]    lightweight summaries of recent chats
  [current session window]  sliding window of this conversation's messages

This is a pre-injection read policy: a compact profile plus recent-chat digests sit in every prompt, so nothing needs to be retrieved at answer time. Shlok Khemani's independent analysis likewise described ChatGPT as combining user-controlled memories with "a dense generated summary" of history that the user cannot see. In a 2026 talk he put that profile at roughly 4,000 tokens [22][23]. These are inferences from probing, not documentation, and they may be out of date.

6.3 Failure modes

  • Opacity. Chat-history memory has no user-visible ledger, so users cannot audit why a detail came up. Saved memories, by contrast, are listed and editable [19][21].
  • Memory as an injection persistence channel. In September 2024 Johann Rehberger showed "SpAIware" against the ChatGPT macOS app. A prompt injection planted in untrusted content (a web page or document) wrote attacker instructions into memory. Those instructions then rode along in every future conversation and exfiltrated chat content. OpenAI patched the exfiltration vector [35]. The general lesson: any automatic write policy that runs over untrusted content turns a one-shot injection into a persistent compromise.

7. Consumer Assistant Memory: Claude

7.1 Phase 1 (August 2025): retrieval-only, tool-mediated

Claude's first cross-chat memory used the opposite design to ChatGPT. Each conversation started from a blank slate with no preloaded profile. Recall worked by searching raw past conversations through two visible tools [22]:

  • conversation_search: searches past conversations for relevant context.
  • recent_chats: retrieves recent chats, with sort order, before/after datetime pagination and project filtering.

Because memory access shows up as tool calls, users can see when and how past context is used. Khemani summed up the contrast this way: ChatGPT trades depth for automatic continuity, while Claude trades automatic continuity for on-demand depth [22][23].

7.2 Phase 2 (September 2025 onward): synthesized summaries, then topics

Anthropic added automatic memory for Team and Enterprise on September 11, 2025, and extended it to Pro and Max in October 2025 [36][24]. Claude's help center describes two generations [24]:

  • Legacy memory. Claude summarizes chats outside projects into a memory summary. The synthesis refreshes every 24 hours, while edits the user makes in chat apply immediately. Deleted conversations drop out of the synthesis.
  • New experience (topics). Claude "saves memory as individual topics while you chat, not by summarizing conversations after they end". It saves either on its own initiative or when told to "remember this".

Several controls and scoping rules apply to both [24]:

  • Projects. Each project has its own memory space and summary, so memory does not leak across workstreams.
  • Sensitive topics. Health, politics and similar topics are not saved by default. Some data, such as government IDs and financial account numbers, is never saved.
  • User controls. Users can pause or reset memory, turn it off for a single chat, use incognito chats, and view and edit topics. Import and export are experimental.
  • Deletion semantics. In the new experience, deleting a conversation does not delete the memory entries made from it.

Khemani reported that the later Claude profile is user-visible and about 1,000 tokens, against his estimate of about 4,000 for ChatGPT [23]. Chat search remains a separate, tool-based capability on paid plans [24].

The two phases show a broader convergence. The pure on-demand retrieval design gained a small always-injected profile. The pure pre-injection design (ChatGPT) depends on recency-weighted summaries. Production assistants end up as hybrids: a small, editable profile in every prompt plus retrieval over history when needed.

8. Developer Memory at Anthropic: Files, Context Editing, Auto Memory

8.1 The memory tool (API)

Anthropic announced the memory tool and context editing on September 29, 2025, together with Claude Sonnet 4.5 [25]. The design choices are deliberately minimal [26]:

  • File-based, client-side. The model issues view, create, str_replace, insert, delete and rename commands against a virtual /memories directory. The developer's handler executes them on any backend (disk, database, per-user prefix). Anthropic never stores the memory.
  • Built-in write/read protocol. When the tool is enabled, the API adds an instruction to the system prompt: "ALWAYS VIEW YOUR MEMORY DIRECTORY BEFORE DOING ANYTHING ELSE... ASSUME INTERRUPTION: Your context window might be reset at any moment." Memory works as a checkpoint, not only as a profile.
  • Paging. view truncates text over 16,000 characters, and the model pages through long files with view_range.
  • Security is the integrator's job. The docs recommend validating paths against traversal (/memories/../../secrets.env, URL-encoded variants), capping file sizes, expiring files that have not been accessed, and stripping sensitive data before writes.
  • Multi-session pattern. An initializer session writes a progress log and a feature checklist. Each later session reads them first and updates them before it ends.

Anthropic's internal agentic-search evaluation reported a 39% improvement from the memory tool plus context editing over baseline, and 29% from context editing alone. In a 100-turn web-search evaluation, context editing (automatically clearing stale tool results) let agents finish workflows that otherwise failed from context exhaustion, while cutting token use by 84% [25]. The memory tool also pairs with server-side compaction: compaction summarizes the conversation, and memory holds what must survive that summarization [26].

Anthropic's context-engineering guidance places memory among three long-horizon techniques [28]:

  • Compaction, which suits long back-and-forth sessions.
  • Structured note-taking, which suits iterative work with milestones.
  • Sub-agents, which suit parallel exploration. Each returns a condensed summary, often 1,000-2,000 tokens.

The guide's Pokémon example shows unprompted note-taking at work. Claude kept step tallies over thousands of game steps, maintained maps and strategy notes, and resumed after context resets by reading its own notes [28].

8.2 Claude Code: CLAUDE.md plus auto memory

Claude Code keeps two complementary stores, and both are loaded at session start [27]:

CLAUDE.md files Auto memory
Writer Human Claude
Content Instructions, rules Learnings, patterns
Scope Org / project / user Per repository, shared across worktrees
Load policy Every session; imports via @path (max 4 hops) MEMORY.md index: first 200 lines or 25KB

Auto memory lives in ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/. It holds a MEMORY.md index with one line per memory, plus topic files whose frontmatter records a type: user, feedback, project or reference [27]. Only the index is pre-injected. Topic files are read on demand with ordinary file tools. When the index nears its limit, the harness reminds Claude to "keep one line per entry, move detail into topic files, and merge or drop stale entries" [27].

The documented write policy is explicitly selective [27]:

  • Claude skips anything it can derive from the code or git history, and anything CLAUDE.md already says.
  • It does not save something every session; it saves only what would help in a future conversation.
  • Subagents do not inherit the main conversation's auto memory and keep separate directories.

This design shows the index-plus-lazy-load pattern clearly: a bounded, always-present table of contents with unbounded detail behind it.

9. Other Research Designs Worth Knowing

  • A-Mem (Xu et al., NeurIPS 2025) applies the Zettelkasten method [32]. Each memory becomes a note with LLM-generated keywords, tags, a contextual description, an embedding and links to related notes. Memory evolution means a new note can update the descriptions and attributes of older linked notes. The authors report gains across six foundation models.
  • MemOS (2025) treats memory as a schedulable system resource [33]. It packages memory in MemCubes whose payload is plaintext, activation (KV cache) or parametric (for example, LoRA) memory, with metadata for governance. This extends "memory" beyond retrieved text to cached activations and weights.
  • MIRIX (2025) splits memory across six typed stores (Core, Episodic, Semantic, Procedural, Resource and Knowledge Vault), each run by its own manager agent under a meta memory manager [34]. The authors report 85.4% on LoCoMo, plus 35% higher accuracy than RAG on ScreenshotVQA with 99.9% less storage.
  • LongMemEval (Wu et al., ICLR 2025) is the benchmark most later systems cite [31]. It has 500 questions over timestamped multi-session histories and tests five abilities: information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates and abstention. The authors found that commercial assistants and long-context LLMs lose about 30% accuracy over sustained interactions. They propose session decomposition, fact-augmented key expansion and time-aware query expansion as design fixes. They also note that LoCoMo does not test recall of assistant-provided information or reasoning over updated user information [31].

10. Comparison

System Primary substrate Write policy (who/when) Reconciliation Read policy Public latency/cost signal
MemGPT (2023) [1] Prompt tiers + recall log + vector archive Agent, hot path, pressure-triggered Agent edits working context; recursive summary on eviction Agent pages in via search tools DMR 92.5% (GPT-4) vs 32.1% baseline
Letta / Letta Code [2][3][5] Memory blocks in git-tracked MemFS + message search Agent hot path + sleep-time agent Agent/sleeper rewrites blocks Blocks always in prompt; recall subagent Sleep-time: ~5x less test-time compute [6]
Mem0 v1/v2 (2025) [8] Vector facts (+ graph for Mem0g) Pipeline after each message pair LLM ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NONE Top-k retrieval per query p95 total 1.44 s vs 17.1 s full context
Mem0 v3 (2026) [9] Append-only facts + entity links Single-pass extraction ADD-only, linked_memory_ids Fused semantic + BM25 + entity, time-aware ~7K tokens, ~1 s p50 (self-reported)
Zep / Graphiti [12][13] Bi-temporal KG: episodes, entities, communities Pipeline per episode Edge invalidation with validity intervals Hybrid cosine/BM25/BFS + rerankers ~1.6K vs 115K tokens; 2.58 s vs 28.9 s
LangMem [17] LangGraph BaseStore namespaces Hot-path tools or background manager LLM consolidation; profiles overwrite Semantic search + filters Not published
ChatGPT [19][21] Saved facts + generated history summary Explicit ("remember") + automatic Opaque Pre-injected every turn Not published
Claude apps [22][24] Topics / summary + raw chat search In-chat topic saves (new); 24 h synthesis (legacy) User-editable topics Profile injected; tool search on demand Not published
Claude memory tool [26] Developer-hosted /memories files Agent via file commands Agent str_replace/delete Agent views directory first +39% with context editing (internal eval) [25]
Claude Code auto memory [27] MEMORY.md index + topic files Agent, selective Agent merges/drops stale entries Index pre-loaded (200 lines/25KB); topics lazy Not published

Key Takeaways for System Designers

  1. Design the write path first. Read-side retrieval is mostly a solved RAG problem (hybrid search plus reranking, as in Chapter 5). The differences between memory systems come from what they store, when, and how they reconcile conflicts [8][12][17].
  2. Do not destroy history. LLM-chosen UPDATE/DELETE silently loses facts. Zep's validity intervals and Mem0's 2026 ADD-only redesign converge on append, link, and resolve at read time with temporal ranking [9][12][14].
  3. Make time a first-class field. Store both when a fact was true and when the system learned it. Resolve relative dates against the episode's timestamp. LongMemEval's temporal-reasoning and knowledge-update categories are where naive memories fail [12][31].
  4. Use a small always-on profile plus on-demand retrieval. ChatGPT and Claude converged on this split from opposite starting points. Claude Code's 200-line index with lazy topic files is a concrete, bounded version [21][24][27].
  5. Move consolidation off the hot path. Reflection, deduplication and summarization belong in background or sleep-time jobs. Reserve hot-path writes for facts the user explicitly asked to keep [5][6][17].
  6. Try files and good tools before building a bespoke store. A filesystem agent hit 74% on LoCoMo [7]. Anthropic's memory tool and Letta's MemFS are both file-shaped [3][26]. Files are inspectable, diffable and easy for users to edit.
  7. Scope memory aggressively. Namespace by user, project and agent (LangMem namespaces, Claude project memories, Mem0 user/session/agent scopes). Cross-context leakage is both a quality bug and a privacy bug [9][17][24].
  8. Treat memory writes as a security boundary. Automatic writes from untrusted content make prompt injections persistent (SpAIware). Validate paths, cap sizes, filter sensitive categories, show writes to the user, and allow pause and reset [24][26][35].
  9. Distrust cross-vendor leaderboards. LoCoMo and LongMemEval scores for the same system differ by tens of points across vendor reports, and harness errors have been publicly conceded [11][15]. Run your own evaluation on your own conversation distribution, including knowledge-update and abstention cases.
  10. Budget the ingestion LLM. Graph and fact extraction cost several LLM calls per episode and need structured-output-capable models [13]. Measure write-path cost and failure rate, not only read latency.
