20. Production RAG Operations: Ingestion, Freshness, Migrations, Latency, Cost, Observability, Caching and Debugging

Overview

Most RAG literature is about the query path: how to chunk, embed, retrieve, rerank and prompt. Teams that have run RAG for a year or more report something else. The hard problems live in the data plane and the operations around it:

  • keeping an index synchronized with a changing source of truth, including deletes and permission changes;
  • changing the embedding model without downtime or a recall cliff;
  • keeping a multi-stage pipeline within a latency SLO;
  • predicting and controlling cost at the storage, embedding and generation layers;
  • seeing what happened inside a single failing request, and turning that into a fix.

Barnett et al. summarize the core lesson of their three-case-study experience report: a RAG system's robustness evolves over time and cannot be fully designed in up front, and validation is really only feasible during operation [1]. A 2026 paper by Budigi and Sirigiri makes a similar point from the infrastructure side. It argues that production RAG failures mostly originate in the data layer, not the language model, and names staleness, access-control fragility and "query composition explosion" across split systems as the three dominant failure modes [39].

This chapter treats RAG as an operational system. It covers ingestion and incremental indexing (Section 1), freshness, deletes and permissions (Section 2), index maintenance inside vector engines (Section 3), re-embedding migrations (Section 4), latency budgets (Section 5), cost modeling (Section 6), caching at four layers (Section 7), observability and tracing (Section 8), and failure modes with debugging playbooks (Section 9). Case studies from Notion, Cursor, Uber, Dropbox, Pinecone, turbopuffer and Microsoft GraphRAG are woven through.

A note on sourcing: numbers here come from vendor docs, company engineering blogs and papers. Vendor-reported figures are labelled as such, and figures that only appear in secondary coverage are marked approximate.

1. Ingestion pipelines and incremental indexing

1.1 The canonical ingestion pipeline

Every production system examined here has the same skeleton. It differs mainly in how changes are detected and how much work is skipped.

  sources (wiki, drive, tickets, code, DB)
        |  connectors: full crawl + webhooks / CDC / polling
        v
  +--------------+   +------------+   +-----------+   +------------------+
  | fetch + ACLs |-->| parse /    |-->| chunk +   |-->| change detection |
  | + metadata   |   | normalize  |   | enrich    |   | (hash per doc /  |
  +--------------+   +------------+   +-----------+   |  per chunk)      |
                                                      +--------+---------+
                                     unchanged: skip <---------+
                                                               | changed / new
                                                               v
                              +-------------------+    +----------------+
                              | embed (batch GPU  |--->| upsert vectors |
                              | or API, cached by |    | + lexical idx  |
                              | content hash)     |    | + metadata     |
                              +-------------------+    +-------+--------+
                                                               |
                       record manager / docstore  <------------+
                       (source_id -> {chunk ids, hashes, ts, model ver})
                                                               |
                                    cleanup: delete stale ids  v

The component that separates a demo from a production system is the record manager, sometimes called the docstore, page-state table or manifest. It maps each source document to the chunk IDs and content hashes currently in the index. Without it you cannot answer "which vectors belong to the document that was just edited or deleted?", and the index drifts.

1.2 Framework implementations: LangChain and LlamaIndex

LangChain indexing API. LangChain's index() function pairs a vector store with a RecordManager that records a hash of each document, its write time and its source ID [2]. Its cleanup modes encode the main design choices:

  • None: deduplicate only. Nothing is ever deleted.
  • incremental: as each batch is written, delete older versions of documents from the same source. Stale data is visible only briefly. If one source's chunks span several batches, some work is repeated. The docs say the end state is correct but the process is "not 100% efficient" [2].
  • full: cleanup runs after all batches are written. Any document not seen in this run is deleted, which is the only mode that catches deletions at the source. The loader must therefore return the entire dataset. A partial load would wipe valid content [2].
  • scoped_full (added in langchain-core 0.3.25): full-style cleanup limited to the source IDs seen in the run. It tracks those IDs in memory and suits loaders that cannot return everything at once [2].

The documented caveats are operationally important. Do not use the API on a store that was populated by other means, because the record manager cannot know about those vectors. The vector store must support add-by-ID and delete-by-ID. Cleanup depends on a time-based mechanism (write timestamps), so clock skew between writers matters. Document IDs are derived from hashes and cannot be user-specified [2].

LlamaIndex IngestionPipeline. LlamaIndex attaches a persistent docstore to an ingestion pipeline and offers three strategies [3][4]:

  • UPSERTS (the default): re-run transformations when a document ID is new or its hash has changed.
  • DUPLICATES_ONLY: skip only exact hash duplicates.
  • UPSERTS_AND_DELETE: also delete documents missing from the current input.

Older versions silently fall back to DUPLICATES_ONLY when no vector store is attached [4], a quiet behavioral change worth checking in tests. The pipeline also caches transformation outputs, so re-running unchanged nodes through the same transformations, including embedding, costs nothing.

Lesson. Both frameworks make deletion an explicit, opt-in mode that needs a complete view of the source. That is the root cause of many "ghost document" incidents, discussed in Section 2.

1.3 Case study: Notion's dual-path pipeline and Page State

Notion's February 2026 retrospective, "Two years of vector search at Notion: 10x scale, 1/10th cost", is one of the most detailed public accounts of operating RAG ingestion at scale [5]. The figures below are from that post and from secondary summaries of it [6].

Launch architecture. Indexing had two paths:

  • an offline path, in which Spark batch jobs chunked existing pages, called an embedding API and bulk-loaded vectors into the vector database;
  • an online path, in which Kafka consumers processed individual page edits in near real time.

To add capacity, Notion chose not to reshard under live traffic. It created new index clusters tagged with a generation ID and routed new workspaces to them [5][6].

  page edits --> Kafka --> online consumers --+
                                              |      +-------------------+
  historical pages --> Spark batch -----------+----> | embed + upsert to |
                                                     | vector DB (gen N) |
  routing table: workspace_id -> generation  ------> +-------------------+

Redesign. Over two years Notion reports roughly 10x scale at about one-tenth the cost [5]. The secondary summaries attribute this to several changes [6]:

  1. A migration to turbopuffer, an object-storage-first engine, including a full re-index and a move to a newer embedding model. Each namespace is an independent index, so the sharding and generation-routing logic disappeared. Reported savings were 60% on search-engine spend and 35% on AWS EMR compute.
  2. A Page State system that hashes page text and metadata separately. Only changed spans are re-embedded, a reported 70% reduction in data volume sent for embedding.
  3. A move of the near-real-time embedding pipeline from Spark plus an external embedding API to Ray on Anyscale with self-hosted models, starting July 2025. CPU preprocessing and GPU inference run in one pipeline, removing an S3 hand-off.
  4. Query latency improving from about 70-100 ms to about 50-70 ms (approximate, per secondary summaries).

Lessons.

  • Change detection at sub-document granularity is the biggest cost lever in ingestion.
  • Choosing a storage engine whose unit of isolation (the namespace) matches the tenant boundary removes a whole class of operational work.
  • A full re-index is easiest to justify when it is bundled with an engine or model migration you were going to do anyway.

1.4 Case study: Cursor's Merkle-tree sync and index reuse

Code indexing is an extreme incremental-indexing workload: many clients, frequent small edits, and near-duplicate corpora. Cursor's "Securely indexing large codebases" post describes the approach [7].

  • Merkle-tree change detection. The client computes a cryptographic hash of every file. Each folder hash is derived from its children's hashes. Client and server compare trees from the root down and descend only where hashes differ, so an edit costs O(depth) comparisons rather than a full scan [7].
  • Index reuse across teammates. Clones of the same repository average 92% similarity across users within an organization. Cursor therefore reuses an existing teammate's index instead of building from scratch, cutting time-to-first-query on the largest repos "from hours to seconds" [7].
  • Matching and seeding (secondary source). A third-party analysis reports how the matching works [8]. The client computes a simhash summarizing its file-hash distribution, and the server finds the nearest existing index. If similarity exceeds a threshold, the new namespace is seeded with turbopuffer's copy_from_namespace. The same analysis says content hashes double as embedding-cache keys, so unchanged chunks are never re-embedded.
 client                                   server
 +-----------------+   root hash      +----------------------+
 | Merkle tree of  |----------------->| stored tree per      |
 | file hashes     |<-- diff paths ---| namespace            |
 +--------+--------+                  +----------+-----------+
          | changed files only                    |
          v                                       v
   chunk (AST) -> hash -> [embedding cache hit?] -> embed -> upsert

Lesson. Content-addressed chunks give you three properties at once: delta sync, embedding caching and cross-tenant deduplication. Where data is legitimately shared, as with identical code, deduplication can turn a cold-start problem into a copy.

1.5 Case study: Uber Genie's Spark ETL

Uber's on-call copilot Genie ingests internal wiki (Engwiki) and Stack Overflow content through a custom Spark application [31]. Data prep produces a dataframe of (source link, content). Embeddings are computed on Spark executors and pushed into Uber's in-house vector database. Secondary coverage names it Sia and describes a "pusher" with bootstrap and merge jobs [32]. A separate ETL joins Genie's responses, from Hive, with Slack metadata and user feedback, and feeds an LLM-as-judge evaluator [31].

The pattern to note is that the evaluation pipeline is itself a batch data pipeline that sits alongside ingestion. A later Uber iteration, Enhanced Agentic RAG, reported a 27% relative increase in acceptable answers and a 60% relative drop in incorrect advice in the security/privacy domain [32].

1.6 Case study: GraphRAG incremental updates

Graph-based indexes are harder to maintain incrementally because new content can change global structure. Microsoft's GraphRAG 1.0 added an update command. It computes deltas between the existing index and new content and merges them "to minimize re-indexing". Microsoft also notes that new content can alter the community structure enough that much of the index must be recomputed anyway [35]. LLM caching is on by default, so re-runs over unchanged content are much cheaper. By default, update outputs go to a separate update_output/ directory so the live index is not overwritten [35]. The archived Azure GraphRAG Solution Accelerator does not support incremental indexing; adding documents there means a re-index [36].

Lesson. Derived artifacts such as summaries, community reports and contextualized chunks have their own invalidation rules, which can be far coarser than per-chunk hashing.

2. Freshness, deletes and permissions

2.1 Measuring freshness

Treat freshness as an SLO with three measured lags:

  t_src_change --(detect lag)--> t_event --(pipeline lag)--> t_indexed
           --(engine visibility lag)--> t_queryable

Each lag has a different owner:

  • Detection lag depends on the connector. Webhooks or change data capture (CDC) take seconds. Polling takes as long as the polling interval. Nightly full crawls take up to 24 hours.
  • Pipeline lag depends on queueing, batching and embedding throughput.
  • Engine visibility lag depends on the store. Pinecone's serverless architecture acknowledges a write once it reaches a write-ahead log on object storage. An index builder pulls up to 10,000 records at a time into an in-memory memtable, and those records are queryable before they are flushed. Pinecone says "seconds is the norm" for freshness [9][10]. Pinecone also offers an eventually consistent read mode that bypasses the memtable for lower latency and higher availability, at the cost of a small amount of staleness [10]. turbopuffer writes each batch as a WAL file in object storage, and a namespace commits at most one WAL entry per second, with concurrent writes batched [11].

Dropbox Dash relies on periodic syncs plus webhooks for real-time changes. Secondary coverage notes that index-based retrieval "presents freshness challenges if rate limits aren't managed well" [34]: source API rate limits often set the floor for detection lag.

2.2 Deletes: the most common correctness bug

Practitioner write-ups repeatedly identify deletes as the main freshness failure [40]:

  • Ingestion code is usually written for inserts, with updates and deletes added later.
  • A row that has been hard-deleted from the source cannot be queried, so a timestamp-polling connector never learns it is gone. The orphaned vectors stay retrievable indefinitely.

The fixes, in increasing order of robustness:

  1. Full-scan reconciliation. Periodically list all source IDs and delete index entries not in the set. This is LangChain full/scoped_full or LlamaIndex UPSERTS_AND_DELETE [2][3]. It is correct but expensive, and dangerous if the listing is partial.
  2. Log-based CDC. Tools such as Debezium emit explicit delete events from the database log [40].
  3. Soft deletes with tombstones in the source, propagated as a deleted=true metadata update and filtered at query time, then physically purged later.
  4. Idempotent keys. Key every write by (source_id, version), so retries and out-of-order events converge instead of duplicating [40].

A subtle variant is the edit that shrinks a document. If a 10-chunk page becomes 7 chunks and the pipeline upserts chunks 0-6 by position, chunks 7-9 survive as orphans. The record manager must delete the full previous chunk-ID set for the source, not only overwrite it.

2.3 Permission freshness

Access-control lists (ACLs) are freshness-sensitive data with security consequences:

  • A nightly sync can let a departed employee query sensitive documents for hours [43].
  • Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases' managed ACL filtering says explicitly that it is not a security boundary. Permission changes are not reflected until the next ingestion job unless the connector supports real-time ACL verification [37].
  • Azure AI Search documents that changing SharePoint permissions without triggering an update leaves stale ACLs on already-ingested files [43].

Recommended practice [42][43]:

  • Store ACL principals as chunk metadata and filter inside the vector query. Post-filtering wastes context and can silently collapse recall when most of the top-k results are unauthorized.
  • Subscribe to permission-change events and run periodic full reconciliation.
  • Set an explicit staleness target, for example five minutes.
  • Include the permission scope in every cache key (Section 7).

Budigi and Sirigiri go further. They argue for one transactional store, PostgreSQL with pgvector and HNSW, so that similarity, freshness, filtering and tenant isolation are evaluated in a single SQL query, removing the cross-system consistency gaps [39].

3. Index maintenance inside the vector engine

3.1 Graph indexes under churn

HNSW and similar graph indexes are optimized for reads, not mutation. Most engines implement delete as a tombstone: the node stays in the graph for routing but is filtered from results, and a background job repairs the graph later. Consequences seen in practice:

  • Recall drift. As the deleted fraction rises, searches route through dead nodes, and neighbor lists fragment under insert/delete cycles. Practitioners recommend incremental writes plus periodic full rebuilds, for example weekly or monthly [40].
  • Cleanup cost. Weaviate runs tombstone cleanup periodically, every cleanupIntervalSeconds. Newer versions expose TOMBSTONE_DELETION_MIN/MAX_PER_CYCLE and a concurrency knob that defaults to half the available cores. For around 300M objects per shard, Weaviate's guidance suggests starting at 1M/10M per cycle [13]. Users report CPU spikes at tombstone_cleanup_begin after bulk deletes [13].
  • Disk not reclaimed. One Weaviate forum report describes deleting about 600k vectors with no change in LSM store size even after cleanup finished. A maintainer explained that space is not freed until segments compact [14].
  • Non-determinism after compaction. Rebuilding a graph after compaction can yield different neighbors, because insertion order and deletion state shape the edges. Golden-set retrieval tests can therefore change after a compaction with no code change.

3.2 Log-structured engines

Object-storage-first engines turn mutation into an LSM-style problem. In Pinecone, the memtable flushes immutable L0 "slabs" to object storage, and compaction merges L0 slabs into larger L1 slabs [9][10]. turbopuffer keeps object storage as the source of truth, with NVMe and RAM caches for hot namespaces [11][12]. Deletes and updates become log entries, and compaction absorbs the graph-repair cost. Operationally you trade in-place graph repair for compaction scheduling, and cold-cache latency becomes the main tail-latency risk (Section 5).

4. Re-embedding migrations

Changing the embedding model invalidates every stored vector: the old and new vector spaces are not comparable. Changing chunking settings has the same effect. Elastic's semantic_text documentation states that updated chunking settings are not applied to existing documents until they are reindexed [17]. A practitioner essay adds a quieter risk: even a "better" model silently re-ranks the whole corpus, so queries that used to work can regress [41].

4.1 Strategy catalogue

Strategy Downtime Extra serving cost Recall during migration Rollback Notes / sources
In-place re-index Yes, or a mixed state None Broken while mixed Hard Rarely acceptable
Blue-green collection + alias swap None ~2x storage during copy Old model until cutover Swap alias back Dual-write during backfill; needs the source text [15]
Named-vector side-by-side None Extra vector per point Old model until cutover Trivial Collection must use named vectors; updates must write both [15]
Shadow index + gradual traffic shift None ~2x during ramp Measured per cohort Feature flag Ramp by percentage while watching retrieval metrics [41]
Query-side adapter (Drift-Adapter) Near zero Adapter cost only ~95-99% of re-embed recall (paper) Remove adapter Defers full re-embedding [16]

4.2 Blue-green and named vectors (Qdrant pattern)

Qdrant's zero-downtime guide gives two concrete recipes [15]:

  1. New collection. Create a second collection for the new model, dual-write all changes to both, backfill by re-embedding the original text (from the primary database, or from payloads stored on the points), then switch search over.
  2. Named vectors. Add a second named vector to each point in the existing collection, backfill it, and switch the query to the new vector name. No data copy is needed and rollback is trivial. Two conditions apply: the collection must have been created with named vectors, and the dual-write logic must update both vectors on every update, or they diverge [15]. The guide notes that deletes are naturally safe in the named-vector approach, but must be mirrored to both collections in the blue-green approach.
            writes ---------------+-------------------+
                                  v                   v
                         +--------------+     +--------------+
   queries --> alias --> | coll_v1      |     | coll_v2      | <-- backfill
               "docs"    | (model A)    |     | (model B)    |     worker
                         +--------------+     +--------------+
   cutover: point alias "docs" -> coll_v2 ; keep v1 for rollback window

Operational checklist distilled from these sources:

  • Persist the raw chunk text and chunk boundaries. Without them you cannot re-embed.
  • Store embedding_model_version on every vector, and refuse queries that mix spaces.
  • Freeze or dual-write during backfill, and reconcile the deletes that landed during the copy.
  • Run the golden-set retrieval evaluation on both indexes before cutover, then ramp traffic gradually and never flip 100% at once [41].
  • Budget beyond the embedding API bill: re-chunking, write amplification, index build CPU, and double storage for the rollback window [41].

4.3 Drift-Adapter: bridging spaces instead of re-embedding

Vejendla's Drift-Adapter (EMNLP 2025) takes a different route. It learns a lightweight map from new-model query embeddings into the legacy space, so the existing ANN index keeps serving while full re-embedding is deferred or skipped [16]. Three parameterizations are compared: orthogonal Procrustes, low-rank affine, and a small residual MLP. Each is trained on a small sample of paired old/new embeddings. On MTEB text corpora and a 1M-item CLIP image upgrade, the paper reports recovery of 95-99% of full-re-embedding Recall@10/MRR, under 10 microseconds of added query latency, and over 100x lower recompute cost than full re-indexing or dual-index serving [16].

Treat these as the authors' own results. The approach also caps quality at what the old document embeddings can express, so it is a bridge, not a destination.

5. Latency budgets

5.1 Where the time goes

A typical synchronous RAG request is a chain of network hops:

 client
   |-- auth/ACL lookup ............ 5-50 ms   (often underestimated)
   |-- query rewrite (LLM, opt.) .. 100-500 ms
   |-- query embedding ............ 5-50 ms
   |-- ANN + BM25 (parallel) ...... 5-100 ms  (cold object-store: 100s of ms)
   |-- rerank (cross-encoder) ..... 30-400 ms (depends on candidates x length)
   |-- prompt assembly + fetch .... 10-80 ms
   |-- LLM prefill  -> TTFT ....... dominant for long contexts
   '-- LLM decode ................. dominates total wall time

The ranges in the diagram are illustrative. The sourced numbers are these:

  • NVIDIA's enterprise RAG sizing guide attributes about 80% of RAG time-to-first-token (TTFT) to LLM prefill over the augmented prompt. Reranking is about 10%, embedding about 5%, and vector search and the RAG server each under 2% [27]. It suggests scaling a component once it exceeds those shares, for example the reranker above 10% of TTFT [27].
  • A ZeroEntropy playbook works through a 700 ms p95 search-request budget: first-pass retrieval 30-50 ms, a large cross-encoder reranker 300-400 ms, assembly and network 40-80 ms, and an LLM summary 150-300 ms. It notes that about half the reranker time is per-batch model-load and tokenization overhead [28].
  • Dropbox Dash reportedly targeted sub-2-second responses for over 95% of queries [34]. Dropbox's earlier search-engine work found that metadata fetches for ACL checks and result decoration, not retrieval itself, drove much of the latency. The team found this only by instrumenting each component [33].
  • turbopuffer's docs report a p50 of 874 ms for a first query against a 1M-document namespace read cold from object storage, versus 14 ms once cached on NVMe [11]. Cache warmth is therefore a first-class tail-latency variable for object-storage engines, and turbopuffer introduced namespace pinning (billed in GB-hours) for hot namespaces in 2026 (approximate, per secondary sources) [11].
  • RAGCache, discussed in Section 7, overlaps retrieval with inference to hide retrieval latency [23].

5.2 Budgeting practice

  1. Set a p95 budget per stage, not just end-to-end. Track percentiles per stage in traces, since averages hide the cold-cache and reranker-batch tails.
  2. Run lexical and dense retrieval in parallel, and bound the reranker's candidate count. Reranking around 20 candidates with a small cross-encoder is a commonly cited compromise [28].
  3. Stream tokens. For chat, TTFT is the user-perceived metric, and it is dominated by prefill, which grows with context length. Retrieving fewer, better chunks therefore reduces latency directly.
  4. Pre-warm caches for tenants likely to be active, or pin hot namespaces on object-storage engines.
  5. Make ACL and metadata lookups batchable and cacheable. They are a known hidden cost [33].

6. Cost modeling

6.1 Cost components

A useful model splits cost into one-time, steady-state and per-query terms:

 C_total = C_ingest_once + C_reembed_per_migration
         + months * (C_storage + C_index_compute + C_churn_embedding)
         + queries * (C_query_embed + C_search + C_rerank + C_llm_in + C_llm_out)

Reference points from public sources:

  • Embedding. OpenAI lists text-embedding-3-small at $0.02 per 1M tokens and text-embedding-3-large at $0.13 [20]. Third parties report a 50% Batch API discount, to $0.01 per 1M, which is not confirmed on the page as extracted. Treat it as approximate. For most corpora, the initial embedding bill is small next to LLM generation. The operational cost is churn re-embedding and migrations, which is why Notion's hash-based Page State (reported 70% volume reduction) mattered [6].
  • Contextualized chunks. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval prepends LLM-generated context to each chunk. Secondary coverage reports an estimated one-time cost of about $1.02 per million document tokens using prompt caching, with failed top-20 retrievals reduced by about 35% (contextual embeddings), about 49% (plus contextual BM25) and about 67% (plus reranking) [38]. Enrichment like this multiplies ingestion cost and must be re-run on every content change, so it has to be included in the churn term.
  • Storage tiers. turbopuffer's documentation gives approximate per-GB-month prices of about $0.02 for object storage, about $0.08 for SSD and about $2 for DRAM [11]. This roughly 100x spread is the economic argument for object-storage-first engines when most namespaces are cold. Notion's reported 60% search-engine savings after moving to turbopuffer is a concrete instance [6].
  • Vector compression. Hugging Face and Mixedbread report that int8 scalar quantization gives 4x smaller vectors and binary quantization gives 32x. For mxbai-embed-large-v1, roughly 97% (int8) and roughly 96% (binary, with rescoring) of float32 retrieval performance is retained (approximate, from benchmark tables quoted secondhand) [18]. The recommended pattern is to search a binary index, then rescore the top candidates with int8 or float32 vectors. Matryoshka truncation keeps 95.8% of performance at 3x compression for a Nomic model [18]. Vespa documents combining Matryoshka with binary quantization [19]. The int8 calibration set strongly affects quality, so recalibrate after domain shift [18].
  • Generation. LLM input tokens usually dominate per-query cost, because retrieved context is long. Anthropic's prompt caching prices cache reads at 0.1x the base input price and 5-minute cache writes at 1.25x (1-hour writes at 2x) [21][22]. Anthropic advertised cost reductions of up to 90% and latency reductions of up to 85% for long prompts. In its own test, a cached 100k-token prompt reportedly dropped from 11.5 s to 2.4 s [21].

6.2 Cost levers ranked by typical impact

  1. Fewer, better context tokens per query, through reranking and tighter top-k. This also cuts latency (Section 5).
  2. Prompt caching for stable prefixes, such as system prompts, tool definitions and frequently reused documents.
  3. Change detection that avoids re-embedding and re-enriching unchanged content.
  4. A storage tier matched to the access pattern: object storage for cold tenants, RAM or SSD only for hot ones.
  5. Quantization and dimension truncation, with rescoring.
  6. Self-hosting embedding models once volume justifies GPUs. Notion's Ray migration is an example [6].

7. Caching

RAG systems can cache at four layers. Each has its own invalidation problem.

Layer Key Value Hit-rate driver Invalidation risk Sources
Embedding cache hash(chunk text, model ver) vector content churn Model change: must include model version [7][8]
Retrieval / semantic cache query embedding (+ tenant, ACL scope) retrieved ids or final answer repeated intents Stale answers after doc change; false positives; cross-tenant leaks [25][26][42]
Provider prompt cache exact prompt prefix provider-side KV state stable prefix reuse within TTL Any byte change in the prefix misses [21][22]
KV cache of retrieved docs chunk id (+ position) attention KV tensors popular chunks Non-prefix reuse needs recomputation [23][24]

7.1 Semantic caches

A semantic cache returns a previous answer when a new query embeds close to a cached one. GPTCache's documentation notes that such caches produce false positives on hits and false negatives on misses, and it reports hit ratio, latency and recall as the metrics to watch [25]. Vendor guidance on similarity thresholds varies widely, from about 0.75 to 0.97 cosine. One vendor table pairs 0.95 with a 15-25% hit rate and 1-3% false positives, and 0.90 with a 35-55% hit rate and 7-15% false positives [26]. These are vendor figures without a published method.

The defensible practice is to label several hundred real query pairs from your own traffic, choose the threshold that meets a precision target, and consider per-category thresholds [26]. Two operational rules:

  • Scope cache keys by tenant and permission set. A shared namespace with a loose threshold can serve one tenant's answer to another [42].
  • Invalidate or TTL entries whose supporting documents changed. This requires storing the source document IDs alongside each cached answer.

7.2 Provider prompt caching

For RAG, put stable content first (system prompt, instructions, tool schemas, sometimes a fixed "core corpus") and retrieved chunks after it. Anthropic's cache has a short default lifetime that is refreshed on each hit, and the 1.25x write premium means sparse traffic can make caching cost more than it saves [21][22].

7.3 KV caching of retrieved knowledge

Two systems papers address the fact that retrieved chunks appear in different combinations and orders, which defeats ordinary prefix caching:

  • RAGCache (Peking University and ByteDance) organizes the KV states of retrieved documents in a "knowledge tree" across GPU and host memory. It uses a replacement policy aware of RAG retrieval patterns and overlaps retrieval with inference. It reports up to 4x lower TTFT and up to 2.1x higher throughput than vLLM with Faiss [23].
  • CacheBlend (EuroSys 2025 best paper) reuses precomputed per-chunk KV caches even when they are not a prefix, and selectively recomputes a small subset of tokens to restore cross-attention. It reports 2.2-3.3x lower TTFT and 2.8-5x higher throughput, with quality comparable to full prefill. Sources differ on whether the baseline is prefix caching or full recompute [24]. Because recomputation is pipelined with KV loading, caches can live on SSD; the LMCache team frames this as approaching a 100% KV-cache hit rate for RAG [24].
 retrieved: [c7][c2][c9]  ---> KV store (GPU/CPU/SSD) lookup per chunk
                                   |hit       |hit       |miss
                                   v          v          v
                              [KV c7]    [KV c2]   prefill c9
                                    \        |        /
                                selective recompute of ~few % tokens
                                             v
                                       decode answer

8. Observability and tracing

8.1 What to trace

A RAG trace should let an engineer replay any answer. At minimum, each request records:

  • the raw query, the rewritten queries and the router decision;
  • for each retriever: index name, embedding model version, filters (including ACL scope), top-k IDs with scores, and latency;
  • the reranker's input and output IDs, scores and the cut-off;
  • the final prompt (or a hash plus template version), model, token counts in, out and cached, and TTFT;
  • citations emitted and links to the source document versions;
  • user feedback and any online evaluator scores.

8.2 Standards: OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference

The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions define gen_ai.operation.name values, including embeddings [29], and metrics for token usage and operation duration [29]. Some vendor instrumentation docs also list retrieval as an operation name (approximate; check the current registry). A third-party timeline places a retrieval span and cache-token attributes in recent convention releases (approximate). The conventions remain in Development status, and as of May 2026 they were reported to have moved to a dedicated semantic-conventions-genai repository. Pin a version, and expect attribute renames.

OpenInference, Arize's OpenTelemetry-based convention used by Phoenix, explicitly covers retrieval from vector stores and tool use. Its helpers extract retrieved documents and question/answer/reference triples from spans into dataframes, so evaluators such as Ragas faithfulness and context precision can run over production traces [30].

 app (LangChain / LlamaIndex / custom)
   | OTel SDK + GenAI / OpenInference instrumentation
   v
 OTel collector --> trace store (Phoenix / Langfuse / APM vendor)
                      |
                      +--> sampled traces --> offline evaluators (faithfulness,
                      |                       context precision, citation check)
                      +--> dashboards: p95 per span, cache hit %, $/query,
                                       empty-retrieval %, index lag

8.3 Online metrics worth alerting on

  • Freshness: index lag (p50 and p95 of t_queryable - t_src_change), connector error rate, delete-propagation lag, ACL sync age.
  • Retrieval health: empty or low-score retrieval rate, top-1 score distribution drift (a sudden shift often means a model or index change), percentage of queries with no reranked chunk above threshold.
  • Generation: refusal or "I don't know" rate (high is FP1 Missing Content, low with bad answers is hallucination), citation coverage, answer length drift.
  • Cost and latency: tokens in, out and cached per request, cache hit rates per layer, per-stage p95, cold-namespace query rate.

Uber's Genie shows the loop closing: production responses, Slack metadata and user feedback flow through an ETL into an LLM-as-judge evaluator [31]. Dash-style systems reportedly mine failed retrievals from production traces into test sets [34].

9. Failure modes and debugging playbooks

9.1 A taxonomy

Barnett et al.'s seven failure points come from three deployments in research, education and biomedical settings [1]. Commonly cited labels are:

  1. FP1 Missing Content: the answer is not in the corpus, and the system answers anyway instead of declining.
  2. FP2 Missed Top-Ranked Documents: the answer is in the corpus but ranks below the cut-off.
  3. FP3 Not in Context (consolidation limits): the document was retrieved but dropped during context assembly.
  4. FP4 Not Extracted: the answer is in the context, but the model fails to extract it.
  5. FP5 Wrong Format.
  6. FP6 Incorrect Specificity: the answer is too general or too specific.
  7. FP7 Incomplete.

Operations adds failure classes that the paper does not separate:

  • stale content (index lag);
  • ghost content (undeleted orphans);
  • permission leakage or over-filtering;
  • mixed embedding spaces after a partial migration;
  • cache poisoning or false-positive semantic hits;
  • silent recall drift from index churn or compaction;
  • cold-cache tail latency.

9.2 Triage flow

 bad answer reported
   |
   v
 1. Replay trace. Is the correct source doc in the corpus?  --no--> FP1 / ingestion
   |yes                                                         (connector, parser,
   v                                                             filter, ACL?)
 2. Is the current version indexed? compare src hash vs index --stale--> freshness
   |yes                                                                 playbook
   v
 3. Was it in retriever top-N (pre-rerank)? --no--> FP2: query rewrite, hybrid,
   |yes                                              chunking, model version mix?
   v
 4. Survived rerank / context assembly?  --no--> FP3: reranker, top-k, token budget
   |yes
   v
 5. In prompt but answer wrong?  --yes--> FP4-FP7: prompt, model, format, citations
   |
   v
 6. Was a cache involved? semantic hit / stale prompt cache --> cache playbook

9.3 Playbooks

Playbook A: "It cites a document we deleted."

  1. Look up the chunk IDs in the record manager. If they are missing, they are orphans written outside the indexing API, which LangChain explicitly warns against [2].
  2. Check whether the connector emits delete events. If it polls timestamps, it cannot see hard deletes [40].
  3. Run a scoped full reconciliation for that source.
  4. Purge semantic-cache entries that reference the IDs.
  5. Add a canary: a synthetic document that is created and deleted hourly, with an alert if it remains retrievable after the SLO.

Playbook B: "User saw something they should not have."

  1. Treat it as a security incident first.
  2. Compare the chunk's ACL metadata with the live source ACL. A mismatch means sync lag [37][43].
  3. Check whether a cache served the answer without a permission-scoped key [42].
  4. Fix the filter-in-query path, shorten the ACL sync interval, and consider real-time ACL verification on the final candidates. AWS describes its managed ACL filtering as not a security boundary [37].

Playbook C: "Retrieval quality dropped overnight; no deploy."

  1. Check the top-1 score distribution and the empty-retrieval rate for a step change.
  2. Check whether a background compaction or rebuild ran, since HNSW rebuilds can change neighbors, and whether tombstone counts are rising [13][14].
  3. Check whether any vectors carry a different embedding_model_version, which indicates a partially applied migration [15].
  4. Check whether a parser or connector update changed the chunk text, and therefore the hashes, causing a mass re-embed with a new chunking.
  5. Re-run the golden set against a snapshot if your engine supports one.

Playbook D: "p95 latency doubled."

  1. Break the latency down per span [27][33].
  2. Typical culprits are:
    • cold namespaces on object storage [11];
    • reranker batch size or candidate inflation [28];
    • longer contexts increasing prefill [27];
    • a prompt-cache miss caused by a changed prefix, for example a timestamp in the system prompt [22];
    • ACL lookup fan-out [33].

Playbook E: "Costs jumped."

  1. Split by ingestion and query.
  2. On the ingestion side, look for churn spikes, such as a source that rewrites metadata on every sync and invalidates hashes. Notion's separate hashing of text and metadata addresses this [6]. Also check for enrichment re-runs [38] and GraphRAG community recomputation [35].
  3. On the query side, look at the context-token growth and cache hit rate per layer.

9.4 Comparison: operational posture of reference designs

Design Change detection Delete handling Freshness (public) Migration approach Cost lever highlighted
LangChain indexing API [2] Doc hash + source id incremental / full / scoped_full cleanup Batch-dependent Re-index into a new store Skip unchanged docs
LlamaIndex IngestionPipeline [3] Doc id + hash in docstore UPSERTS_AND_DELETE Batch-dependent Re-run pipeline Transformation cache
Notion [5][6] Hashes of page text and metadata Online Kafka path + rebuilds Near real time Full re-index during engine move 70% less embed volume; 60% search savings
Cursor [7][8] Merkle tree of file hashes Tree diff Periodic client sync (interval undisclosed) Seeding from similar index Index reuse; embed cache
Pinecone serverless [9][10] Client-side WAL + compaction Seconds (vendor) Client-side Object storage + slabs
turbopuffer [11][12] Client-side WAL entries 1 WAL commit/s per namespace copy_from_namespace (reported) ~$0.02/GB-mo object storage
Qdrant migration guide [15] n/a Must mirror in blue-green n/a Collections or named vectors Rollback safety
GraphRAG 1.0 [35] New/changed input files Delta merge Batch update to separate output LLM cache on by default

10. Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Build the record manager first. A durable map from source document to chunk IDs, hashes, embedding-model version and ACLs is what makes updates, deletes, migrations and debugging possible. Neither LangChain nor LlamaIndex will delete anything unless you opt in with a complete view of the source [2][3].
  2. Deletes and permissions are the freshness SLO that matters. Prefer CDC or webhooks with explicit delete events, run periodic full reconciliation, filter ACLs inside the query, and measure delete- and ACL-propagation lag separately from insert lag [37][40][43].
  3. Hash at the finest granularity you can afford. Separate content hashes from metadata hashes. Notion's selective re-embedding and Cursor's Merkle diffing show this is the largest ingestion cost lever [6][7].
  4. Plan every embedding change as a migration. Version every vector, keep the raw text, and use alias or named-vector cutovers with dual writes and a rollback window [15]. Evaluate before and during the ramp. Adapters such as Drift-Adapter can buy time but cap quality at the old index [16].
  5. Expect index entropy. Tombstones, compaction and rebuilds change recall and disk usage without code changes [13][14]. Schedule rebuilds, and re-run golden sets after them.
  6. Budget latency per stage, with percentiles. Prefill usually dominates TTFT, so fewer, better context tokens save both latency and money [27]. Watch the hidden costs: ACL and metadata fetches [33], reranker batches [28] and cold object-storage reads [11].
  7. Model cost in three terms: one-time, churn and per-query. Enrichment such as contextual chunks and graph summaries moves cost into the churn term [35][38]. Storage-tier choice and quantization change the steady-state term by an order of magnitude [11][18].
  8. Cache at the right layer, with the right key. Embedding caches are keyed by content and model version. Semantic caches need tenant and ACL scope plus a doc-change invalidation path [26][42]. Prompt caches need byte-stable prefixes [22]. KV-cache systems such as RAGCache and CacheBlend target prefill directly [23][24].
  9. Make every answer replayable. Trace retriever inputs, outputs, scores, model versions and prompt versions with OpenTelemetry GenAI or OpenInference conventions. Pin the convention version, because the spec is still in Development status [29][30].
  10. Debug with a fixed decision tree. Walk each case through: in corpus, then current, then retrieved, then survived rerank, then in prompt, then extracted. Each failure point maps to a different owner and fix [1]. Feed every resolved incident back into the evaluation set [31][34].

21. RAG System Design Interview Playbook: Enterprise Q&A, Support Bots, Code Assistants, and Web Answer Engines

Overview

"Design a retrieval-augmented assistant" has become a standard prompt in ML, AI-engineer, and forward-deployed-engineer interviews. Typical versions include "design a system that answers employee questions from our internal wiki", "design a customer-support bot", "design context retrieval for a coding assistant", and "design a Perplexity-style answer engine" [1][2][3]. Prep platforms and candidate reports agree on what separates strong answers. Strong candidates treat retrieval as the hard part and generation as the easy part. They scope the corpus (size, change rate, formats such as scanned PDFs and tables) before naming any technology. They spend the closing minutes on evaluation and failure diagnosis: "a wrong RAG answer is either a retrieval failure or a generation failure, and the interview is mostly about proving you can tell which" [2][4][5].

This chapter is a playbook built on publicly documented production systems. It covers:

  1. A reusable interview framework: the 45-60 minute arc, the requirement questions, and a canonical component diagram.
  2. Back-of-envelope sizing formulas with worked numbers. These are illustrative arithmetic based on published prices and index-memory formulas.
  3. Four reference designs, each anchored to real systems:
    • Enterprise Q&A: Glean, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Uber Genie, Dropbox Dash.
    • Customer support: LinkedIn's knowledge-graph RAG, DoorDash, Klarna, Intercom Fin.
    • Code assistants: GitHub Copilot, Sourcegraph Cody, Cursor, Augment.
    • Web answer engines: Perplexity on Vespa, plus the FreshLLMs line of research.
  4. A comparison table, a bank of common follow-up questions with model answers, and takeaways.

The other chapters of this atlas go deep on components: chunking (Ch. 2), embeddings (Ch. 3), vector databases (Ch. 4), hybrid search (Ch. 5), evaluation (Ch. 11), and security (Ch. 16). This chapter covers how to assemble them under interview time pressure and defend the tradeoffs.

1. The interview framework

1.1 The 45-60 minute arc

One published mock-interview transcript for a corporate RAG platform uses checkpoints at roughly minutes 10, 30, 45, and 60 [3]. Its main advice is to connect each design decision back to a stated requirement or scale number rather than listing technologies. A workable arc:

Minutes Phase What to produce
0-8 Requirements and scoping Users, corpus, freshness, ACLs, latency SLO, quality bar
8-15 Back-of-envelope sizing Chunks, index RAM, QPS, tokens per query, cost per query
15-30 High-level design Offline ingestion path and online answer path, drawn separately
30-45 Deep dives (interviewer picks) Retrieval quality, permissions, freshness, hallucination control
45-55 Evaluation and operations Offline eval set, online metrics, LLM-as-judge, feedback loop
55-60 Follow-ups and evolution Scale x10, multilingual, agentic multi-hop, long context vs RAG

1.2 Requirement questions that change the design

Ask questions whose answers change the architecture. Generic questions do not earn credit.

  • Corpus: How many documents, and how many tokens on average? What formats (HTML, PDF with tables, scans, slides, code, tickets)? What is the change rate? A static manual set and a constantly edited wiki need different ingestion pipelines [2].
  • Permissions: Is the data public to all users or ACL-scoped per user or group? In enterprise settings this is the defining constraint. Educative's framing of enterprise RAG puts access control, citation traceability, and answer accuracy at the center [1].
  • Freshness: Is minutes-stale acceptable (wiki), or must answers reflect seconds-old changes (code edits, stock prices, news)?
  • Latency SLO: Time to first token versus full answer. Interactive chat typically tolerates 1-3 s to first token. IDE autocomplete tolerates far less.
  • Quality bar and risk: Is a wrong answer an annoyance (internal wiki) or a compliance incident (payments support)? This determines whether you need a pre-delivery guardrail and human fallback.
  • Answer form: Free text with citations, structured action (refund, ticket), or code edit?
  • Traffic: Daily active users, queries per user per day, and peak-to-mean ratio.

1.3 The canonical component diagram

Almost every RAG design question reduces to two paths. Draw them separately; interviewers check that you know ingestion is a separate, asynchronous system [3].

OFFLINE / ASYNC INGESTION PATH
 sources --> connectors/crawlers --> parse & clean --> chunk --> enrich
 (wiki, tickets,  (incremental,       (OCR, tables,    (struct-   (title, path,
  code, web)       webhooks, ACLs)     dedupe)          aware)     context blurb)
                                                                  |
          +-------------------+------------------+----------------+
          v                   v                  v
     lexical index       vector index       metadata / ACL store
     (BM25 / inverted)   (HNSW / IVF / BQ)  (doc->groups, freshness)

ONLINE ANSWER PATH
 user --> auth --> query understanding --> hybrid retrieve --> fuse (RRF)
          |        (rewrite, condense,     (BM25 + dense,     |
          |         route, decompose)       ACL pre-filter)   v
          |                                              rerank (cross-enc.)
          |                                                   |
          +--> conversation memory          context assembly (top-k, order,
                                            dedupe, token budget)
                                                   |
                                                   v
                         LLM generation with citations --> guardrails --> user
                                                   |
                        logs, feedback, LLM-judge <-+--> eval sets, dashboards

Each box maps to a documented technique:

  • Contextual enrichment of chunks: Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval prepends an LLM-generated context blurb to each chunk before embedding and BM25 indexing [6].
  • Rank fusion: reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) combines lexical and dense result lists using ranks only, with k typically 60 [7].
  • Reranking: a cross-encoder rescoring stage [6].
  • Retrieval-quality gating: Corrective RAG (CRAG) uses a lightweight evaluator that decides whether to use, refine, discard, or supplement retrieved evidence with web search [8].

1.4 Numbers worth memorizing

Interviewers reward candidates who anchor choices in published data:

  • Contextual Retrieval [6]: contextual embeddings cut the top-20 retrieval failure rate about 35% (5.7% to 3.7%). Adding contextual BM25 brings the reduction to about 49% (2.9%). Adding a reranker brings it to about 67% (1.9%). Gains vary by domain. A critique notes the reduction falls to about 41% on a vague-codebase category [9].
  • Long context vs RAG [10]: the Google DeepMind / Michigan EMNLP 2024 study found long-context models outperform RAG on average when resourced sufficiently, but RAG is far cheaper because it shrinks input tokens. Their Self-Route method routes each query to RAG or long context based on the model's self-reflection, keeping comparable accuracy at much lower cost.
  • Lost in the middle [11]: accuracy follows a U-shape over the position of relevant evidence in the prompt. It is best at the start or end and degrades as context grows. This argues for small, well-ordered contexts rather than stuffing.
  • Binary quantization [12]: 1-bit embeddings cut memory 32x. Rescoring a larger binary candidate set with float32 query vectors preserves about 96% of retrieval quality.
  • RRF [7]: score(d) = sum over lists of 1/(k + rank). k = 60 is the default in many engines.
  • The seven failure points [13]: missing content, missed top-ranked documents, not in context (consolidation), not extracted, wrong format, incorrect specificity, incomplete answer. Barnett et al. also conclude that RAG robustness "evolves rather than is designed in", and that validation is only feasible during operation.

2. Back-of-envelope sizing toolkit

All numbers in this section are illustrative arithmetic. They combine published unit prices and index-memory formulas with assumed workloads. State your assumptions aloud in the interview.

2.1 Corpus to chunks

chunks = documents x avg_tokens_per_doc / (chunk_size - overlap)

OpenAI's hosted file search defaults to 800-token chunks with 400-token overlap. Overlap may be at most half the chunk size, and chunk size ranges from 100 to 4,096 tokens [14]. With a 50% overlap the effective stride is 400 tokens, so chunk count doubles compared with non-overlapping chunks. Say this when you justify a smaller overlap at scale.

2.2 Embedding cost

Third-party price trackers list text-embedding-3-small at about $0.02 per million input tokens, about $0.01 via batch, with 1,536 default dimensions [15]. Embedding cost is therefore usually negligible compared with LLM generation. The real ingestion costs are parsing (OCR, table extraction) and optional LLM enrichment. Anthropic estimated contextual chunk generation at roughly $1.02 per million document tokens with prompt caching [6][9].

2.3 Vector index memory

OpenSearch-style HNSW sizing for float32 vectors is approximately 1.1 x (4·d + 8·M) bytes per vector, where d is the dimension and M the graph degree [16]. Its binary-quantized variant uses 1.1 x (d/8 + 8·M) style terms. The exact constants differ by engine. ScyllaDB, for example, uses N x (D x B + 16m) x 1.2 [16].

Worked example (d = 1,536, M = 16): 1.1 x (6,144 + 128) ≈ 6.9 KB per vector, so about 6.8-6.9 GB per million vectors in RAM.

Chunks float32 HNSW (approx.) Binary-quantized vectors only (d/8 = 192 B)
1 M ~6.9 GB ~0.2 GB (+ graph links)
100 M ~690 GB ~19 GB (+ graph links)
1 B ~6.9 TB ~190 GB (+ graph links)

The lesson: past roughly 100M chunks, a float32 in-memory HNSW is a multi-node, high-RAM deployment. Propose quantization (binary or product quantization) with float rescoring from disk [12], dimension reduction, or sharding by tenant.

2.4 Traffic and tokens

avg_QPS   = DAU x queries_per_user_per_day / 86,400
peak_QPS  ~ 3-10 x avg_QPS (state assumption)
input_tok = system_prompt + history + k_chunks x chunk_tokens + question
LLM_cost  = (input_tok x p_in + output_tok x p_out) x queries

Example: 50,000 employees x 5 questions/day = 250,000 queries/day, which is about 2.9 QPS on average and perhaps 30 QPS at peak. Each query carries 8 chunks x 500 tokens plus about 1,000 tokens of instructions and history, so about 5,000 input tokens. That totals about 1.25 billion input tokens per day. The point to make in the interview: generation tokens, not vector search, dominate cost and latency. The levers are fewer, better chunks (reranking), prompt caching of static prefixes, smaller models for routing and condensation, and caching frequent answers.

2.5 Latency budget (interactive chat, illustrative)

auth + ACL lookup           10-30 ms
query rewrite (small LLM)   100-300 ms   (skip when query is self-contained)
hybrid retrieval            20-100 ms    (BM25 + ANN in parallel)
rerank top-50..100          50-200 ms    (cross-encoder, GPU)
LLM time-to-first-token     300-1000 ms  (depends on model and prompt size)
guardrail check             50-500 ms    (cheap similarity first, LLM judge if needed)

Dropbox's Dash team describes a retrieval target of completing more than 95% of requests within roughly 1-2 seconds. They treat retrieval as the layer that shapes both speed and answer quality [17].

3. Design A: Enterprise Q&A assistant

3.1 Problem

"Employees should ask questions in natural language over wiki, drive, tickets, chat, and email, and get cited answers. They must never see content they lack permission to read."

3.2 Requirements that dominate

  • Permissions are the hard constraint. Microsoft 365 Copilot's semantic index inherits Microsoft Graph security trimming, so users only receive content they can already open [18]. Microsoft's own ISE guidance for custom RAG over SharePoint copies document ACLs (Entra ID object IDs) into index fields at ingestion. It then filters on them at query time, and the ingestion app uses least-privilege Graph permissions (Sites.Selected) [19]. A practitioner warning makes the risk concrete: get ACLs wrong and "you've just built a single search index that ignores years of permission work in the source system" [20].
  • Heterogeneous connectors with incremental sync. Glean describes the foundation as a robust, scalable crawler that connects to all enterprise data, together with its permission rules [21].
  • Mixed query types: navigational ("the Q3 OKR doc"), factual ("what is our parental leave policy"), and people/expertise queries. Glean argues that vector search alone is insufficient. It combines a self-learning language model, lexical search, and a knowledge graph, with authority signals inspired by PageRank [21][22].

3.3 Architecture

 +-----------+   webhooks / polling   +-------------------+
 | SaaS apps |----------------------->| connector workers |--+
 | (wiki,    |   (per-source rate     | fetch content +   |  |
 |  drive,   |    limits, backoff)    | ACLs + activity   |  |
 |  tickets) |                        +-------------------+  |
 +-----------+                                               v
                       +----------------------------------------------+
                       | normalize -> chunk -> embed -> index         |
                       | per-chunk fields: tenant, acl_principals[],  |
                       | source, updated_at, author, doc_type         |
                       +---------------------+------------------------+
                                             |
         +---------------+-------------------+--------------+
         v               v                                  v
   inverted index   vector index (tenant-sharded)   knowledge graph
   (BM25)           with ACL filter fields          (people, docs, teams,
                                                     activity edges)
 ONLINE:
 user -> SSO -> expand principals (user + groups, cached) -> query rewrite
      -> parallel BM25 + ANN with filter acl_principals IN user_principals
      -> RRF -> rerank (+authority/recency/graph features) -> top 5-10
      -> LLM answer with inline citations -> post-check: cited doc still visible?

3.4 Key techniques and tradeoffs

  • Pre-filter versus post-filter for ACLs. Pre-filtering (ACL principals as index filter fields) is safe and gives full recall within the user's visible set. It requires ANN engines that handle selective filters well, and an ACL change triggers re-indexing of metadata. Post-filtering (retrieve top-N, drop unauthorized) is simpler but leaks through timing and counts. It can also return empty results when the user sees only a small slice of the corpus. Third-party analyses of Glean describe it as filtering by permission from the start rather than retrieve-then-filter [23]. Treat that as commentary, not official documentation. Always add a final "can this user still read the cited doc?" check at render time, because ACLs change between indexing and query.
  • RAG over fine-tuning. Glean argues fine-tuning is poorly suited to factual recall and permissioning, and recommends a centralized, permission-aware index with RAG [21]. Uber chose RAG for its on-call copilot Genie mainly for time to market, since fine-tuning needs curated examples and ongoing compute [24].
  • Hybrid retrieval plus reranking is table stakes. Use the 35% / 49% / 67% failure-reduction ladder from Contextual Retrieval to justify each added stage [6].
  • Agentic escalation for hard questions. Dropbox Dash pairs RAG for fast single-shot answers with multi-step agents (planning plus a custom interpreter) for complex tasks [17]. Uber later moved its security and privacy domain to an "Enhanced Agentic RAG" design. After traditional RAG fell short on a curated 100+ query test set, it reported about 27% relative more acceptable answers and about 60% relative fewer incorrect-advice answers (as summarized secondhand) [25].

3.5 Scale and outcomes (public)

Uber Genie launched in September 2023. Secondary summaries of Uber's reports say it served 154 Slack channels and answered more than 70,000 questions, with a 48.9% helpfulness rate and an estimated ~13,000 engineering hours saved [24][25]. Take two lessons from these numbers. A useful internal assistant need not be "right" on every question. And helpfulness must be measured explicitly, because Genie built a user-feedback pipeline and LLM-as-judge evaluation [24].

3.6 Failure modes to name

  • Permission leakage through stale ACLs, flattened group membership, or a non-delegated service connection. Microsoft's guidance warns that a non-delegated Azure AI Search connection has no security trimming [18].
  • Duplicate and outdated documents (five versions of a policy). Mitigate with recency/authority features and dedupe at ingestion.
  • Missing content, the first of Barnett's seven failure points [13]. The system should say "I couldn't find this" rather than synthesize an answer.
  • Tables and scanned PDFs parsed badly. This is a corpus-scoping question to raise early [2].

4. Design B: Customer support bot

4.1 Problem

"Deflect a large share of inbound support conversations with accurate, policy-compliant answers. Hand off to humans gracefully."

4.2 What is different from enterprise Q&A

  • The corpus is smaller and curated: help-center articles, macros, resolved tickets. Permissions are simpler, usually per-tenant or per-customer-account.
  • Risk is higher. Wrong refund or policy statements create financial and compliance exposure, so pre-delivery guardrails and escalation are core components.
  • Conversations are multi-turn. The retrieval query must be distilled from the whole dialogue, not taken from the last message.
  • Actions matter: order lookup, refunds, account changes. The bot needs tools as well as retrieval.

4.3 Reference architectures

DoorDash Dasher support [26]. There are three parts:

  1. A RAG system that condenses the multi-message conversation into the core issue, then retrieves knowledge-base articles and similar previously resolved cases.
  2. An online guardrail. Every response must pass all checks before the Dasher sees it. Summaries describe this as two tiers: a cheap semantic-similarity check, then an LLM evaluator [26].
  3. An offline LLM judge that scores retrieval correctness, response accuracy, grammar, coherence with context, and relevance to the request.

DoorDash reports that the guardrail reduced hallucinations by about 90% and severe compliance issues by about 99%. When guardrail latency is a problem, the system defaults to human agents rather than trade off quality [26].

LinkedIn customer-service KG-RAG [27]. Instead of chunking historical tickets as flat text, LinkedIn builds a knowledge graph from them. The graph preserves each ticket's internal structure (fields such as summary, description, steps to reproduce) as a tree, and links tickets to each other via explicit references and embedding similarity. At query time, the system parses the customer query into entities and intents and retrieves matching ticket sub-graphs. It then generates the answer from those sub-graphs. The paper (SIGIR 2024) reports a 77.6% MRR improvement over a flat-text baseline. After roughly six months in production it reports a 28.6% reduction in median per-issue resolution time.

Klarna [28]. In its first month, Klarna's assistant handled 2.3 million conversations, about two-thirds of its customer-service chats. Klarna equated that to the workload of 700 full-time agents. It operates in 23 markets and more than 35 languages. Klarna reported customer satisfaction on par with humans and a 25% drop in repeat inquiries, with resolution time down from about 11 to under 2 minutes. These are company-reported launch numbers.

Intercom Fin [29]. Third-party guides describe Fin as a bespoke multi-phase RAG pipeline: query refinement, retrieval, reranking, generation, and validation. They say it uses custom retrieval and reranker models trained on customer-service interactions; the phase counts differ between sources. Anthropic's case study reports a 51% average resolution rate across Intercom's customers, and up to 86% for some [29]. Note the metric definition. Guides point out that "assumed" resolutions (the customer leaves after the last answer) count alongside confirmed ones, so headline rates may overstate satisfaction [29]. This makes a strong follow-up talking point about metric hygiene.

4.4 Architecture

 customer msg --> session store (history, account ctx, locale)
       |
       v
 intent + condense (small LLM): "core issue" + entities (order id, product)
       |
       +--> policy router: sensitive intent? (fraud, legal, safety) --> human
       |
       v
 retrieval: help-center (hybrid) + resolved-ticket KG / similar cases
       |                                  + tool calls (order status API)
       v
 rerank --> grounded generation (answer + citations + proposed action)
       |
       v
 guardrail tier 1: similarity(answer, retrieved evidence) >= tau ?
 guardrail tier 2: LLM judge for policy / grounding (only if tier 1 uncertain)
       |pass                                 |fail or timeout
       v                                     v
   send to user                       escalate to agent with summary
       |
       v
 offline: LLM-judge sampling, CSAT, resolution, repeat-contact, reopen rate

4.5 Sizing sketch (illustrative)

At Klarna-like volume (2.3M conversations per month), that is about 77k conversations per day, or about 0.9 conversations per second on average. If each conversation has about 4 bot turns, that is roughly 3.5 LLM turns per second on average, and an order of magnitude more at peak. The knowledge base is typically thousands to tens of thousands of articles plus millions of resolved tickets. The vector index fits on a single node even in float32 (Section 2.3). The cost drivers are LLM turns and guardrail calls, so make the expensive LLM judge conditional on the cheap check.

4.6 Failure modes

  • Retrieval keyed on the last message instead of the condensed issue. DoorDash condenses first for this reason [26].
  • A policy article that is outdated but faithfully cited. Faithfulness metrics such as RAGAS measure consistency with context, not truth [30].
  • Over-deflection: optimizing resolution rate leads to hiding the human-handoff path. Track repeat contacts and CSAT alongside deflection [28][29].
  • Guardrail latency spikes. Use a timeout that falls back to a human, as DoorDash does [26].

5. Design C: Code assistant (autocomplete and chat)

5.1 Problem

"Give completions and chat answers that use the developer's codebase, not just the open file, without leaking code and under tight latency."

5.2 What is different

  • Two products, two latency classes. Inline completion must feel instant and runs on every keystroke pause. Chat can afford seconds.
  • Extreme freshness. The "document" changes as the user types, and per-branch state differs per developer.
  • Code structure (symbols, imports, call graphs) is a stronger signal than semantic similarity of prose.
  • Security. Source code is often the most sensitive asset a company has.

5.3 Reference techniques

  • GitHub Copilot [31]. The prompt is assembled from the current file and "neighboring tabs": other open files are searched for snippets similar to the code around the cursor. A/B tests found a very low inclusion threshold worked best and gave about a 5% relative increase in accepted suggestions. Fill-in-the-middle (sending code both before and after the cursor) gave about a 10% relative boost. Caching let both run without added latency.
  • Sourcegraph Cody [32][33]. Cody frames context retrieval as recommender-style candidate generation followed by ranking. The system must balance recall and precision because only a few items fit. A larger context window does not fully solve this, since it raises inference cost and big codebases still overflow it [33]. Retrievers include keyword search with query rewriting, Sourcegraph code search (with a BM25 variant among its ranking signals), and code-graph context, plus snippets from open IDE files [32]. Sourcegraph also tested a 1M-token Gemini 1.5 Flash context and reported a substantial improvement on its "Essential Recall" benchmark [34]. That result shows long context and retrieval being combined, not one replacing the other.
  • Cursor [35]. Cursor builds a Merkle tree over the workspace: each file is hashed, and each folder's hash derives from its children. Client and server compare trees and sync only the entries that diverge. For a 50,000-file workspace, sending all filenames and SHA-256 hashes would be about 3.2 MB per update, which is what the Merkle comparison avoids. Changed files are split into syntactic chunks and embedded asynchronously, with embeddings cached by chunk content. To reuse a teammate's index safely, the client uploads its own Merkle tree with a similarity hash, and the server filters results against that tree, so users only see code they actually have [35].
  • Augment [36]. Augment claims index updates within seconds of edits (versus "10-minute" delays elsewhere) and custom retrieval models rather than generic embeddings. It keeps per-developer indices to handle branch switching, and shares overlapping index segments between users to control RAM. These are vendor claims.

5.4 Architecture

 IDE plugin                                   server
 +-----------------------------+              +-------------------------------+
 | cursor ctx (prefix/suffix)  |  completion  | low-latency code LLM (FIM)    |
 | open-tab snippet matcher    |------------->| prompt cache                  |
 | local symbol index (LSP)    |  <~ hundreds |                               |
 | Merkle tree of workspace    |  of ms total +-------------------------------+
 +-------------+---------------+
               | diff sync (changed hashes only)
               v
 +---------------------------------------------------------------+
 | chunk by syntax (functions/classes) -> embed (async, cached   |
 | by content hash) -> per-repo/branch vector index + code search |
 | + symbol/code graph                                           |
 +-----------------------------+---------------------------------+
                               |  chat / agent queries
                               v
 retrievers: keyword(+rewrite) | embeddings | graph (defs/refs) | open files
         -> rank (recsys-style) -> pack under token budget -> chat LLM
         -> answer/edit; agent may iterate (grep, read file, run tests)

5.5 Sizing sketch (illustrative)

Take a 100,000-file monorepo averaging 300 lines per file: 30M lines. With function-level chunks of about 40 lines, that is about 750k chunks, roughly 5 GB of float32 HNSW at 1,536 dimensions using the formula in Section 2.3. Per-branch indices multiply this, which is why reusing shared content-addressed chunks and storing only branch deltas matters [35][36]. Re-embedding cost is driven by churn, not repo size, so content-hash caching is the key lever.

5.6 Failure modes

  • Retrieving semantically similar but wrong-version code (other branch, deprecated module).
  • Long-context overconfidence: stuffing the repo and then "losing in the middle" [11].
  • Leakage across repos or users through shared caches. Cursor's server-side filtering against the client's own tree shows the mitigation [35].
  • Evaluating with generic benchmarks instead of product-specific ones. Cody built its own context-recall benchmarks [33][34].

6. Design D: Web answer engine

6.1 Problem

"Answer open-domain questions from the live web with citations, at consumer scale and latency."

6.2 What is different

  • The corpus is the web: billions of documents, adversarial SEO, and continuous change.
  • Freshness is a first-class requirement. FreshLLMs showed all tested LLMs struggle with fast-changing and false-premise questions [37].
  • Scale. Perplexity's research post describes a production search system handling about 200 million daily queries, built on hybrid retrieval, multi-stage ranking, distributed indexing, and a self-improving content-understanding module [38]. That works out to an average of roughly 2,300 QPS (my arithmetic).
  • Granularity. Perplexity argues that a search API for AI should treat sections and spans of documents as retrievable units, not only whole pages [38].

6.3 Reference architecture: Perplexity on Vespa

Perplexity moved its search in-house onto Vespa (announced April 2025). Its stated requirements were: combine keyword and semantic search, filter, rank individual passages, and index new content continuously at consumer latency. It wanted all of this in one platform rather than stitched-together databases, vector stores, and ranking services [39]. Vespa's materials also highlight distributed machine-learned ranking inference that combines many relevance signals [39]. Perplexity published an open evaluation framework (search_evals) and reported a median latency of about 358 ms for its Search API. These are company-run benchmarks [38].

The method lineage is public. FreshPrompt injects search-engine results (answer box, organic results, related questions) into the prompt, ordered by date. With GPT-4 it gave about +49 points of absolute accuracy on FreshQA under strict evaluation. Both the number and the order of evidence snippets mattered, and asking for concise answers reduced hallucination [37]. Trade press has described Perplexity's "online LLMs" as inspired by this work [40].

  crawler fleet --> fetch queue (priority by freshness/authority)
       |                       ^
       v                       | recrawl signals (news, change rate)
  parse + boilerplate removal + spam/quality classifiers
       |
  split into sections/spans --> per-span: text, embedding, signals
       |
       v
  distributed index (sharded by doc id), lexical + vector + attributes
 ----------------------------------------------------------------------
 ONLINE (~hundreds of ms budget for retrieval):
 query --> classify (navigational / fresh / complex) --> rewrite / decompose
       --> fan-out to all shards: hybrid retrieval of spans
       --> stage-1 cheap rank (per shard) --> merge top-N
       --> stage-2 ML ranker (many signals) --> stage-3 cross-encoder (top-K)
       --> LLM synthesize answer with numbered citations (streamed)
       --> complex queries: iterate (search -> read -> search) as agent

6.4 Tradeoffs to discuss

  • Build versus buy search. A third-party search API ships quickly but limits control of ranking, freshness, and cost per query. Perplexity's move in-house shows the trajectory at scale [39].
  • Page versus span indexing. Spans improve precision and context efficiency but multiply index size (10-100 spans per page) [38].
  • Freshness tiers. Use a small, rapidly refreshed news/real-time index next to a large, slowly refreshed index, with the query classifier routing between them.
  • Single shot versus multi-hop. Agentic research modes improve complex answers at several times the latency and cost. Route by query complexity, analogous to Self-Route [10].

6.5 Failure modes

  • Citing low-quality or SEO spam sources. Quality classifiers and authority signals belong before the LLM.
  • False-premise questions answered confidently [37].
  • Citation-answer mismatch, where the claim is not supported by the cited span. Add a post-hoc attribution check.
  • Fan-out tail latency across thousands of shards. Hedge requests and set per-shard timeouts.

7. Comparison of the four designs

Dimension Enterprise Q&A Support bot Code assistant Web answer engine
