Hardest constraint Per-user ACLs Policy correctness, safety Latency + freshness per keystroke Scale + freshness + spam
Freshness need Minutes-hours Hours-days (policy changes) Seconds Minutes for news
Retrieval core Hybrid + graph/authority [21] Condense + hybrid / ticket KG [26][27] Keyword + embeddings + code graph [32] Hybrid span retrieval, multi-stage ML rank [38][39]
Guardrails Render-time ACL recheck Pre-delivery 2-tier guardrail, human fallback [26] Repo/tenant isolation [35] Source quality, attribution
Public outcome numbers Genie: 70k+ Qs, 48.9% helpful [24] DoorDash -90% hallucinations [26]; LinkedIn -28.6% resolution time [27] Copilot +5% (tabs), +10% (FIM) acceptance [31] ~200M queries/day, ~358 ms median [38]
Primary metric Helpfulness, citation precision Resolution, CSAT, repeat contacts Acceptance rate, context recall Answer accuracy, latency, freshness
Typical escalation Agentic multi-step [17][25] Human agent Agent loop (grep/read/test) Multi-hop research mode

8. Common follow-up questions and strong answers

"How do you know if a bad answer is a retrieval or a generation failure?" Log retrieved chunk IDs for every answer. Build a labeled set of question, gold passages, and gold answer. Measure retrieval recall@k against the gold passages separately from answer correctness given gold context. If the gold passage was not retrieved, the failure is retrieval (failure points 1-2 in [13]). If it was retrieved but the answer was wrong, the failure is consolidation, extraction, or generation (points 3-7). Interviewers report this diagnosis skill is the core of the evaluation discussion [4].

"What metrics would you track?"

  • Offline: recall@k and MRR for retrieval (LinkedIn reported MRR [27]); faithfulness, answer relevance, and context relevance via RAGAS-style reference-free LLM judging [30]; context recall when references exist.
  • Online: product metrics such as acceptance rate [31], resolution and CSAT [28][29], and helpfulness votes [24].
  • Monitoring: LLM-judge sampling over production traffic [26].
  • Caveat: faithfulness does not catch faithfully cited stale content [30].

"Why not just fine-tune the model on our docs?" Fine-tuning is weak at factual recall. It cannot enforce per-user permissions, needs retraining whenever content changes, and gives no citations [21][24]. Fine-tune retrievers, rerankers, or style instead. Intercom reportedly trains its own retrieval and reranker models [29].

"Context windows are 1M tokens now. Do we still need RAG?" Long context can win on accuracy when cost is no object. RAG is far cheaper, and hybrid routing (Self-Route) keeps most of the accuracy [10]. Long prompts also suffer position effects [11], and corpora still exceed windows [33]. Best answer: retrieval narrows the corpus, and long context lets you include whole documents or files rather than tiny chunks.

"How do you handle a document whose permissions change?" Store ACL principals per chunk. Propagate ACL change events through the same incremental pipeline as content changes, updating only metadata with no re-embedding. Cache user-to-group expansion with a short TTL, and re-check access at render time [19][20].

"The corpus grows 10x. What breaks first?" RAM for float32 HNSW (Section 2.3). Mitigate with binary or product quantization plus rescoring [12], tenant sharding, and tiered storage. Re-embedding on a model upgrade becomes a multi-day batch, so version the index and dual-write during migration.

"How do you reduce hallucinations?"

  • Retrieval gating: CRAG-style evaluator [8], or abstain when the top rerank score is low.
  • Explicit instructions to answer only from context and to cite.
  • Concise answers [37].
  • Pre-delivery guardrails [26].
  • Human fallback for high-risk intents.
  • Measure faithfulness continuously.

"How do you make it faster and cheaper?"

  • Skip query rewriting for self-contained queries.
  • Run BM25 and ANN in parallel.
  • Rerank only the top 50-100 results.
  • Send fewer, better chunks.
  • Use prompt caching for static system prompts and document prefixes. Anthropic's contextual chunking cost estimate assumes caching [6].
  • Use a small model for routing and condensation.
  • Cache semantically equivalent frequent questions, keyed by ACL set.
  • Stream tokens.

"How do you handle multi-hop questions?" Decompose the query or iterate as an agent. Dropbox [17] and Uber [25] both moved complex queries to agentic flows. Bound the iterations, and route only complex queries there to protect latency.

"How do you prevent prompt injection from retrieved documents?" Treat retrieved text as data:

  • Delimit it clearly in the prompt.
  • Strip active content at ingestion.
  • Restrict tool permissions to the user's own scope.
  • Require confirmation for side-effecting actions in support bots.
  • Run output guardrails.

See Chapter 16 for detail.

9. Interview anti-patterns

  • Drawing "user -> vector DB -> LLM" and stopping. There is no ingestion path, no ACLs, no reranker, and no evaluation [2][3].
  • Choosing a vector database by brand before stating corpus size, QPS, or filter selectivity.
  • Assuming 50% chunk overlap and float32 vectors at a billion scale without doing the RAM math (Section 2.3).
  • Offering "use a bigger context window" as the answer to retrieval quality [10][11][33].
  • Reporting a single headline metric (deflection, resolution) without its definition [29].
  • Ignoring the "missing content" case. The system must be able to say it does not know [13].

Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Draw two systems. Asynchronous ingestion (connectors, parsing, chunking, enrichment, ACL capture) and the online answer path have different SLOs, failure modes, and scaling axes.
  2. The defining constraint picks the architecture:
    • permissions for enterprise Q&A [18][19];
    • policy safety for support [26];
    • keystroke latency and freshness for code [31][35];
    • scale, freshness, and spam for the web [38][39]. Name it in the first five minutes.
  3. Hybrid retrieval plus reranking is the default. Published ablations show each stage cuts retrieval failures: about 35%, then 49%, then 67% cumulative [6]. RRF is the simple fusion baseline [7].
  4. Do the memory math. Float32 HNSW costs about 6.9 GB per million 1,536-d vectors. Quantization with rescoring keeps about 96% quality at 1/32 the vector memory [12][16].
  5. Generation tokens dominate cost and latency. Fewer, better-ordered chunks beat more chunks [11]. Route easy queries cheaply and hard ones to long context or agents [10].
  6. Guardrails and fallbacks are components, not afterthoughts. DoorDash's two-tier guardrail with human fallback is the canonical pattern [26].
  7. Structure beats flat text when the data has it. LinkedIn's ticket knowledge graph improved MRR by about 78% [27], code graphs help code assistants [32], and authority graphs help enterprise search [22].
  8. Evaluate retrieval and generation separately, offline and online. Expect robustness to come from operation, not upfront design [13]. Uber, DoorDash, and LinkedIn all built judge-based evaluation pipelines [24][26][41].
  9. Read headline metrics critically. Resolution and deflection rates depend on definitions [29]. Company benchmarks are self-reported [38][39].

22. Master Index of RAG Engineering Blogs, Talks and Guides

This chapter is the atlas's bibliography in working form. It lists the engineering blogs, conference talks, vendor guides, practitioner essays and papers that people building retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems actually cite, grouped by company and by topic. Each entry has a one-line summary and a numbered reference that carries the full URL. The second half is a flat annotated index of 170+ entries.

The first half reads the most informative primary sources as one body of evidence. It covers the problem each team set out to solve, the architecture they shipped, the numbers they published, and the failures they admitted. The pattern that emerges is consistent across companies. Production RAG wins came mostly from retrieval and data preparation, not from the generator. Systems moved from single-shot "embed, top-k, stuff" pipelines toward agentic retrieval and structured indexes (graphs, Merkle-synced code indexes, page images). Evaluation and guardrails became first-class components rather than afterthoughts.

Method and caveats. The entries were collected through web searches and direct reads of primary sources in October 2026. Many company blogs could not be fetched directly from the research environment. For those posts the facts below come from search-result extracts of the primary page or from clearly labeled secondary summaries; the ZenML LLMOps database is the most common one. Numbers that come from secondary sources are marked "(secondary)". Numbers that could not be checked against the original are marked approximate. Coverage is broad but not complete. Several well-known company posts (for example from Instacart, Spotify, Notion and Shopify) did not show up in searches and are left out rather than cited from memory.

22.2 Deep reads: company engineering case studies

22.2.1 Uber: Genie and Enhanced Agentic RAG

Problem. On-call engineers at Uber asked roughly 45,000 questions a month in Slack help channels. The answers were spread across Engwiki, an internal Stack Overflow and other stores [44]. Uber chose RAG over fine-tuning mainly for time to market: fine-tuning needs curated, diverse examples and recurring compute to stay current [44].

Architecture (v1, 2023-2024). Internal sources go through ETL into chunks, then into embeddings and a vector store. A Slack bot retrieves the top chunks and generates an answer with citations, and users leave helpfulness feedback. According to a secondary summary, Genie reached 154 Slack channels, answered more than 70,000 questions with a 48.9% helpfulness rate, and saved about 13,000 engineering hours (approximate) [164].

Architecture (v2, May 2025: EAg-RAG). Pointed at more than 40 security and privacy policy documents stored as PDFs, the traditional pipeline "revealed significant gaps" [45]. The redesign added richer document processing: custom Google Docs loaders, and LLM-driven content formatting so that tables and structure survive parsing. It also added pre-processing agents (query optimization, source identification) and post-processing agents (context refinement) around a hybrid vector and BM25 retriever [45][165]. The reported result was a 27% relative increase in acceptable answers and a 60% relative reduction in incorrect advice (secondary) [165].

 Slack question
      |
      v
 +-----------------+    +--------------------+    +---------------------+
 | Query optimizer |--->| Source identifier  |--->| Hybrid retrieval    |
 | (agent)         |    | (agent: which docs)|    | vector + BM25 top-k |
 +-----------------+    +--------------------+    +----------+----------+
                                                             |
                     +---------------------------+           v
 answer + cites <----| Generator (LLM)           |<---| Post-processor     |
                     +---------------------------+    | (context refine)   |
                                                      +--------------------+
 Offline: PDF/GDoc loaders -> LLM formatting (tables, headings) -> chunks -> index

Lesson. The jump in quality came from document enrichment plus query-side agents, not from changing the generator. This agrees with the controlled comparison in "Is Agentic RAG worth it?" [37]: agentic retrieval helps on hard, policy-heavy corpora but costs latency and tokens.

22.2.2 DoorDash: RAG with a two-tier guardrail and LLM judge

Problem. DoorDash wanted to automate support for Dashers (delivery drivers) without hallucinated or policy-violating answers [46].

Architecture. The multi-turn chat is first condensed into a single issue statement. That summary drives retrieval over knowledge-base articles and past resolved cases, and an LLM then drafts the reply [46]. DoorDash first tried a more sophisticated guardrail model but found it too slow and too token-expensive. The shipped version has two tiers. The first is a cheap in-house semantic-similarity check between the response and the knowledge-base segments. Only responses that fail it go to an LLM evaluator. A separate LLM Judge monitors quality offline [46][151].

Numbers. Secondary sources cite a 90% reduction in hallucinations and a 99% reduction in compliance issues across thousands of daily requests [153][166]. These were not verified against the original post and should be treated as approximate. A 2025 follow-up extends the knowledge base with user-generated content, because a manually curated knowledge base does not scale [46].

Lesson. Run the expensive grounding check only on the tail. A cheap similarity filter in front of an LLM evaluator keeps guardrail latency close to retrieval latency.

22.2.3 LinkedIn: knowledge-graph RAG for support, and the GenAI product postmortem

LinkedIn's SIGIR 2024 paper argues that treating historical tickets as flat text loses both the structure inside each ticket and the links between tickets [40]. The paper builds a dual-layer knowledge graph. The intra-issue layer is a tree of ticket sections. The inter-issue layer links tickets through explicit metadata and through implicit links inferred from embeddings. Queries are parsed into entities and intents, sub-graphs are retrieved, and the answer is generated from them. Reported results: MRR improved by 77.6%, and median per-issue resolution time fell by 28.6% after deployment on LinkedIn's customer service team [40][171].

The companion "Musings on building a generative AI product" post [47] is one of the most widely quoted postmortems. According to secondhand accounts, the team reached about 80% of the target experience in roughly one month, then spent about four more months pushing past 95%, with each additional 1% "discouragingly" hard because of hallucinations. Earlier LinkedIn posts and a 2025 talk describe the platform that grew out of this work [48][49][150][167].

22.2.4 Pinterest: RAG for table selection in text-to-SQL

Pinterest's text-to-SQL feature lives in Querybook, its open-source SQL tool. The first version assumed users knew which tables to query. The second added RAG for table discovery: an LLM writes a summary of each table from its schema and sample queries, those summaries and historical queries are embedded into a vector index, and only "top-tier" tables are indexed so that low-quality datasets never reach the prompt [50][51][53]. At query time, the question is embedded and matched against the index. An LLM re-selects the best tables from the candidates, the user confirms them, and SQL is generated. Reported impact: 35% faster task completion and a first-shot acceptance rate that rose from about 20% to over 40% [50][52]. A later Pinterest write-up on unified context-intent embeddings for analytics tables (covered in Korean by [54]) and academic follow-ups such as CSR-RAG [38] continue the line.

22.2.5 Ramp and Grab: RAG as a constrained classifier and an analytics engine

Ramp's January 2025 post (by Ryne Carbone) rebuilds industry classification as RAG over the NAICS taxonomy [57]. Retrieval restricts the LLM to valid six-digit codes, which turns open generation into a multiple-choice question. A secondary summary describes two stages: optimized embeddings produce candidate codes, then a dual-prompt LLM makes the final selection. The same summary reports about 60% better recommendation retrieval and 5-15% better final accuracy (secondary) [168]. Ramp's engineering index also lists a separate post on transaction embeddings trained with triplet loss [58].

Grab's Integrity Analytics team paired an internal LLM tool (Spellvault) with a data middleware layer (Data-Arks) that exposes vetted SQL and API outputs as retrievable context. A secondary summary reports savings of 3-4 hours per report and fraud investigations shortened to minutes [55][56].

22.2.6 Harvey: vector-store selection for legal RAG

Harvey's February 2025 post describes three data scales [66][68]:

  • Ad-hoc uploads of about 1-50 documents
  • Project "vaults" of about 100-100,000 documents
  • Third-party corpora of millions of legal documents, which a related talk puts at tens of millions [67]

Harvey runs two vector stores in parallel. Postgres with pgvector uses brute-force KNN, which gives high accuracy at small-to-medium scale. LanceDB uses an IVF-PQ index with tunable recall versus latency, and its decentralized storage can sit in per-customer cloud buckets, which matters for confidentiality and customer isolation [66]. The comparison table quotes LanceDB latency at 15M rows with metadata filtering [66].

Lesson. In regulated domains, tenancy and retention shape the index topology as much as recall does.

22.2.7 Code assistants: GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Sourcegraph

GitHub (2025). A new Copilot embedding model raised the average retrieval score from 0.362 to 0.498 (37.6%) and lifted code-acceptance ratios for C# users in VS Code by 110.7% [59]. InfoQ adds that index throughput doubled and memory dropped eightfold [60]. Training on "hard negatives" (code that looks right but is wrong) is reported by weaker sources [59][60].

Cursor. Cursor hashes every file and builds folder hashes from their children's hashes, forming a Merkle tree. Client and server compare trees and sync only the branches that differ. Changed files are split into syntactic chunks and embedded in the background, with embeddings cached by chunk content [61]. Third-party write-ups add that a new teammate's index can be bootstrapped by copying a similar existing index from the team namespace, and that the vector store is reported to be Turbopuffer [62][63]. These details are unverified.

Sourcegraph Cody. Sourcegraph chose RAG over fine-tuning because code changes too quickly for a fine-tuned snapshot to stay current [64]. Context comes from three sources: keyword search with automatic query rewriting, the Sourcegraph search backend, and a code graph that follows structural relationships. Users can also pull context in explicitly with @-mentions [65].

      Cursor-style incremental code index
 local repo --hash--> Merkle tree --diff vs server--> changed files only
                                                          |
                                         syntactic (AST) chunking
                                                          |
                         content-hash cache hit? --yes--> reuse vector
                                    | no
                                    v
                           embed -> vector namespace (per repo / team)

22.2.8 Enterprise search: Glean and Dropbox Dash

Glean's posts describe a knowledge graph built from three pillars: content, people and activity. It is assembled per customer from 100+ connectors through continuous crawling rather than federated search [69][70]. The RAG layer runs plan, retrieve, generate. The planner learns to query Glean's own hybrid engine (semantic search, lexical search and the graph) and to rewrite queries with knowledge of the enterprise. Retrieval enforces permissions, so the LLM never has blanket access to company data [69][71]. The "Scholastic" semantic model is fine-tuned on each customer's corpus and click data [71]. Newer posts move to agentic reasoning built on the same retrieval layer [72].

Dropbox's engineering blog lists "How Dash uses context engineering for smarter AI" (November 2025), a December 2025 post on the feature store behind Dash, and a January 2026 post on knowledge graphs, MCP and DSPy in Dash [75]. A podcast with Dropbox's VP of Engineering covers the "context engine" in more depth [74]. The Dropbox posts themselves could not be fetched, so no numbers are reported here.

22.3 Deep reads: model-provider and research-lab blogs

22.3.1 Anthropic

Contextual Retrieval (September 2024) [91].

  • Before indexing, Claude 3 Haiku reads the whole document and writes a 50-100 token context for each chunk. That context is prepended to the chunk before both embedding and BM25 indexing.
  • With top-20 retrieval, the baseline failure rate was 5.7%. Contextual embeddings alone cut failures by 35% (to 3.7%). Adding contextual BM25 brought the cut to 49% (2.9%). Adding a reranker brought it to 67% (1.9%).
  • With reranking, the top 150 chunks are retrieved and reranked down to 20. Twenty chunks beat 5 or 10.
  • Prompt caching brings the one-time indexing cost to about $1.02 per million document tokens.
  • Cohere's reranker was used in the tests.
  • Secondary coverage [155][156], and a critique arguing that context is "not all you need" [157], are indexed below.

Citations (2025) [92]. The API splits PDF and text sources into sentences and returns grounded citations. Anthropic reports up to 15% better recall accuracy than most custom citation implementations. Endex reports that source hallucinations and formatting issues fell from 10% to 0%.

Building effective agents (December 2024) [95]. The post frames the "augmented LLM" (retrieval, tools, memory) as the basic building block of agentic systems. It notes that a single call with retrieval and in-context examples is often enough, so agentic complexity is not always needed.

Multi-agent research system (June 2025) [94]. A lead agent plans and spawns parallel subagents that search and compress what they find. A citation agent then attributes each claim to a source. This setup beat single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal research eval, but used about 15x the tokens of a chat interaction. Token usage alone explained about 80% of the variance on BrowseComp. The post explicitly contrasts its adaptive multi-step search with static top-k RAG.

Effective context engineering (September 2025) [93]. The post argues for "just-in-time" retrieval. The agent holds lightweight references (paths, queries, links) and loads content through tools such as glob and grep when it needs it. A hybrid approach preloads a little context (for example CLAUDE.md files) and explores the rest at runtime, which avoids stale indexes. The trade-off is that runtime exploration is slower than querying a pre-built index.

DRIFT search [99] Oct 2024 Primer -> follow-up local searches -> ranked hierarchy Beats local search 78% (comprehensiveness), 81% (diversity)
Dynamic community selection [100] Nov 2024 Cheap LLM prunes irrelevant communities top-down ~77% average cost reduction for global search
LazyGraphRAG [101] Nov 2024 NLP noun-phrase graph, no LLM summaries at index time Indexing ~0.1% of GraphRAG cost; >700x cheaper global queries
BenchmarkQED [102] Jun 2025 AutoQ / AutoE / AutoD benchmarking suite LazyGraphRAG won 96/96 comparisons; beat 1M-token vector RAG 
 GraphRAG (eager)                         LazyGraphRAG (deferred)
 docs -> LLM entity/rel extraction        docs -> noun-phrase extraction (NLP)
      -> graph -> Leiden communities           -> concept graph -> communities
      -> LLM community summaries          query -> LLM expands to 3-5 subqueries
 query -> map over summaries                    -> best-first chunk ranking
       -> reduce -> answer                      -> LLM relevance tests (budget)
                                                -> map claims -> reduce answer
 cost paid at index time                  cost paid at query time, tunable

The arc of this series is instructive. Microsoft first showed that global "sensemaking" questions need structure [17][96]. It then spent a year driving down the cost of that structure [98][100][101], and finally built a benchmark that measures it without hand-written test sets [102]. The BenchmarkQED result is relevant to the long-context debate: expanding vector RAG's context from 8k to 1M tokens did not close the gap on global queries [102].

22.3.3 Databricks, AWS, Google, Microsoft Azure, OpenAI

  • Databricks [77][24]. More than 2,000 experiments on 13 LLMs (20 in the paper). Llama-3.1-405B performance starts to fall after 32k tokens of retrieved context and GPT-4-0125-preview after 64k. Failure modes vary by model: some answer incorrectly, some fail to follow instructions, and some refuse.
  • AWS Generative AI Innovation Center [78][79]. Part 1 covers text RAG: hybrid search, preprocessing that enriches context, query rewriting, and both quantitative and qualitative evaluation. Part 2 extends to tables, databases and images. AWS prescriptive guidance [80] and the Bedrock Knowledge Bases documentation [81] cover the managed path.
  • Azure [82][83] and Google Cloud [84][85][86] publish reference architectures and design guides. OpenAI's accuracy guide frames RAG, prompting and fine-tuning as separate levers to tune [87], and its file-search documentation describes the managed retrieval tool [88].

22.4 Deep reads: infrastructure vendors and techniques

  • Late chunking (Jina, August 2024) [117][21]. Run a long-context embedding model (8,192 tokens) over the whole document, then split into chunks after the transformer and just before mean pooling. Each chunk vector is then conditioned on the surrounding document. The paper is co-affiliated with Weaviate.
  • ColPali on Vespa [112]-[116][20]. Embed page screenshots as multi-vectors, which skips OCR and chunking. Vespa reports better ViDoRe results than BM25 and BGE-M3. For billions of pages, it adds a Hamming-distance MaxSim over binary-quantized vectors inside a phased ranking pipeline [112].
  • Hybrid fusion (Weaviate) [109][110]. Run BM25 and vector search in parallel, normalize, and fuse. Weaviate offers rankedFusion and relativeScoreFusion; the latter has been the default since v1.24. AutoCut (v1.20) trims the tail of the result list.
  • Two-stage retrieval (Pinecone) [105]-[108]. A bi-encoder retrieves candidates and a cross-encoder reranks them. Pinecone hosts rerankers such as bge-reranker-v2-m3 as a separate inference step.
  • Decoupled chunks (LlamaIndex) [123]. Use different chunks for retrieval and for synthesis: embed small units for precision, then expand to a window or the parent section before generation ("small-to-big").
  • Query transformations (LangChain) [125][126]. Multi-query, RAG-Fusion, decomposition, step-back and HyDE [9], plus a multi-vector retriever that indexes summaries but returns the full documents.

Comparison of headline techniques by evidence

Technique Primary source Where it acts Reported gain Cost profile Main failure mode
Contextual Retrieval Anthropic [91] Index time -49% failures (-67% with rerank) ~$1.02/M doc tokens once Context generation quality; reindex cost on churn
Late chunking Jina [117] Embedding Gains on BEIR (paper) [21] One long-context pass Needs a long-context embedder
Hybrid + rerank Weaviate/Pinecone [109][105] Query time Qualitative; widely adopted Reranker latency per query Reranker domain mismatch

LazyGraphRAG MSR [101] Query time Matches global quality at >700x lower query cost Vector-RAG-level indexing Relevance-test budget tuning

22.5 Practitioner canon: essays, courses, talks

  • Eugene Yan [139][140]. Seven patterns for LLM systems, with RAG as the pattern for adding fresh external knowledge. His 2023 AI Engineer keynote covers evals, RAG, guardrails and feedback.
  • Applied LLMs [141][142]. Written by Yan, Bischof, Frye, Husain, Liu and Shankar (May-June 2024). Do not neglect keyword search, prefer RAG over fine-tuning for new knowledge, and long-context models will not make RAG obsolete.
  • Jason Liu [144][145][146]. Treat RAG as a recommender system. Measure retrieval precision, recall and MRR on synthetic evaluation sets, and separate leading from lagging metrics.
  • Hamel Husain [143]. A multi-part "Stop saying RAG is dead" series featuring guest talks.
  • Chip Huyen [147]. Places retrieval inside a full GenAI platform reference architecture.
  • Simon Willison [148]. A running tag archive of RAG experiments and commentary.
  • Jerry Liu, AI Engineer [149]. A production-ready RAG talk: start with table-stakes tuning (chunk size, metadata filters, hybrid search), then move to small-to-big retrieval and agents.

22.7 Cross-cutting lessons from the corpus

The same failure modes come up again and again across the sources:

  1. Parsing loses structure. Uber's policy PDFs [45], the messy-PDF warnings in [160], and the ColPali line of work [20][112] all point at ingestion as the first place quality drops.
  2. Chunks lose their document. Contextual Retrieval [91], late chunking [117] and small-to-big retrieval [123] are three answers to the same problem at different points in the pipeline: before embedding, inside the encoder, and after retrieval.
  3. Lexical signals still matter. Hybrid BM25 plus vector search shows up at Uber [45], Glean [69], Anthropic [91] and AWS [78], and in Applied LLMs' advice [141].
  4. Global questions break top-k. GraphRAG [96][97] and BenchmarkQED [102] show that bigger context windows do not substitute for structure on whole-corpus questions. Databricks [77] shows that quality falls past 32-64k tokens for many models.
  5. The last 20% is most of the work. LinkedIn's 80%-to-95% timeline [47] and Genie's 48.9% helpfulness rate [164] suggest planning for months of evaluation-driven iteration.
  6. Agentic retrieval is a cost decision. Anthropic's 15x token multiplier [94] and the Uber and EAg-RAG trade-offs [45][37] put agentic retrieval in the "high-value queries only" tier.

22.8 Key takeaways for system designers

  • Start from retrieval metrics, not answer vibes. Build a labeled or synthetic retrieval set and track recall@k, MRR and failure rate before tuning prompts [91][124][144]. Anthropic's 5.7% to 1.9% failure progression is a template for this kind of ablation.
  • Default to hybrid retrieval plus a reranker, and over-fetch before reranking (for example 150 candidates down to 20) [91][105][109].
  • Fix context loss at index time when the corpus is stable (Contextual Retrieval at about $1.02 per million tokens) and at query time when it churns (just-in-time agent retrieval) [91][93].
  • Choose index topology by question type. Use vectors for local lookups. Use graph or community structures for global sensemaking, and prefer budgeted, deferred variants (LazyGraphRAG) when indexing cost matters [101][102].
  • Constrain the output space when you can. Ramp's NAICS classification and Pinterest's table selection turn generation into choosing among retrieved candidates, which removes whole classes of hallucination [57][50].
  • Put cheap checks first. Use a similarity guardrail before an LLM evaluator, and a cheap LLM to prune communities before an expensive one [46][100].
  • Tenancy is architecture. Permission-aware retrieval (Glean) and per-customer storage (Harvey with LanceDB) must be designed in from the start [69][66].
  • Code RAG is an indexing problem. Incremental Merkle sync, syntactic chunking, content-hash caches and domain-trained embedders give the largest gains [59][61].
  • Treat agentic RAG as a tier, not a default. Route only complex or high-stakes queries through multi-step agents [94][95][37].
  • Benchmark continuously and automatically. Synthetic query generation and LLM-judge pairwise evaluation (BenchmarkQED, Ragas, ARES) make regression testing affordable [102][28][29].

  167. Building and Scaling a Production Generative AI Assistant for Professional Networking (LinkedIn case). ZenML. n.d. https://www.zenml.io/llmops-database/building-and-scaling-a-production-generative-ai-assistant-for-professional-networking
  168. RAG-Based Industry Classification System for Financial Services (Ramp case). ZenML. n.d. https://www.zenml.io/llmops-database/rag-based-industry-classification-system-for-financial-services
  169. Enterprise-Grade RAG Systems for Legal AI Platform (Harvey case). ZenML. n.d. https://zenml.io/llmops-database/enterprise-grade-rag-systems-for-legal-ai-platform

23. Canonical RAG and Retrieval Paper Reading List: 120+ Papers (2017-2026) by Theme, with System-Design Takeaways

Overview

This chapter is a curated reading list. It is not a bibliography dump. Each entry was chosen because it changed how production retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems are built: it introduced a component that is now standard (dense retrievers, rerankers, late interaction, HNSW), set a failure model that engineers design against (lost in the middle, distractor sensitivity, single-vector capacity limits), or defined a benchmark that teams still use. The list covers 2017 to 2026. It begins with retrieve-then-read open-domain QA (DrQA) and ends with RL-trained search agents, KV-cache-level RAG decoding and the 2026 agentic RAG systematizations.

The papers fall into fourteen themes:

  1. Foundations: retrieve-then-read and retrieval-augmented language models
  2. Dense, sparse and late-interaction retrievers, and general-purpose embedders
  3. Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexing
  4. Reranking
  5. Query transformation and synthetic training data
  6. Context construction: chunking, ordering, compression, hierarchy
  7. Adaptive, iterative and agentic retrieval
  8. Training generators for RAG
  9. Graph and structured RAG
  10. Long context, KV caching and RAG decoding
  11. Multimodal (visual document) retrieval
  12. Evaluation and benchmarks
  13. Security and privacy
  14. Surveys and engineering experience reports

Each theme has a short design narrative and a table with venue, year, a reference link (cited as [n] and listed in full under References) and a single takeaway for system design. Deeper notes follow for the papers whose numbers matter most. Every figure below comes from the cited paper or from the primary-source analyses in earlier chapters of this atlas. Approximate figures are marked "about" or "approx.".

A suggested reading order

Most readers do not need all 120 papers. The following path gives a working mental model in about 25 papers. The rest of the list is for going deeper on one theme.

  2017-2020 FOUNDATIONS          2020-2023 RETRIEVER STACK       2023-2024 CONTEXT + CONTROL
  DrQA [1] -> ORQA [2]           DPR [4] / BM25 baseline         Lost in the Middle [53]
     -> REALM [3] -> RAG [5]     ColBERT/ColBERTv2 [14][15]      RAPTOR [57], Contextual [59]
     -> FiD [6] -> RETRO [9]     SPLADE [20], Contriever [21]    IRCoT [63] -> FLARE [64]
     -> Atlas [10]               BEIR [102], MTEB [103]          Self-RAG [65] -> CRAG [66]
                                 HNSW [35], DiskANN [39]         GraphRAG [81], HippoRAG [83]
                                 monoT5 [44] -> RankGPT [45]

  2024-2026 SCALE + AGENTS                                         EVALUATE EVERYTHING
  Self-Route [90], CAG [93], CacheBlend [95], REFRAG [97]          RAGAS [107], ARES [108]
  Search-o1 [68] -> Search-R1 [69] -> DeepResearcher [72]          CRAG bench [111]
  LIMIT [34] (why single vectors are not enough)                   BrowseComp-Plus [115]

1. Foundations: retrieve-then-read and retrieval-augmented LMs

Problem. Language models store knowledge in their weights. That knowledge is hard to update or attribute, and it is weak on rare facts. The 2017-2022 papers separated where knowledge lives (an external, swappable corpus) from how it is used (a reader or generator).

Architecture lineage. DrQA [1] fixed the two-stage template: a TF-IDF/bigram-hash retriever over Wikipedia feeds an RNN reader. ORQA [2] made the retriever learned and treated the retrieved block as a latent variable. REALM [3] pushed that latent retrieval into pre-training with an asynchronously refreshed MIPS index. DPR [4] showed that a supervised BERT dual encoder alone beats BM25 by a wide margin. RAG [5] coined the name: a DPR retriever plus a BART generator, with marginalisation over documents per sequence or per token. FiD [6] encodes each passage independently and fuses them in the decoder, so reader cost grows linearly with passage count. RETRO [9] and Atlas [10] scaled retrieval to trillion-token datastores and few-shot settings. In-Context RALM [11] and REPLUG [12] marked the API era: retrieval works with a frozen, black-box LM through the prompt alone.

 Query --> [Retriever: sparse | dense | latent] --> top-k passages
                                                       |
            +------------------------------------------+-------------------+
            | concat in prompt     | FiD: encode each,  | RETRO: chunked    |
            | (RAG, RALM, REPLUG)  | fuse in decoder    | cross-attention   |
            +----------------------+--------------------+-------------------+
                                                       |
                                                  Generator --> answer
# Paper Venue, year Key system-design takeaway
1 DrQA: Reading Wikipedia to Answer Open-Domain Questions [1] ACL 2017 A cheap sparse retriever plus a strong reader is a viable baseline; retriever recall caps end-to-end accuracy.
2 ORQA: Latent Retrieval for Weakly Supervised Open-Domain QA [2] ACL 2019 The retriever can be trained from answer-only supervision; Inverse Cloze Task pre-training bootstraps it.
3 REALM [3] ICML 2020 End-to-end retriever training requires periodic index refresh; stale indexes hurt.
4 DPR: Dense Passage Retrieval [4] EMNLP 2020 In-batch negatives plus one BM25 hard negative are enough for a strong dual encoder.
5 RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP [5] NeurIPS 2020 Swapping the document index updates model knowledge without retraining.
6 FiD: Leveraging Passage Retrieval with Generative Models [6] EACL 2021 Accuracy keeps rising with more passages (up to 100) when the reader fuses them in the decoder.
7 FiD-KD: Distilling Knowledge from Reader to Retriever [7] ICLR 2021 Reader cross-attention scores are a free relevance label for retriever training.
8 kNN-LM: Generalization through Memorization [8] ICLR 2020 Interpolating a token-level datastore lowers perplexity with no retraining; the datastore can be domain-swapped.
9 RETRO: Improving LMs by Retrieving from Trillions of Tokens [9] ICML 2022 Retrieval can substitute for parameters: a 7.5B model competes with models about 25x larger.
10 Atlas: Few-shot Learning with Retrieval-Augmented LMs [10] JMLR 2023 Jointly pre-training retriever and reader gives strong few-shot QA (64-shot NQ 42.4 EM).
11 In-Context RALM [11] TACL 2023 Prepending retrieved text to a frozen LM is a large, free win; retrieve often, with short query windows.
12 REPLUG [12] NAACL 2024 Treat the LM as a black box and tune only the retriever from LM likelihood feedback.
13 WebGPT [13] arXiv 2021 Browsing plus quoted references makes answers verifiable and lets humans judge factuality.

Deeper notes. DPR's headline figure is top-20 retrieval accuracy on Natural Questions of 78.4% against 59.1% for BM25 [4]. That 19-point retrieval gain carried through to end-to-end QA. It was the result that moved industry from pure lexical search to dense retrieval. REALM used a 330M-parameter model to reach 40.4 EM on NQ-Open. Its ablations showed that a much staler index (refreshed far less often) fell below the baseline [3]. That is the first published evidence that index freshness is a correctness issue, not only an ops issue. RETRO splits text into 64-token chunks and retrieves neighbours from a 2-trillion-token database with a frozen BERT plus SCaNN. Neighbours enter through chunked cross-attention. DeepMind summarised the result as GPT-3-level performance with 25x fewer parameters [9]. RETRO also warned that test-set leakage into the retrieval corpus inflates scores, which matters for anyone benchmarking a RAG system on public data.

Lessons. (a) Freeze the document encoder whenever you can. REALM, RAG, Atlas and RETRO all did, at some stage, to avoid costly re-indexing. (b) Reader architecture decides how many passages you can use. (c) The API era made retrieval a prompt-construction problem. Most later work optimises what goes into the prompt.

2. Retrievers and embedding models

Problem. Dense retrievers trained on one dataset generalise poorly. BEIR [102] showed BM25 beating many neural retrievers zero-shot. Single-vector models also compress a whole passage into one point. Three answers emerged: better negatives and distillation (ANCE, RocketQA, TAS-B), different representations (late interaction, learned sparse), and massive weakly supervised or LLM-based pre-training (Contriever, E5, GTE, BGE, Gecko, NV-Embed, Qwen3, Gemini Embedding).

# Paper Venue, year Key system-design takeaway
14 ColBERT [14] SIGIR 2020 Late interaction (per-token vectors, MaxSim) keeps cross-encoder-like quality with precomputed documents.
15 ColBERTv2 [15] NAACL 2022 Residual compression shrinks multi-vector indexes by about 6-10x; distillation from a cross-encoder adds quality.
16 PLAID [16] CIKM 2022 Centroid pruning before full MaxSim scoring makes late interaction fast enough to serve.
17 ANCE [17] ICLR 2021 Hard negatives mined from an asynchronously refreshed ANN index beat random/BM25 negatives.
18 RocketQA [18] NAACL 2021 Cross-batch negatives, denoised hard negatives and cross-encoder-labelled data improve dual encoders.
19 TAS-B [19] SIGIR 2021 Topic-aware batch sampling plus balanced margin distillation trains strong retrievers cheaply.
20 SPLADE [20] SIGIR 2021 Learned sparse expansion runs on inverted indexes and gives exact-term matching with semantic recall.
21 Contriever [21] TMLR 2022 Unsupervised contrastive pre-training gives a robust zero-shot dense retriever.
22 E5 [22] arXiv 2022 Weakly supervised pairs mined from the web (CCPairs) produce general embedders; use query/passage prefixes.
23 E5-Mistral: Improving Text Embeddings with LLMs [23] ACL 2024 A decoder LLM fine-tuned on synthetic multilingual data becomes a top embedder.
24 GTE [24] arXiv 2023 Multi-stage contrastive learning (pre-train, then fine-tune) is the standard recipe.
25 C-Pack / BGE [25] SIGIR 2024 Open data, models and training recipes made strong open embedders the default.
26 BGE-M3 [26] arXiv 2024 One model can emit dense, sparse and multi-vector outputs; hybrid retrieval from one forward pass.
27 Matryoshka Representation Learning [27] NeurIPS 2022 Nested embeddings let you truncate dimensions for cheap first-pass search and rerank at full size.
28 Gecko [28] arXiv 2024 Distil LLM knowledge into a compact embedder by having the LLM generate and relabel training pairs.
29 NV-Embed [29] ICLR 2025 Latent-attention pooling and two-stage instruction tuning make decoder LLMs strong embedders.
30 Qwen3 Embedding [30] arXiv 2025 Open embedding and reranking models built from one foundation family; synthetic data at scale.
31 Gemini Embedding [31] arXiv 2025 Initialising from a frontier LLM gives broad multilingual and code retrieval quality.
32 Promptriever [32] ICLR 2025 Retrievers can follow per-query natural-language instructions like an LM.
33 ReasonIR [33] arXiv 2025 Reasoning-intensive retrieval needs purpose-built synthetic training data, not only web pairs.
34 LIMIT: Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval [34] arXiv 2025 The number of top-k subsets a single-vector embedder can represent is bounded by its dimension.

Deeper notes. LIMIT (Google DeepMind) is the most consequential 2025 result for architecture choices [34]. It proves a dimension-dependent bound on which combinations of documents can be returned as top-k. It confirms this with "free embedding" optimisation and a deliberately simple dataset on which state-of-the-art single-vector embedders fail. BM25 and multi-vector models do much better there. The practical reading: single-vector dense retrieval is a recall layer, not a complete solution. Keep a lexical or multi-vector path and a reranker for combinatorial and exact-match queries. ColBERTv2's residual compression [15] and PLAID's centroid-interaction pruning [16] are the reason late interaction is deployable at all. Matryoshka embeddings [27] are the reason "truncate to 256 dims for ANN, rescore at full width" became a common storage pattern.

3. Approximate nearest neighbour indexing

Problem. Exact maximum inner product search over 10^8 to 10^10 vectors is too slow and too memory-hungry. Each index family makes a different trade-off between memory, update cost, filtering and recall.

# Paper Venue, year Key system-design takeaway
35 HNSW [35] TPAMI 2018 (arXiv 2016) A layered proximity graph gives log-like search and excellent recall; RAM-heavy, and deletes are awkward.
36 Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs (Faiss) [36] IEEE TBD 2019 (arXiv 2017) GPU IVF-PQ with k-selection makes billion-scale brute-force-like search practical.
37 The Faiss library [37] arXiv 2024 A design-space map of IVF, PQ, graph and refine stages; index choice is a memory/recall/latency trade-off.
38 ScaNN: Anisotropic Vector Quantization [38] ICML 2020 Quantisation loss should weight the error component parallel to the query; better MIPS recall per byte.
39 DiskANN [39] NeurIPS 2019 A Vamana graph on SSD with compressed vectors in RAM serves a billion points from one node.
40 FreshDiskANN [40] arXiv 2021 Graph indexes can absorb streaming inserts and deletes with background merges.
41 SPFresh [41] SOSP 2023 In-place incremental rebalancing of cluster-based indexes avoids costly global rebuilds.
42 ACORN [42] SIGMOD 2024 Predicate-agnostic filtered vector search by denser graph construction and filtered traversal.

Deeper notes. DiskANN reported serving about 1 billion points on a 64 GB RAM workstation with high recall and millisecond-scale latency (approx.) [39]. That result is why SSD-resident graph indexes now underpin several managed vector databases. Filtered search (ACORN [42]) is the most common production pain point: post-filtering an HNSW result list collapses recall when the filter is selective. Chapter 04 covers this in depth.

4. Reranking

Problem. First-stage retrievers optimise recall at low cost. Precision at the top of the list, which is what the LLM actually reads, needs a more expensive model over a short list.

# Paper Venue, year Key system-design takeaway
43 monoBERT: Passage Re-ranking with BERT [43] arXiv 2019 A cross-encoder over (query, passage) pairs gives large precision gains over BM25 lists.
44 monoT5: Document Ranking with a Pretrained Seq2Seq Model [44] Findings EMNLP 2020 Scoring relevance as the probability of a "true" token transfers well zero-shot.
45 RankGPT: Is ChatGPT Good at Search? [45] EMNLP 2023 LLMs rerank well listwise with sliding windows; distil into small rankers to cut cost.
46 RankZephyr [46] arXiv 2023 An open 7B listwise reranker can match proprietary LLM reranking.
47 Rank1: Test-Time Compute for Reranking [47] arXiv 2025 Reasoning traces before a relevance judgment help on reasoning-heavy retrieval, at a latency cost.

Lesson. The two-stage cascade (cheap recall, then expensive precision on 50-200 candidates) has been stable from monoBERT to Rank1. What changes is the scorer's cost per pair. Budget reranking latency explicitly; it is often the largest retrieval-side cost.

5. Query transformation and synthetic training data

# Paper Venue, year Key system-design takeaway
48 HyDE: Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels [48] ACL 2023 Embed an LLM-written hypothetical answer instead of the query; helps zero-shot, risks hallucinated anchors.
49 Query2doc [49] EMNLP 2023 Expand the query with a pseudo-document; helps both BM25 and dense retrieval.
50 InPars [50] arXiv 2022 Few-shot LLM prompting generates synthetic queries to train domain rerankers.
51 Promptagator [51] ICLR 2023 Eight task examples plus LLM query generation train task-specific retrievers.
52 GPL: Generative Pseudo Labeling [52] NAACL 2022 Generated queries plus cross-encoder pseudo-labels adapt dense retrievers to new domains without labels.

Lesson. HyDE and Query2doc add one LLM call to the query path, so they trade latency for recall. InPars, Promptagator and GPL move the LLM cost offline into training-data generation. For high-QPS systems the offline route usually wins. Chapters 06 and 17 compare the two.

6. Context construction: chunking, ordering, compression and hierarchy

Problem. Retrieval quality is necessary but not sufficient. How retrieved text is cut, ordered and compressed decides whether the generator uses it.

# Paper Venue, year Key system-design takeaway
53 Lost in the Middle [53] TACL 2024 Accuracy is U-shaped in evidence position; put the best evidence at the start or end.
54 The Power of Noise [54] SIGIR 2024 Related-but-irrelevant distractors hurt more than random noise; rerank to remove near-misses.
55 RECOMP [55] ICLR 2024 Extractive and abstractive compressors cut prompt length a lot with little accuracy loss, and may return nothing.
56 LongLLMLingua [56] ACL 2024 Question-aware token pruning and reordering reduce cost and mitigate position bias.
57 RAPTOR [57] ICLR 2024 Recursive cluster-and-summarise trees let one query retrieve at several levels of abstraction.
58 Late Chunking [58] arXiv 2024 Embed the whole document with a long-context encoder, then pool per chunk to keep cross-chunk context.
59 Contextual Retrieval (Anthropic) [59] Engineering blog, 2024 Prepend an LLM-written 50-100 token context to each chunk before embedding and BM25.
60 Is Semantic Chunking Worth the Computational Cost? [60] Findings NAACL 2025 Semantic chunking's gains over fixed-size chunking are inconsistent and often not worth the cost.

Deeper notes. Anthropic's contextual retrieval write-up is one of the few publicly quantified chunking interventions [59]. Across its test corpora, the top-20 retrieval failure rate fell from 5.7% to 3.7% with contextual embeddings (35% lower), to 2.9% with contextual embeddings plus contextual BM25 (49% lower), and to 1.9% with reranking added (67% lower). The one-time preprocessing cost was about $1.02 per million document tokens with prompt caching, assuming 800-token chunks and 8k-token documents. RAPTOR reported a 20% absolute accuracy gain on the QuALITY benchmark when paired with GPT-4 [57]. Its tree is an index-time cost that must be rebuilt when documents change. Lost in the Middle [53] is the single most cited reason for "fewer, better chunks" designs.

   doc --> chunk --+--> [contextualize: LLM adds 50-100 tok header] --+--> embed --> ANN
                   |                                                  +--> BM25 index
                   +--> [late chunking: embed whole doc, pool spans] ------> ANN
                   +--> [RAPTOR: cluster -> summarize -> recurse]   -------> tree index
   query --> hybrid recall --> rerank --> order (best at edges) --> compress --> LLM

7. Adaptive, iterative and agentic retrieval

Problem. One retrieval pass fails on multi-hop questions and wastes compute on easy ones. The field moved through four control strategies. Fixed loops came first (IRCoT). Then came uncertainty-triggered retrieval (FLARE), self-critique (Self-RAG, CRAG), and complexity routing (Adaptive-RAG). Since 2025, learned policies have been trained with reinforcement learning against live or simulated search (Search-R1 and successors).

  2022-23 fixed loop      2023 trigger         2023-24 critique       2025-26 learned policy
  IRCoT: CoT step ->      FLARE: retrieve      Self-RAG: reflection   Search-R1: RL on
  query -> retrieve       when next-sentence   tokens; CRAG: T5       <search>/<answer>
  -> next CoT step        confidence is low    evaluator + web        with outcome reward
# Paper Venue, year Key system-design takeaway
61 ReAct [61] ICLR 2023 Thought/Action/Observation is the interface nearly every search agent still uses.
62 Toolformer [62] NeurIPS 2023 Models can self-supervise when to call tools (including search) by keeping calls that lower loss.
63 IRCoT [63] ACL 2023 Use each chain-of-thought sentence as the next retrieval query for multi-hop QA.
64 FLARE [64] EMNLP 2023 Retrieve only when the model's predicted next sentence has low-confidence tokens; requires logprobs.
65 Self-RAG [65] ICLR 2024 Train one LM to emit retrieve/relevance/support/utility tokens; controllable at inference.
66 CRAG: Corrective RAG [66] arXiv 2024 A light retrieval evaluator triggers refine, discard or web fallback; quality bounded by the evaluator.
67 Adaptive-RAG [67] NAACL 2024 A small classifier routes no-retrieval / single-step / multi-step, trading accuracy against cost.
68 Search-o1 [68] EMNLP 2025 Reasoning models can call search mid-thought; a Reason-in-Documents step condenses results first.
69 Search-R1 [69] COLM 2025 RL with outcome-only reward and masked retrieved tokens teaches when and what to search.
70 R1-Searcher [70] arXiv 2025 Two-stage outcome-supervised RL elicits search without SFT cold-start data.
71 ReSearch [71] arXiv 2025 Search calls become part of the reasoning chain, trained with RL and no supervised reasoning steps.
72 DeepResearcher [72] arXiv 2025 End-to-end RL against the real web beats prompt-engineered and local-RAG-trained agents.
73 WebThinker [73] NeurIPS 2025 A deep-web explorer that navigates pages lets reasoning models write research reports.
74 Anthropic multi-agent research system [74] Engineering blog, 2025 An orchestrator with parallel subagents scales breadth-first research at a large token cost.

Deeper notes. Self-RAG 13B reported 55.8 accuracy on PopQA and 69.3 on TriviaQA, beating retrieval-augmented baselines of the time [65]. Its inference cost varies with how often the model chooses to retrieve. CRAG's lightweight T5-large evaluator classifies retrievals as correct, incorrect or ambiguous [66]. The authors note that the method is only as good as that evaluator. Search-R1 [69] defines the 2025-2026 template. The policy LLM emits <search> queries; retrieved passages are inserted and masked out of the RL loss; a rule-based exact-match reward on the final answer drives PPO or GRPO. Its follow-ups differ mainly in the environment: local Wikipedia, simulated search (ZeroSearch), or the live web (DeepResearcher). On Anthropic's internal research evaluation, the multi-agent configuration (Opus 4 lead, Sonnet 4 subagents) beat single-agent Opus 4 by about 90%. Anthropic also reported that such systems use roughly 15x the tokens of a chat interaction and that token usage explained most of the performance variance (approx. figures from the post) [74].

Failure modes. Uncertainty triggers depend on logprob access, which hosted APIs often restrict. Critic-based loops multiply LLM calls. RL agents can over-search or reward-hack exact-match rewards. Chapter 08 covers each in detail.

8. Training generators for RAG

# Paper Venue, year Key system-design takeaway
75 RA-DIT [75] ICLR 2024 Two light fine-tunes (LM learns to use retrieved text; retriever learns LM preferences) retrofit any LLM.
76 RAFT [76] COLM 2024 Fine-tune with oracle plus distractor documents and cited chain-of-thought answers for domain RAG.
77 ChatQA [77] NeurIPS 2024 Two-stage instruction tuning makes an open model competitive on conversational RAG.
78 RankRAG [78] NeurIPS 2024 One instruction-tuned LLM can both rerank contexts and generate the answer.
79 Fine-Tuning or Retrieval? [79] EMNLP 2024 For injecting new facts, RAG consistently beats unsupervised fine-tuning.
80 Does Fine-Tuning LLMs on New Knowledge Encourage Hallucinations? [80] EMNLP 2024 Models learn new facts slowly through fine-tuning, and doing so raises hallucination; prefer retrieval.

Lesson. Fine-tuning and RAG are complements. Fine-tune for behaviour: ignoring distractors, citing, abstaining. Retrieve for facts. RAFT [76] and RA-DIT [75] are the two recipes to start from. Chapter 17 expands on this.

9. Graph and structured RAG

Problem. Chunk-level similarity cannot answer global, corpus-wide questions ("what are the main themes?"). It also struggles with multi-hop entity paths. Graph approaches extract entities and relations at index time, then traverse or summarise at query time.

# Paper Venue, year Key system-design takeaway
81 GraphRAG: From Local to Global [81] arXiv 2024 LLM-built entity graphs plus hierarchical community summaries answer global sensemaking queries; indexing is costly.
82 LightRAG [82] EMNLP 2025 Dual-level (entity and theme) keys with incremental graph updates cut GraphRAG's cost.
83 HippoRAG [83] NeurIPS 2024 OpenIE triples plus Personalized PageRank give single-step multi-hop retrieval.
84 HippoRAG 2: From RAG to Memory [84] ICML 2025 Adding passages to the graph and filtering recognised triples improves factual, sense-making and associative memory together.
85 G-Retriever [85] NeurIPS 2024 Retrieve a subgraph via prize-collecting Steiner tree and pass it to the LLM as soft graph tokens plus text.
86 KAG (Ant Group) [86] arXiv 2024 Professional domains need schema-constrained KGs and logical-form reasoning, not only open extraction.
87 RAG vs. GraphRAG: A Systematic Evaluation [87] arXiv 2025 Graph methods win on multi-hop and global queries; plain RAG often wins on single-hop detail.
88 RAG with KGs for Customer Service QA (LinkedIn) [88] SIGIR 2024 Ticket-structure-aware KGs improved retrieval and cut per-issue resolution time in production.

Deeper notes. HippoRAG reported up to 20% better multi-hop QA than prior methods while being 10-30x cheaper and 6-13x faster than iterative retrieval (IRCoT) [83]. That cost profile is why graph retrieval is often a replacement for agent loops, not an addition to them. GraphRAG's community summaries are costly to build. Microsoft's later LazyGraphRAG work (covered in Chapter 07) reported indexing cost at about 0.1% of full GraphRAG by deferring LLM work to query time. Treat graph RAG as a query-type-specific tool. Systematic comparisons [87] show no universal winner.

10. Long context, KV caching and RAG decoding

Problem. As context windows passed 128K tokens, teams asked whether to retrieve at all. The research answer: long context and RAG are complementary. When the corpus is small and stable, preloading wins. Otherwise retrieval wins, and the serving stack should exploit RAG's structure (independent chunks, sparse relevance).

# Paper Venue, year Key system-design takeaway
89 Retrieval meets Long Context LLMs [89] ICLR 2024 Retrieval with a 4K window can rival a 16K long-context model, and helps long-context models too.
90 Self-Route: RAG or Long-Context LLMs? [90] EMNLP 2024 Industry Let the model judge if retrieved chunks suffice; fall back to long context only when needed.
91 LongRAG [91] arXiv 2024 Retrieve long units (about 4K tokens) to shrink the corpus and shift work to a long-context reader.
92 Long-Context LLMs Meet RAG [92] ICLR 2025 More retrieved passages first help, then hurt, because of hard negatives; reorder and fine-tune for robustness.
93 CAG: Don't Do RAG [93] 2025 (short paper) For a small, bounded knowledge base, precompute the KV cache once and skip retrieval.
94 RAGCache [94] arXiv 2024 Cache KV states of popular retrieved documents in a knowledge tree across GPU and host memory.
95 CacheBlend [95] EuroSys 2025 Reuse per-chunk KV at non-prefix positions by recomputing a small subset of tokens.
96 TurboRAG [96] arXiv 2024 Precompute chunk KV caches offline and fine-tune the model to tolerate independent chunk attention.
97 REFRAG [97] arXiv 2025 Compress retrieved chunks into embeddings and expand only the selected ones; large time-to-first-token gains.

Deeper notes. CacheBlend recomputes KV for only a small fraction of tokens (Chapter 09 cites roughly 10-20%) whose attention deviates most. This recovers cross-chunk attention while keeping most of the reuse savings [95]. REFRAG (Meta) feeds a lightweight encoder's chunk embeddings to the decoder in place of full token sequences. An RL policy decides which chunks to expand. The paper reports large time-to-first-token speedups (around 30x, approx.) and an extended effective context [97]. The common thread: RAG contexts are block-sparse, and serving systems that know chunk boundaries can skip most cross-chunk attention.

   Classic RAG:   [sys][q][chunk1 tokens][chunk2 tokens]...[chunkK tokens] -> full prefill
   Prefix cache:  [sys cached][q][chunks recomputed]                       (APIs today)
   CacheBlend:    [sys][q][KV1*][KV2*]...  (* reused; ~10-20% tokens recomputed)
   REFRAG:        [sys][q][e1][e2][chunk3 tokens][e4]... (e = one embedding per chunk)
   CAG:           [entire KB KV cached][q]                  (no retriever at all)

11. Multimodal (visual document) retrieval

# Paper Venue, year Key system-design takeaway
98 ColPali [98] ICLR 2025 Embed page images with a VLM and late interaction; skip OCR/layout pipelines for visually rich PDFs.

ColPali (PaliGemma-3B base) produces about 1,030 vectors per page and introduced the ViDoRe benchmark. In the colpali-engine listing, v1.0 and v1.3 score about 81.3 and 84.8 [98]. The storage cost of multi-vector pages is the main deployment concern. Binary quantisation and token pooling are the usual mitigations (Chapter 10).

12. Evaluation and benchmarks

Problem. RAG has two failure surfaces: retrieval (did we fetch the evidence?) and generation (did we use it faithfully?). Benchmarks have moved from extractive QA to attribution, robustness, multi-hop reasoning and deep-research agents.

# Paper Venue, year Key system-design takeaway
99 MS MARCO [99] arXiv 2016 The training set behind most neural rankers; shallow labels mean many false negatives.
100 HotpotQA [100] EMNLP 2018 Multi-hop questions with supporting-fact labels; the standard testbed for iterative retrieval.
101 KILT [101] NAACL 2021 One Wikipedia snapshot across 11 datasets and 5 tasks; scores provenance as well as output.
102 BEIR [102] NeurIPS 2021 D&B Zero-shot evaluation over 18 datasets; BM25 is a strong out-of-domain baseline.
103 MTEB [103] EACL 2023 The 8-task, 58-dataset embedding leaderboard; retrieval average is not your domain.
104 MMTEB [104] ICLR 2025 Community-built multilingual extension to 500+ tasks; reduced, cheaper benchmark variants.
105 BRIGHT [105] ICLR 2025 Reasoning-intensive retrieval where lexical and semantic overlap fail; reasoning rewrites help.
106 RGB: Benchmarking LLMs in RAG [106] AAAI 2024 Tests noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration and counterfactual robustness.
107 RAGAS [107] EACL 2024 Demo Reference-free faithfulness, answer relevance and context relevance via LLM judges.
108 ARES [108] NAACL 2024 Fine-tuned judges plus prediction-powered inference give confidence intervals from few labels.
109 ALCE: Generating Text with Citations [109] EMNLP 2023 Score citation recall and precision via NLI; citation quality lags fluency.
110 RAGChecker [110] NeurIPS 2024 D&B Claim-level metrics separate retriever errors from generator errors.
111 CRAG: Comprehensive RAG Benchmark (Meta) [111] NeurIPS 2024 D&B Mock web and KG APIs, dynamic and long-tail questions; hallucination is penalised.
112 FRAMES [112] arXiv 2024 Unified test of fact retrieval, multi-hop reasoning and numerical reasoning; multi-step retrieval helps sharply.
113 MultiHop-RAG [113] COLM 2024 Multi-hop queries over news; exposes single-shot retrieval limits.
114 TREC 2024 RAG Track nugget evaluation [114] arXiv 2024 Automatic nugget extraction and matching approximates human RAG judgments at scale.
115 BrowseComp-Plus [115] arXiv 2025 A fixed, curated corpus makes deep-research agent evaluation reproducible and separates retriever from agent.

Lesson. Evaluate the retriever (recall@k against labelled evidence) separately from the generator (faithfulness, citation precision). Then evaluate end to end on a held-out, time-split slice. RAGChecker [110] and ARES [108] are the best published patterns for attributing errors and putting confidence bounds on LLM-judge scores. Chapter 11 has the full treatment.

13. Security and privacy

# Paper Venue, year Key system-design takeaway
116 Not What You've Signed Up For: Indirect Prompt Injection [116] AISec 2023 Retrieved content is an attack channel; treat every document as untrusted input.
117 PoisonedRAG [117] USENIX Security 2025 A few crafted passages injected into a large corpus can steer answers to target questions.
118 Text Embeddings Reveal (Almost) As Much As Text [118] EMNLP 2023 Embeddings can be inverted to recover text; vector stores need the same protection as raw documents.

Lesson. Enforce ACLs at retrieval time. Keep provenance on every chunk. Isolate retrieved text from instructions. Never treat embeddings as anonymised data (Chapter 16).

14. Surveys, frameworks and engineering experience reports

# Paper Venue, year Key system-design takeaway
119 RAG for LLMs: A Survey [119] arXiv 2023 Introduced the Naive / Advanced / Modular RAG taxonomy used across industry.
120 Seven Failure Points When Engineering a RAG System [120] CAIN 2024 Missing content, missed top-k, not in context, not extracted, wrong format, wrong specificity, incomplete.
121 Agentic RAG survey [121] arXiv 2025 (rev. 2026) Taxonomy of single-agent, multi-agent, hierarchical and graph-based agentic RAG.
122 SoK: Agentic RAG [122] arXiv 2026 2026 systematization of agentic RAG architectures, evaluation and open problems.
123 FlashRAG [123] WWW 2025 Companion One toolkit reimplements dozens of RAG methods under uniform settings; many gains shrink.
124 DSPy [124] ICLR 2024 Declare RAG pipelines as modules and compile prompts/demos against a metric.

Deeper notes. The Seven Failure Points paper [120] came from three real deployments (research, education and biomedical). It concludes that RAG systems are validated in operation, not at design time, and that robustness evolves rather than being designed in. FlashRAG's uniform reproductions [123] give a sobering check. Under identical retrievers and generators, several celebrated adaptive methods score close to a well-tuned standard RAG baseline. Always re-baseline before adopting a method from a paper.

Cross-theme comparison

The table below compresses the list into the decisions a system designer actually makes. Each row names the representative papers and what they imply for cost, latency and quality.

Design decision Representative papers Quality lever Cost / latency impact Main failure mode
Sparse vs dense vs hybrid recall BM25 in [4][102], DPR [4], SPLADE [20], BGE-M3 [26], LIMIT [34] Hybrid closes lexical and semantic gaps Dense needs ANN memory; sparse uses inverted index Single-vector capacity limit; domain shift
Single- vs multi-vector ColBERTv2 [15], PLAID [16], ColPali [98] Token-level matching, robust zero-shot Index often several x larger; extra scoring Storage blow-up
Reranker monoT5 [44], RankGPT [45], Rank1 [47] Top-k precision 10s-100s of ms per query; LLM rerankers more Latency budget overrun
Chunking / contextualisation Contextual Retrieval [59], Late Chunking [58], RAPTOR [57] Fewer retrieval misses (-35% to -67% failure in [59]) One-time index cost (about $1/M tokens in [59]) Re-index on every doc change
Context ordering / compression Lost in Middle [53], RECOMP [55], LongLLMLingua [56] Higher use of evidence Fewer prompt tokens Compressor drops key facts
When to retrieve FLARE [64], Self-RAG [65], Adaptive-RAG [67], Self-Route [90] Skip noise on easy queries Saves calls on easy, adds on hard Router miscalibration
Iterative / agentic IRCoT [63], Search-R1 [69], DeepResearcher [72], [74] Multi-hop and open-web research Many LLM and search calls; about 15x tokens in [74] Over-searching, loops, cost spikes
Graph index GraphRAG [81], HippoRAG [83], LightRAG [82] Global and multi-hop questions High index cost (GraphRAG); cheap query (HippoRAG) Extraction errors, stale graph
No retrieval (preload) CAG [93], long-context studies [89][92] No retriever errors Huge prefill unless cached Doesn't scale past context window
KV-level RAG serving RAGCache [94], CacheBlend [95], TurboRAG [96], REFRAG [97] Same quality, lower TTFT Large TTFT reductions Model or kernel changes required
Train the generator RA-DIT [75], RAFT [76], ChatQA [77], RankRAG [78] Distractor robustness, citation Training cost; ties you to a model Overfitting to the domain snapshot

Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Recall is the ceiling, and lexical recall is not obsolete. DPR's 19-point top-20 gain over BM25 [4] started the dense era. BEIR [102] and LIMIT [34] explain why hybrid (lexical plus dense, or multi-vector) remains the safe default.
  2. Always cascade. Cheap recall over millions of candidates, then a cross-encoder or LLM reranker over at most a few hundred [43][44][45]. Spend the latency budget where the LLM reads.
  3. Fix chunks before you fix models. Contextualising chunks cut retrieval failures by up to 67% at a one-time cost of about $1 per million tokens [59]. That beats most retriever swaps on cost-effectiveness.
  4. Fewer, better passages. Position bias [53], near-miss distractors [54] and the "more passages first help then hurt" curve [92] all argue for aggressive reranking, deduplication and edge placement over large top-k.
  5. Make retrieval conditional. Routers and self-assessment [64][65][67][90] save compute on easy queries and spend it on hard ones. Calibrate the router on your own traffic.
  6. Agentic search is now trained, not prompted. Search-R1 and its successors [69]-[73] show that RL against a search tool learns when and what to query. Budget for the token multiplier [74] and add hard caps on turns and tool calls.
  7. Pick graph RAG by query type. It wins for global and multi-hop questions and often loses on single-hop detail [81][83][87]. Its index cost must be justified by those queries.
  8. Exploit RAG's block structure in serving. Chunk-level KV reuse and compression [94]-[97] are where 2025-2026 latency gains come from. Preloading (CAG [93]) is right only for small, stable knowledge bases.
  9. Fine-tune for behaviour, retrieve for facts [75][76][79][80].
  10. Evaluate in layers and re-baseline. Separate retriever and generator metrics [110], add statistical bounds on judge scores [108], and reproduce methods under uniform settings before adopting them [123]. Treat every retrieved document as untrusted input [116][117].
